translations.text: Ecclesiastical History, that is, the histories of the Church, by Mar Eusebius of Caesarea.
The first book of the histories of the Church.
First chapter: what the subject of its beginning is. / Second:
Summary headings of what is said concerning the pre-existence of the divinity of our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. / Third:
On the name of Jesus and of Christ: that it was known and honoured among the holy prophets.

/ Fourth [?]: That the teaching of the fear of God which he proclaimed was not a shadow or something foreign. / Fifth: On the times in which he appeared among human beings. / Sixth: That in his times, as prophecy said, the former rulers ceased, those who were from of old
from the line of succession of the ancestors of the Jews. Leaders from among themselves had been over them, and there became king over them, from the gentiles, first of all Herod. / Seventh.
On the book of the genealogy of Christ, in which the evangelists are thought not to agree with one another. / Eighth:
On the murderous plot that Herod devised against the infants of Bethlehem, and what evil end he came to. / Ninth:
On the times of Pilate.
Tenth: On the high priests of the Jews in whose days our Lord taught.
/ Eleventh: On the testimonies that are spoken about John the Baptist and about Christ. / Twelfth:
On the disciples of our Saviour.
/ Thirteenth: An account concerning the king of Edessa.
First chapter: what the subject of its beginning is.
I wish to set down in a book the succession of the apostles from the days of our Saviour until our own time;

and how many and what kind of deeds were done that are related in the histories of the Church; and who were those who gloriously were leaders and governors in the well-known churches; and who were those who in each generation proclaimed the word of God, either without writings or in writings;

and who, and how many, and at what times, out of love of novelty, sprang up as teachers of the error of falsely named knowledge, and who without mercy, like destructive wolves, attacked the flock of Christ;

and along with these, what befell the Jewish people all at once because they attacked and were insolent toward our Saviour; and how and at what times the teaching of God was persecuted by the Gentiles;

and which men at all times endured the contest for the sake of the name of our Lord, with tortures and torments and the shedding of blood; and along with these also the martyrs who have been in our own day, and the helps of the mercy of our Saviour that have come at all times. Since I wish to write these things, it is fitting that I make the beginning of the account
from the first dispensation of our Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

But I ask that the discerning understand on my behalf, for I confess that this is beyond my strength, to fulfil this promise completely; for we are indeed the first to venture upon this subject, like a man who travels on an untrodden road.
And we pray that God may be our guide and that the power of our Lord may be our help. For we have not found clear footprints of other men who travelled this path before us,
but only small fragments of the narratives of particular individuals, in the times in which they lived, which they left us piece by piece;

and as if from a distant watchtower, with the gleams of their voices, they cry out as from a resting-place on high, and command by which way we should go, and direct the course of our account for us without error.

All these things, then, that we consider fitting for this narrative, from among those scattered in the records of the early writers, we shall gather, as from rational meadows, the flowers of their voices, and embody them in the account of our history, and complete the succession of the apostles of our Savior, whose memory is preserved in the well-known churches until our day,
even if not of all of them, at least of those who are known. The labor of this narrative which has been laid upon us is very [?], because of the early writers who were in the Church

we have not perceived that there was any diligence concerning the writing of this narrative. I think, moreover, that it will be of profit to those who love the learning of the account of this history. Even before now, indeed, it was noted by us from this narrative in the histories of former times, which we set down in brief summaries. Now, however, I have been eager to complete fully this history which has been laid upon us.
[Chapter] two. Summary sections
which are spoken concerning the pre-existence of the divinity of our Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. I will begin, then, the account, as I said before,

from the exalted and glorious divinity of Christ, which is prior to this dispensation in the body. For it is right for anyone who is going to hand down in writing the histories of the affairs of the Church
to begin his account of our Lord from above. For it is from his divinity that his humanity received this title of Christ.
For his form has two distinct aspects and can be compared to a body: his divinity is the head,

and his humanity is compared to the feet [?]… which he put on for the sake of our salvation. If, then, we make the beginning of our account from the pre-existence of his divinity, the history will be complete in its proper order.
By this, moreover, the antiquity and ancient origin of the Christians will also become known:

that even from of old it was glorious before God, and it is not, as some people think, that it has appeared newly just now. Concerning the birth and the honour of the being of Christ, however, there is no word sufficient to tell of it,
as the Spirit of God said in prophecy: "Who shall declare his generation?" For just as no one knows the Father except the Son,
so no one is able to know the Son as he is, except the Father alone, who begot him.

For the Light that is before the world, and the Wisdom that is a perfect hypostasis, and the living God the Word, who was with his Father from the beginning — who is able to conceive of him worthily, except the Father?
Him who alone is the offspring of the Godhead,

who is prior to all creatures, visible and invisible; to the chief of the powers of the immortal heavenly hosts; to him who is the Wonderful and the Counselor; to the executor of the hidden will of the Father; to him who is the Creator of all together with the Father; to him who is the cause of all that came to be;
to him who is the true and only-begotten Son of God.

He who is over all, Lord and God and King, who equally has lordships and authorities, together with power and divinity and honor, from the nature of the being of the Father, according to the mystery which the Scriptures speak concerning his divinity.
"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Everything came into being through him, and without him not even one thing came into being."

This same thing Moses also, the first and chief of the prophets, when he wrote by the Spirit of God about the coming into being and the ordering of creation, wrote concerning Christ: that he is the creator and orderer of all things.
That is, concerning God the Word, who was begotten from the beginning, and whom he made his partner in the fashioning of man.
For God said to him: "Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness." And another prophet set his seal on this word,
when he said about God in the Psalms: "He spoke, and they came into being;
he commanded, and they were created." That is, the Son shares with the Father in his will. This one [?], however, the head of the kingdom…
All those who have been renowned for righteousness and for the praiseworthy conduct of the fear of God, those of the time of Moses and before him:
Abraham and his sons,
and the righteous men and prophets who appeared after them, saw him with the luminous eye of the mind and recognized him, and offered him the worship due to him as the Son of God.
And he became the teacher of all concerning the knowledge of the Father. For it says:
The Lord God appeared as an ordinary man to Abraham, while he was sitting by the oak of Mamre.
He fell down and worshipped. And though with his eyes he saw a man, he worshipped him as God, and entreated him as Lord, and confessed that it was not hidden from him who he was.
When he spoke in these words: "Lord, Judge of all the earth, shall this judgment not be done?" Now the God and Lord who judges all the earth appeared in the form of a man.
Who else is called by this name except God the Word, he who was from of old?
Concerning whom it is said in the Psalm: He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from destruction.
Concerning this, that he is truly Lord together with the Father, Moses says clearly: The Lord rained fire and brimstone upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah from before the Lord.
to this one who appeared to Jacob in the form of a son of man.
Scripture calls God. For he said to Jacob, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but your name will be Israel, because you have prevailed with God.”
Jacob called that place “Vision of God,” for he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life has been spared.”
For as for the appearances of God that have been recorded, to suppose that they were appearances of subordinate, ministering angels

It is not permitted to us. For whenever one of them appeared to human beings, Scripture does not conceal his name; for it does not call them Lord or God, but angels, as one can easily learn from many passages. This one
Joshua also, who took over from Moses, [calls] as ruler over the angels of heaven.
the archangels, and the glorious powers, calls “commander of the Lord’s armies,” when he saw him in human form.
For it is written that when Joshua was in the plain of Jericho, he raised his eyes and saw a man standing opposite him, with his sword drawn and held in his hand.
And Joshua drew near to him and said to him, "Are you one of us, or one of our enemies?"
And he said to him, "I am the Captain of the host of the Lord, and now I have come."
And Joshua fell on his face on the ground and said to him, "My lord, what do you command your servant?"

And the chief of the hosts of the Lord said to Joshua: Loose your sandals from your feet, because the place on which you are standing is holy. From this it is made known from the words that this one was not [?] he who appeared to Moses.
For the Scripture says that these same words were spoken also to him, when the Lord saw that Moses drew near to see.
the Lord called to him from the bush and said, 'Moses, Moses.' And he said, 'Here I am.'"
And he said, ‘Do not come any closer. Take your sandals off your feet, because the place where you are standing is a holy place.’
And he said to him, ‘I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob.’” Thus it was already known
that before the world there existed a living being, complete in its own person, which shared with the Father and God of all in the formation of everything that was created.
which was called the Word of God and Wisdom.
So then, the Word, God, existed from of old;

and he appeared to certain individuals, though not to all people. These things we have said briefly. But as to why he was not proclaimed to all peoples of old as he is now, let us understand clearly: the first way of life of humankind was not able to receive the teaching of the glorious wisdom of Christ.
For when the first man despised the commandment of God,
he was deprived of that glorious life and immediately cast into this short-lived mortal life. He exchanged that delight in God for this accursed earth.

and those also who came after him and filled the whole earth were found to be worse than he, except for one or two; and, as in the manner of beasts, they chose for themselves a life that was not life.
But neither a city nor a way of life nor wisdom did they bring into their thoughts.
Laws and judgments, or the excellence of wisdom, they did not accept, not even its name; but like herds in the wastelands and savage creatures in the wilderness they roamed about.
And they corrupted the natural reasonings which are right and the gentle seed of the knowledge of the soul, through the great wickedness of their will.

And they gave themselves over fully to every abomination: at times they destroyed one another, at times they killed one another, at times they ate human beings; and in the wars of the giants, those which are spoken of by everyone.
they even planned to build a tower from the earth to heaven, and in the madness of their minds they made ready to go up from their place to make war with Him who is God over all.
Because they behaved in this way, God brought punishment upon them through floods of water and fire, as though they were forest thickets spread over the whole earth.

And with continual [? floods], with pestilences, with wars, and with fire coming down from above, He was destroying them; and He was chastising the evil disease of souls with the bitter medicine of punishments.
But when wickedness had spread over almost everyone and, like a powerful drunkenness, overshadowed and darkened human souls,
Then the Wisdom of God, who is the eternal Word, he who exists from of old, in his great mercy toward human beings, at times through a vision of angels,
and at times that very Power of God, who is our Savior, appeared in the likeness of a son of man to one or two of the ancients who loved him; for they were not able to see him in any other way.
And when, through these things, the seeds of the fear of God had been sown among the multitude of humankind, one whole people, that of the Hebrews, turned to the fear of God.

To these people, then, because they were still conducting themselves according to many of the former customs of the nations, he introduced, through Moses the prophet, the likeness and mystery of the Sabbath and of circumcision and other types, without, however, fulfilling the very truth of the mystery. But when the law which was laid down for these was proclaimed,
and was carried like a sweet fragrance among all people,

then from these, the majority of the nations too, through lawgivers and philosophers who arose in every place, turned from that harshness and brutishness. The minds of many were changed to peace and gentleness, so that there was great peace
and love and fellowship with one another.
And from then on, for all people, for all the nations in creation, as for people who had already been helped beforehand and were now able to receive the knowledge of the Father,
he, that teacher of virtues and glorious things, the one who shares with the Father in all good things, the Word of God and his Wisdom,

put on a body and became a door for the human race. He appeared at the beginning of the Roman Empire, and did and endured the things that agreed with the words of the prophecies. For he had foretold and said through the prophets

that God [?] would come into the world as a man; also that he would be a doer of glorious deeds and the teacher of all the nations who worship the Father. He also foretold and spoke about the excellence of his knowledge, his new teaching and his wonderful deeds. And along with these,
he also spoke about the manner of his death, his resurrection from the dead, his ascension to heaven, and how his humanity was brought to completion in his divinity.
Concerning his kingdom at the end, Daniel saw in the Spirit a divine vision and depicted it for us in human terms.
For he says: I was looking, and thrones were set up, and the Ancient of Days sat down.
His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head was like pure wool. His throne was a flame of fire, its wheels were burning fire. A river of fire flowed and came out from before him.
A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court sat, and the books were opened.”
And afterward he said, “I watched as one like a son of man came on the clouds of heaven and [?] as far as the Ancient of Days.
And he was brought near before him. And to him was given dominion, honour and kingship, and all peoples and languages will serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that does not pass away,
and his kingdom will not change." These things clearly apply to our Saviour.
who was in the beginning with God, the Word who is God, and who was called the Son of Man because he put on our humanity in the last days.

But since in another treatise we have gathered and collected from all the prophets the things said about our Saviour Jesus Christ, in this section these will suffice. Now it is time to show, concerning the name of Jesus Christ, how it was honoured among the prophets, the beloved of God.
Of the third [chapter]: On the name of Jesus and of Christ,
That he was known and honored among the holy prophets, and that the name of Christ was worshipped and praised, Moses first shows.

in heavenly types, and in shadows and likenesses on earth, as that voice said to him: "See that you make everything carefully in this way, according to the likeness that was shown to you on the mountain." And when he presented the high priest of God, and as far as it was possible among human beings for him to be named, he called him "Christ" (Anointed). And to this honour of greatness, which was exalted among human beings above all ranks,
he gave the name of Christ, for honour and glory. That is how convinced he was.
that the name of Christ is a divine name. Moses himself, again,
He also foresaw the name Jesus through the Spirit of God and bestowed it on him as a distinguished title, a name that had never before been used among human beings,
... until the name of Jesus was made known to Moses. And this name of Jesus he first gave

to the one who, in likenesses and symbols, received the leadership over the whole people after his death. He gave him the name, although he had previously had another name, the one given him by his family.
That is, Hoshea son of Nun. But Moses himself called him Jesus, as an honour greater than the crown of kingship.
For this Jesus son of Nun bore the likeness of our Saviour.
[?] He alone received the leadership of the completion of the service of truth, which had been handed down to Moses in mystery and symbols.
Moses, then, [gave it] to two men who were with him, who surpassed the whole people in excellent conduct:

to the one in the greatness of his priesthood, and to the other who received the leadership after him. He conferred on them the name of our Saviour, Jesus Christ, as an honour. The prophets who came after these also
clearly proclaimed the Christ by name in advance, and also what he was going to suffer at the hands of the Jews.

And again they also testified in advance about the calling of the Gentiles, which was to come about through him. In the time of Jeremiah, he said this: "The breath of our nostrils, the Lord's Anointed, was taken in their pits, he of whom we said, 'In his shadow…'"
we shall live among the nations.’” Again, David, astonished at these things, said: “Why have the nations raged and the peoples plotted in vain?
The kings of the earth and its rulers rose up and took counsel together against the Lord and against his anointed.” After this, he spoke as though in the person of Christ:
"The Lord said to me, 'You are my Son;
today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.'"
And it was not only those honoured with the high priesthood, who were anointed in a mystery with perfumed oil, through whom the name of Christ was adorned among the Hebrews,
but also the kings, whom the prophets anointed as if in a divine mystery,
making them anointed ones, as holders of a shadow. For they too bore the likeness of him who alone is the true Christ, who reigns over all: the likeness of kingship, authority and leadership.
Again, some of the prophets who were anointed were also called anointed ones, as if in a type. For these held these types
that pointed to him who is the true Christ, God the Word, who alone is high priest over all, alone king over all creation, and alone the chief prophet of the Father.
And the proof of this is that none of the ancients who were anointed in a mystery, whether priests, kings or chief prophets, acquired a glorious divine power like this
that our Saviour Jesus showed, he who alone is the true Christ.

And not one of these, even though they held ranks of honour and were praised among their people in every generation, was called "Christian" by those under their authority, from that borrowed type which they had. Nor was the honour of worship given to any of them by those who obeyed them.
Nor after their death did people show toward them such a disposition of love that they would be ready to die on their behalf.
Nor, among all the nations under heaven, had there ever been such [?] for any one of those who came before.
For neither did their symbolism possess such power as to accomplish anything like this, as truth itself demonstrated through our Savior.
He did not receive the insignia and symbols of the high priesthood from anyone, nor did he belong by bodily descent to a priestly family.
Nor did he establish his kingdom through armed men, nor was he called a prophet like those who had come before.
Nor did he have any rank or authority of any kind among the Jews. Yet not in a mystery but in truth he was adorned by the Father with all these things, as I said before.
He was not made equal to all these things like those men, nor was he called Christ for that reason. Rather, it is because he alone is the true Christ.
And from his holy and glorious name he named the whole world and filled it with Christians.
No longer types or likenesses, but revealed truth, heavenly conduct and the glory of his commandments: these he handed on to those who obey him. And the anointing was not one prepared with perfumes,
but by the Spirit of God, as befits God. He received it from the very being of the Father's divinity.
And Isaiah also teaches this. Speaking as if in the person of Christ, he proclaimed: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor,
and has sent me to proclaim release to the captives and sight to the blind."
And not only Isaiah, but David also proclaimed about him: "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever;

"A sceptre of uprightness is the sceptre of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above those who were anointed."
In the first verse of the passage he calls him God, and in the second he honours him with "the sceptre of your kingdom."

And again, when he comes down in his account, after the power of divinity and kingship, in the third rank, he shows concerning him that he became Christ, not furnished with oil made from created things,

but with that oil of gladness which is in God. He showed the excellence of his anointing, which was distinct from that of those earlier ones who were anointed with bodily things, in mysteries and in likenesses. And in another place he again says thus concerning him:
"The Lord said to my Lord, 'Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies as a footstool under your feet.'"
"And in the splendours of holiness, from the womb and from of old, I begot you. The Lord has sworn and will not lie:
'You are a priest forever, after the likeness of Melchizedek.'" Now this Melchizedek, whom the Scriptures show to be a priest of God Most High,

is not shown to have been anointed with fragrant oil. Nor was he descended from the line of the family that belonged to the priesthood of the Hebrews. For this reason our Saviour is named Anointed and Priest after his likeness, and not after those who existed in shadows and types. Instead, he was named so by the oaths he received. For this reason the history [?] does not record that he was anointed bodily by the Jews either.
nor that he came from a priestly family, but that he was begotten of God himself before created things,

and he holds a priesthood that does not die and does not grow old, forever and ever. That he received the spiritual and divine anointing, its great and manifest proof is this: that of all who have lived in all generations up to this day, he alone is called Christ among all people who are in the whole world.

And everyone bears witness to him and confesses him by this name, Greeks [?]; and up to now the whole creation, all who confess him, honours him as a king, and he is spoken of with greater wonder than the prophets.
And he is glorified as being truly the high priest of God,
And beyond all these things, he is God the Word, begotten before all ages. By nature he has from his Father the honor of worship, and he is worshiped as God.
since he truly is so, from that [?], because he is truly God. And what surpasses everything is that those who love him honour him not only with acclamation or with the sound of words,
but with the perfect love of the soul, and his martyrdom is to us more precious even than life.

We have rightly set all these things before us before the narrative of the history, so that no one may suppose that our Saviour Jesus Christ is young and his teaching new because of the circumstances of the time of his humanity.
[?] it is necessary [to show] that the teaching of the fear of God which our Saviour proclaimed was not young or foreign.

Again, so that no one may suppose that he is foreign and his teaching young, as if it had been spoken anew, or as if he were in no way different from the rest of humankind, we will also say a little about this.
For since the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ only recently shone forth to all people, we admit that our people is new. However, it is not a small or weak people set in some corner of the earth.
Rather, they are present among all nations and are numerous, fearing God and neither destroyed nor overcome.
And God is with it at all times with his help. And so this people, honoured with the name of Christ, has suddenly appeared to everyone.

One of the prophets also marvelled at this. With the eye of the Holy Spirit he foresaw what was going to happen, and he said: "Who has heard such things as these, and who has seen such a thing as this?"
That the earth should travail in one day, and a people be born in one hour!"
This same prophet also made known the name, saying, “You who fear my name will be called by a new name, which will be blessed on earth.”
But although we are new, and the name of Christians has only recently become known among all nations,

But its way of life, its power, and the foundation of its religion were not recently fashioned by us. Rather, from the beginning of the formation of humankind they were established by the first men, the friends of God, as if from a natural understanding. How this is so, let us now show.
The people of the Hebrews was not new; rather, its antiquity is honoured among men, for it is a well-known people.

It has in its words and writings accounts of the first men, who were rare and few in number, but who excelled in righteousness, in the fear of God, and in all the rest of glorious conduct, each one of them before the flood; and after it, others who were of his sons.
of Noah and his descendants, down to Abraham, in whom the Hebrews boast as the chief of their forefathers.
Now [?] all these to whom testimony of uprightness is given, from Abraham back to the first man: if anyone says that they were Christians in their deeds, even if not in name,

he does not depart from the truth. For what this name requires of a Christian man is this: the knowledge of Christ and his teaching, chastity and righteousness, endurance in good conduct, and the confession of the fear of God.
to acknowledge that there is only one God over all. In all these things, those people of ancient times were no less diligent than we are.
For they were not concerned about bodily circumcision, just as we are not, nor about observing Sabbaths, just as we are not,

Nor did they care about the distinction of foods, or about the other things which Moses first began and handed down to be kept through shadows by those who came after him, just as Christians now do not keep such things either. But they also clearly knew Christ, the Son of God.
For see, it has been made known that he appeared to Abraham, gave oracles to Isaac, and spoke with Israel, and with Moses and with the prophets who came after him. From this, then, you can know
that those beloved of God were counted worthy to be [?] called anointed ones (Christians), as the word that is spoken about them says:
"Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not harm my prophets." So it is clear that this religion of God, which has now been proclaimed to all nations through the teaching of Christ,
should rightly be considered the first and ancient one,
belonging to all those men of the house of Abraham who were beloved of God.
And if it is said of Abraham that he received the commandment of circumcision after a long time, scripture testifies of him that before this he was justified by faith, as the word of God said of him:
"Abraham believed in God, and it was counted to him as righteousness."
While he was in this state, before circumcision, God appeared to him—that is, Christ, the Word of God—and spoke to him
about those who would later be justified as he was, in these words of promise to him: “In you all the families of the earth will be blessed,”
and that he would become a great and numerous people, and that all the peoples of the earth would be blessed in him.
How these things have been fulfilled is plain from this:
For he was justified by faith in the one who appeared to him, who is the Word of God. He distanced himself from the idols of his fathers and from his former ways of error.
He confessed the One who is God over all, and he served him with praiseworthy deeds, not with the observances of the law that was given through Moses.
And that all the families of the earth and all the peoples are blessed in him
has now been made known by deeds that are known and plain, more than by words: that praiseworthy way of life is found only among Christians. From now on, what is there to stop us from confessing

that we, who received it from Christ, have one and the same way and pattern of the religion of God as those first ones who were beloved of God? So his teaching should not be considered new and foreign. Rather, as is right, one should say truly
that this alone is the first and true religion of God,
the religion that has been handed down to us through the teaching of Christ.

Fifth: On the times in which he appeared among human beings. After this setting-out, which had to be placed before the history of the church, let us now speak of our Savior's appearance in the body. Then, as if following the course of the road, let us approach the history.
Let us call upon God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ our Savior, the Word of God, that he may help us establish the truth of these accounts.
It was the forty-second year of the reign of Augustus,
twenty-eight years after Egypt was subjugated and Antony and Cleopatra died, and the dynasty called that of the house of Ptolemy came to its end,

when our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea, according to the prophecy that had been made about him. This was at the first census, which took place at that time while Quirinius was governor of Syria.
Flavius Josephus also mentions this census, which took place in the years of Quirinius. He was a famous man, one of the history writers among the Hebrews.
He also follows it with another account concerning the sect of the Galileans that arose at that time.
Luke also mentions this for us in Acts, saying, “After him Judas the Galilean arose in those days of the census,
and some of the people followed him. He too perished, and those who had been persuaded by him were scattered.”

This man whom we spoke of before also agrees with these things, putting it in his words like this: "Quirinius was a man of those who gather in the council (boulē). He had held other offices and passed through all of them, and became consul, and he was also great in honors in other respects.
came to Syria with a few companions, having been sent by Caesar to be an impartial judge of the people and an assessor of their property.” A little later he says:
"Judas, a Gaulanite man from a city named Gamala, took Saddok, a Pharisee, with him and was eager to stir up a rebellion among the people. For they were saying that this census brings slavery,
And they would comfort and encourage the people with the hope of freedom.

And in the second book of the history of the Jewish war he wrote these things about this man: "In the years of this man, it says, a Galilean man named Judas arose. He was drawing the people into rebellion and pronouncing woe on the people over the [?]."
if they agreed to pay a poll tax to the Romans and, after God, to have mortal masters over them.” These are the words of Josephus.
At that time Herod received the kingship over the Jews. He was the first of foreign descent to become king over them. With him the prophecy given through Moses was fulfilled, which said:
"The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs,

and he shall be the expectation of the nations." What had been said beforehand was not fulfilled as long as they were permitted to have rulers over them from their own people. These rulers began with Moses and continued until the reign of Augustus.
in whose days Herod, the first ruler from among the Gentiles, received authorization from the Romans to rule over the Jewish people.

For, as Josephus shows, he [Herod] was an Idumaean by race on his father's side and an Arab on his mother's side. Africanus also shows this. He too was no ordinary man, and was one of the writers of histories, as those who are well acquainted with him say.
They say that Herod's father, whose name was Antipater, was the son of a certain Herod of Ascalon, and that he was one of those who served in the temple of Apollo.
This Antipater was taken captive by Idumaean raiders when he was a child, and he stayed with them, because his father, who was poor, could not afford to pay for him and ransom him.

After he had been brought up in their customs, he later came to be on friendly terms with Hyrcanus, the high priest of the Jews. The son of this Antipater was Herod, who lived in the days of our Saviour.
When the kingship of the Jews came to this man of such origins, the one awaited by the nations was now at the door, as the prophecy had said.
So from his days, it was as if those from whom the rulers and governors had come were removed. These had begun with Moses in succession. Before their captivity and their removal to Babylon,
they began to have kings over them, first Saul and David.
Before the kings and rulers, they were governed by those who were called judges. These also began after Moses and Joshua, who succeeded him.
After their return from Babylon, government did not cease from them either, for high priests were in charge of their affairs.
until Pompey, the Roman general, rose against them, captured Jerusalem, plundered it, and defiled their sanctuary.
He even entered the Holy of Holies. And the man named Aristobulus, who held the kingship by succession from the days of their ancestors,
when he sent him in bonds to Rome with his sons, and handed over the high priesthood to Hyrcanus, this man's brother. And from then on the whole people of the Jews
he made to pay tribute to the Romans. And again, Hyrcanus too, with whom the succession of the high priests came to an end, was led away into captivity by the Parthians.
Then, as I mentioned earlier, he received kingship over the Jewish people from [?] the Roman Senate and from Emperor Augustus.
In his days Christ came, the hope of salvation arrived, and the calling of the nations was fulfilled, as had been declared in prophecy.

Now [?] in his times, as the prophecy said, the rulers ceased: those who of old, in the succession of their fathers, had supplied the governors over them. And Herod became the first king over them who came from the Gentiles.

After the rulers and governors ceased from the people of the Jews, the high priesthood too was suddenly thrown into confusion in the times of our Lord. From the days of their fathers it had been kept among those who received it in succession through all generations.

You have a trustworthy witness to these things in Josephus. He shows that when Herod received the kingdom from the Romans, he no longer appointed high priests from that original family, but gave this honour to obscure men.

Archelaus his son also threw the high priests into confusion, just as Herod did, and after him so did the Romans, who took over the government of the Jews. The same Josephus also shows that the holy robe of the high priests
was first shut up by Herod, who put it under his own control.
He did not allow it to remain in the custody of the high priests. Archelaus did the same, and after him the Romans.
We have said these things to demonstrate the final prophecy, which was fulfilled when our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, appeared.
Moreover, this is stated plainly in Daniel, in the specified number of weeks that he set as the limit until the Messiah, the ruler.
We have discussed these elsewhere. He prophesied that, after they were completed, the anointed succession that had existed among the Jews would be destroyed.
This shows clearly that [the prophecy] was fulfilled at the time of the birth of our Saviour, our Lord Jesus.
These things are to be kept as confirmation of the truth about the times.

Seventh: On the account of the genealogy of Christ, in which the evangelists are thought not to agree with one another. Matthew and Luke the evangelists handed down the genealogy of Christ to us in different ways, and many think that they contradict each other. Every believer who has not been persuaded of the truth of this matter is eager to find explanations. So let us set out the account we have received about this.

which Africanus, whom we mentioned a little earlier, wrote in a letter to Aristides. He also wrote about the agreement of the genealogies recorded in the Gospels. He refutes the opinions that many held about this, as false and as doing violence to the truth, and he set out the account he had received in these words:
"Since the names of the generations were counted in Israel either by nature or by law,
by law, the one who was born to raise up children for a brother who had died without children, so that he might raise up a name for him.

For since a clear hope of the resurrection of the dead had not yet been given, they represented [?] the promise that was to come in the resurrection by a mortal resurrection, so that the name of the one who had died would not pass away.

Now among those whom we have recorded in this book of genealogies, there are sons who are reckoned from their fathers by nature, and there are some who were born of others and became the sons of others. So the names of both were recorded:
both of those who begot and of those to whom sons were born.

For this reason neither of the evangelists lied, since each counted the lineages both by nature and by law. For the lineages of Solomon and of Nathan were mixed with each other, through those who raised up sons for their brothers who had died, and through those who took two wives. And rightly these sons were considered to be the sons of those who had died, as by law,
and to be the sons of those from whom they were born, as by nature.
How both of these accounts of the lineages truly agree concerning Joseph,

even if differently, yet precisely. To make clear what we are saying, they recounted the succession of the generations. Counting the generations from David through Solomon, Matthan is found third from the end,
who begot Jacob, the father of Joseph. But from Nathan son of David, as Luke shows, Melchi is found third from the end.
For Joseph was the son of Heli, the son of Melchi.
Now let us set ourselves to show about Joseph how the account shows us that both of these men, from whom the lines descend, are his fathers.
Jacob from Solomon, and Heli from Nathan;
and how Jacob and Heli were brothers, and before them how their fathers were Matthan and Melchi.
Both of them took one woman, whose name was Estha, and they begot two brothers from one mother.
For the law did not forbid a woman who was widowed, or a woman who was divorced from her husband, from belonging to another man. First Matthan, whose lineage is traced from Solomon, begot Jacob.

And when Matthan died and she was widowed, Melchi took her. His lineage is traced from Nathan; he was from the same tribe, but from another lineage, as we said before. And when he took her, he begot Heli.
So when we separate these two lineages, we find that Jacob and Heli are brothers from one mother.
When his brother Heli died without children, Jacob took his wife and begot from her Joseph, the third, who is his own son according to nature.
And for this reason it is written that Jacob begot Joseph. But according to the law he is the son of Eli, for Jacob raised up offspring for him, because he was his brother.
Therefore the record of his generations was not broken off. And in listing it, Matthew says that Jacob begot Joseph.

But Luke, reckoning from the bottom upward, says: "As was supposed, he was the son of Joseph, son of Eli, son of Melchi." For of that line, which is according to the law and not according to nature, he could not say "begot."

But since it came about as if by adoption, he kept silent about "begot," until he had taken it back up to Adam, and said, "son of Adam, son of God," and so on. And these things they did not say as something without proof or as mere conjecture. Rather, those who are of the family of our Savior according to the flesh, or his relatives, taught it in a plain way. Indeed, they truly handed down these things along with this.
The Edomites [?] attacked Ashkelon, a city in Palestine, and took captive from the temple of Apollo, which stood beside the city wall,
that Antipater the son of Herod, who was a temple servant in the temple of idols, was carried off with the rest of the other captives, and they led him away and left. And this Herod was a priest.
Because he did not have the means to pay a ransom for his son, Antipater was brought up in the customs of the Idumeans. Later he formed a friendship with Hyrcanus, the high priest of the Jews.

He became an envoy for him to Pompey and freed his kingdom for him, which was being cut off and destroyed by his brother Aristobulus. Having succeeded in this, he became epimelete, that is, guardian of Palestine.
His son Herod succeeded Antipater after he was treacherously murdered out of envy for his great success.
He then [?] by decree of Antony, of Augustus the king, and of the senate became king over the Jews. He had sons: Herod the tetrarch and these other tetrarchs.
These things also agree with the history of the Greeks.

The genealogies of the Hebrews were recorded in the archives up to that time, even those of the proselytes, such as Achior the Ammonite and Ruth the Moabite, and the mixed people who came up with them from Egypt.
But Herod, because he had nothing counted to him in the lineage of the house of Israel,

And because his ancestry stung him with the baseness of his lineage, he burned all the records of the families of the Jews. He thought that he would appear to be of good lineage if there was no one else who could produce his family from the public records and trace it back to the heads of the patriarchs,
either from the proselytes, or from the mixed people who were among them.

But a few of the diligent among them made private records of the genealogies for themselves, either because they remembered the names, or because they already had copies in their possession—those of whom we spoke before. And they were honored as the Lord's kin [literally "lordships"; ?] because of their connection with the family of our Savior.
And they were from Nazareth and Cochaba, villages of Judea.

And when they went out to other lands, they recounted it diligently, as far as they were able, from the Book of Days, that is, from the Book of Genealogies. Whether this is so or otherwise, I do not think that anyone else can find a clearer account than this. And everyone who is discerning in this matter should strive at it earnestly.
Even if it has no testimony, no one can tell a better or truer account than this. But the Gospel is true in truth. And at the end of this letter he added these things:
Matthan, who was descended from Solomon, fathered Jacob.
And when Matthan died, Melchi, who was descended from Nathan, also fathered Eli by her, by the same woman. So Eli and Jacob were brothers, sons of one mother. Eli died without children,
and Jacob raised up seed for him, for he fathered Joseph, who was his own son by nature
but Eli's son by law. In this way Joseph was the son of both of them.
All these things were said by Africanus.
Since Joseph is recorded in the genealogies, it follows that Mary is also known, along with him, to have been from the same family.

For according to the law of Moses they were not permitted to mix the tribes with one another. He commanded that a woman should be joined to a man from the same people and the same tribe, so that the portion of inheritance of a [?] would not pass from tribe to tribe. This much is enough on this subject.

Eighth: On the treacherous slaughter that Herod plotted against the children of Bethlehem, and what evil end came upon him. Now when Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea, according to the testimony of prophecy, in the times we described earlier,
Magi came from the east and were asking, "Where is the king who has been born to the Jews? For we have seen his star."

And this was the reason for the whole long journey that they made with great eagerness: to come and worship the one who had been born, as God. But Herod was greatly disturbed by this matter, for he thought that his rule would be taken from him.
He asked the people’s teachers of the law where they expected the Christ to be born. When he learned that Micah’s prophecy said Bethlehem,
So with a single order he commanded that all the infants in Bethlehem and in all its districts, from two years old and under, should be killed, matching the time that the Magi had told him.
And he thought that Jesus too would perish along with those children.
But a vision of an angel forestalled his plot, informing Jesus’ family of what was about to happen. They took him and fled to Egypt.
These things the holy scripture of the Gospel teaches...
But it is right to see what happened to Herod because of his audacity against Christ and against those children of Bethlehem: the just judgment of God overtook him at once.
While he was still alive in the world, it showed him here in advance what he was going to suffer after he departed from the world.
And the prosperity of the kingdom that he thought was his was overtaken by many mournings over the murders he committed in his own house: of his wife and of his sons,

and of the rest of those who were dear to him and close to him by kinship. We cannot list them now, because Josephus tells the whole story of them at length in the histories that he wrote. Along with that treacherous slaughter that he carried out against our Saviour and against those children,

the stroke of God overtook him and pursued him until death. It would not be amiss for us to hear the words of that writer, who wrote these words about the evil end of his death: that Herod's illness grew extremely bitter for him, for God was exacting from him the penalty for the wicked things he had done.

For a mild fever was burning in him, which did not show its heat on the outside as much as its torment grew greater on the inside. And he also longed to take some food with a longing that would not stop [? text garbled], because it would not pass through him.
There was an ulcer and severe pain in his intestines, and a watery swelling in his feet. His genitals, he says, had rotted and swarmed with worms.
The shortness of breath that afflicted him also tormented and distressed him, with a foul smell and frequent, labored gasping.
Severe pains struck him from every side, and he had no strength to endure them. It was said by those who spoke as though from God,

And some of those who foretell such things by wisdom said that because of the many wicked murders he had committed, God exacted punishment from him, from the king. And again in other histories similar to these.
This writer says about him
For when the disease seized him, from there it spread through his body as various pains. For there was on him a fever that was [?], and an eating sore without limit over his whole body,
and severe pain in his bowels, and in his feet a swelling like that of a person who retains water, and in his groin a rotting that bred worms.

And there was also shortness of breath, which is called in Greek orthopnoea and dyspnoea, and severe convulsions in all his limbs. Those who speak from God said that this disease was a punishment. But he, though tormented by all these pains, struggled to live and looked for deliverance,
and he sought out remedies for himself.
He crossed the Jordan and bathed in the hot springs that are at Callirrhoe.
whose waters flow into the Asphalt Lake and are sweet and pleasant to drink. The physicians thought it best to bathe his whole body there in oil.
And when he had been immersed completely in a vessel full of oil, he went limp and his eyes rolled back. And there was a great commotion among his servants. But in pain, fifty [?]
to his soldiers, fifty each by weight, and much gold to the commanders and to his friends.
Then he turned back and came to Jericho. And he was angry and embittered, and fought against death.
He then set his mind on a plot for an evil deed. For he gathered from all the villages of Judea the notable men into the place called the Hippodrome, and ordered that they be confined there.
He called his sister Salome and her husband Alexas and said to them, “I know that my death will be a festival for the Jews.
But I can have others mourn for me and make the mourning over me splendid, if you are willing to carry out my command.
"As for these men who are confined, the moment I die, set soldiers on them and kill them, so that all Judea and every household will weep for me, even against their will."

And after a little while he said again that he was in distress because he could not take food, and he was racked by a severe fit of coughing. And when he felt his pains, he wished to hasten the day of his end.

He took an apple and asked for a knife, for he was accustomed to cut it up and eat it that way. Then he looked around to see whether there was anyone who would stop him, and raised his right hand as if to kill himself.

... And besides all these things, this writer relates that a short time before he died he killed one of his sons; together with the two others whom he had killed up to then, he killed this third one as well, and then he died in bitter pain.
Such was the end of the death of Herod, who was repaid with a just judgment for having killed those children of Bethlehem in the plot that was plotted against our Savior.
After that an angel appeared to Joseph in Egypt and told him to take the child and his mother and go to the land of Judea, and told him that those who sought the child's life were dead.
After this, the evangelist says that he heard that Archelaus had become king in place of his father Herod, and he was afraid to go there.
And he saw in a dream that he should go to the region of Galilee.
Concerning the reign of Archelaus after Herod, the writer we mentioned before agrees,
telling how, through the will of his father Herod and the commands of Augustus Caesar, he received the kingship over the Jews,

and also on how, after he had completed ten years, he fell from his kingdom, and his brothers were ruling tetrarchies, that is, each one of four parts of the land of Israel: Philip, Herod the younger, and Lysanias.

[?] that he relates about the times of Pilate. And this same Josephus also said in his history that in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar (for Tiberius received authority and the whole kingdom after the fifty-seven years of the rule and dominion of Augustus)

Pontius Pilate received authority over the land of Judea, and remained there ten years, until Tiberius died. So the error of those who fabricated those memoirs against our Savior [?] is plainly refuted.
They circulated them some time ago. First, the very date recorded by those who fabricated this falsehood exposes their lie.
For in the fourth year of the consulship of Tiberius, which was the seventh year of his reign,

they wrote that the passion of our Savior took place. In what they dared to write, they are refuted, since at that time Pilate had not yet even begun to govern in Judea, if it is right to trust the testimony of Josephus, who wrote as we have recounted above.
that in the twelfth year of Tiberius’s reign Pilate became governor of Judea by Tiberius’s command.
And in these years, as the evangelist said, in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate governed one of the four divisions of Israel,
and the tetrarchs Herod, Lysanias, and Philip were governing the rest of Judea,
Our Savior and our Lord Jesus, the Christ of God, was beginning to be about thirty years old, and he came to the baptism of John.
And from then on he began the preaching of the gospel.

Tenth: On the high priests of the Jews in whose days our Lord taught. The holy scripture says of our Savior that the whole period of his teaching was completed during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas. That is, within the years that run from the high priesthood of Annas to the beginning of the high priesthood of Caiaphas.
The time in between was not even four years.

Because the ordinances of the law had been destroyed for them, the old rule was dissolved from then on. Under that rule a man held the office of high priest for all his days, as an inheritance from the fathers.

Instead, they received appointment to the high priesthood from the Roman governors from time to time. And they did not remain from time to time the appointment of the high priesthood [?] [the text repeats this phrase]. And they did not remain in it for more than one year.
Josephus relates that after Annas there were four high priests before Caiaphas.

For in the same book of his history he says this: Valerius Gratus removed Annas from the high priesthood, and after him he appointed Ishmael son of Phabi as high priest. And after a short time he removed this one too,
and appointed Eleazar son of Annas high priest. And when this one too had completed a year, he removed him and appointed Simon son of Camithus.
And when this man too had completed his year, Joseph, who is Caiaphas, received the office after him."
Therefore the whole period of our Savior's teaching does not even fill four years.
For four high priests completed four years from Annas until Caiaphas took office, each of them serving his year.
As for Caiaphas the high priest, the Gospel makes it clear that he was high priest in the year in which our Savior suffered.
From this we learn that the period of our Savior's teaching was as we have already said.
Now our Savior and Lord, a short time after the beginning of his proclamation, called the twelve apostles.
These alone, above all his other disciples, he named apostles as a special honor.
And afterward he appointed seventy others, whom he also sent ahead of him two by two to every place and town where he was going to go. ...

Eleventh: On the testimonies spoken about John the Baptist and about Christ. A short time later Herod the tetrarch cut off the head of John the Baptist. The holy scripture of the Gospel mentions this. Josephus also relates it, and he mentions Herodias by name.
saying that she was his brother's wife and that Herod took her as his wife, wronging his first wife, whom he had lawfully married.
She was the daughter of Aretas, king of the people of Petra. He separated Herodias from her husband while her husband was still alive.
For her sake he also killed John. He went to war with Aretas because his daughter had been cast aside.
In this war, when battle took place, Herod’s entire army was destroyed. These things happened to him because of the evil plot he carried out against John.
Josephus also, more than other people, acknowledges that John was an exceedingly righteous man and a baptizer, in what he testified about him, just as is written about him in the holy Gospel.
He also relates that Herod fell from his kingdom because of Herodias. Herod was driven out with her and cast into exile beyond the border, to live in Vienne, a city of the Gauls.
Josephus writes the following about John:
"To some of the Jews it seemed that Herod's army had perished as if by God's doing,
and that vengeance was justly taken from him for John, the one who was called the Baptist.
For Herod killed this John, who was a good man. John commanded the Jews to practice excellent conduct and justice toward one another,

and, while practicing the fear of God, to attend to his baptism. For it appeared that baptism would be acceptable to God in this way: not as a request for pardon for particular offenses, but for the purity of the body,
once the soul had first been purified by righteousness and by the other things that grow along with it.

People were also greatly stirred up by hearing his words. But Herod feared that all this power John had to persuade people might lead to a desire for rebellion. For they seemed to do everything on that man's counsel. And he considered in his mind [?]
that it was much better to have him killed beforehand, before he could bring about a change, rather than fall into regret after an upheaval had taken place.
Because of this suspicion of Herod’s, John was sent in chains to the prison called Machaerus, and there he was killed.”
This is what he said about John. He also mentions our Savior in this same book of his History, as follows: "There was at this time
a certain wise man whose name was Jesus, if it is right for us to call him a man. For he was a doer of glorious works and a teacher of people who receive the truth eagerly.
And he made disciples of many of the Jews, and of many of the Gentiles as well.

This man was the Messiah. And on the testimony of the men who are leaders among us, Pilate handed him over to be placed at the top of the cross. Yet those who had loved him did not cease from loving him.
For after three days he appeared to them alive again. God’s prophets had spoken these things about him, along with ten thousand other wonders like them.
And to this day the people of the Christians, who are named after him, has not died out. These things
are said by the one who is a writer from among the Hebrews themselves, who earlier set down in his writings an account of John the Baptist and of our Saviour.
What excuse, then, is left to those who have now been refuted and shamed, those who fabricated and put together memoirs (hypomnemata) against themselves? But these things too are enough for now.
Chapter Twelve: On the Disciples of Our Lord. The names of our Savior’s apostles are known to everyone from the Gospel.
About the seventy disciples.

Their names are not recorded anywhere. It is said, however, that Barnabas was one of them. The Acts of the Apostles mentions him by name in many places, and so does Paul when he writes to the Galatians. It is also said
that Sosthenes, whose name is written with Paul's in the Epistle to the Corinthians, was also one of them.

And, as Clement says in his history, there is also Cephas, the one of whom (as Clement says in his history) also Cephas, the one of whom [?] Paul said: "When Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face."
He was one of those seventy and had the same name as Peter the apostle.
And it is said that Tolmai, who was counted with the apostles in place of Judas, and also Justus, who stood with him in the casting of lots, were both among the seventy.
Thaddaeus is also said to have been one of them. A story about him has also come down to us, and I will now set it down.
You can also find more than these seventy who were known to have been disciples of our Savior,
This can be seen from the testimony of Paul, who said that after our Saviour rose from the dead he appeared first to Cephas, and after him to the Twelve,
and after them he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once. Paul said that some of them had fallen asleep, but many of them were still alive when he wrote these things.
After that, Paul says, he appeared to James, who was one of those said to be our Saviour's brothers.
Again, this shows that besides the Twelve there were many who were apostles, as Paul himself was. For he goes on to say
that after these he appeared to all the apostles. These things have been said briefly.
Thirteenth: The story about the king of Edessa. The story about Thaddaeus went like this.
While the divinity of our Savior and our Lord Jesus Christ was being proclaimed to all people,
because of the wonderful mighty works he was doing. Crowds came to him in hope of healing, even from places far from the land of Judea, people who suffered from sicknesses and pains of every kind.
King Abgar also, who was famous for his valor among the peoples east of the Euphrates, had his body ravaged by a severe illness,

for which there was no human cure. And when he heard and learned of the name of Jesus and of the mighty works he was doing, to which everyone alike bore witness, he sent a letter of request by one of his men, entreating him to come and heal him of his disease. But at the time he was called, our Savior did not grant his request. He did, however, think him worthy of a letter.
For he promised him that he would send one of his disciples to heal his diseases.
and give life to him and to all his family. And he did not delay in keeping his promise. After he had risen from the dead and been taken up to heaven, Thomas the apostle, one of the Twelve,
sent Thaddeus, who was himself numbered among Christ's seventy disciples, to Edessa through God's working,
to be a herald and proclaimer of the good news of Christ's teaching. Through him Christ's promise was fulfilled.
You have the testimony of these things in writing, taken from the book of records that was kept in Edessa, for at that time its kingdom still stood. In the documents kept there,

which contained what had been done from the earliest times up to Abgar, these things too are still found preserved there today. But nothing prevents us from hearing them, including these very letters, which were taken from the archive for us
and which read as follows:
which were translated from Aramaic into Greek. Copy of the letter written by King Abgar to Jesus, and sent to him by the hand of Hannan the courier, to Jerusalem.
Abgar the Black, head of the land, to Jesus, the good Saviour who has appeared in the land of Jerusalem: peace. . . .
I have heard about you and about the healing performed by your hands without medicines or roots. For it is said
that you make the blind see and the lame walk, cleanse lepers, and drive out unclean spirits and demons.
And those who are afflicted with long illnesses you heal, and the dead you raise. And when I heard all these things about you, I settled in my mind one of two things:
either that you are God, who came down from heaven and are doing these things.
or you are the Son of God and do these things. For this reason I have written to ask you to take the trouble to come to me
and heal this illness that I have. For I have also heard that the Jews are grumbling against you and want to harm you. I have a small and beautiful city that is large enough for us both.

Copy of the things that were written by Jesus, by the hand of Hannan the courier, to Abgar, head of the land. Blessed is he who has believed in me without having seen me. For it is written concerning me that those who see me will not believe in me, and those who have not seen me, they will believe and live.
As for your request that I come to you, I must complete here everything for which I was sent.

And after I have fulfilled it, then I will be taken up to him who sent me. And when I have been taken up, I will send to you one of my disciples to heal your affliction, and also to give life to you and to those who are with you.
To these letters, moreover, the following is also attached in the Aramaic language.
After Jesus had ascended, Judas Thomas sent him Thaddaeus the apostle, one of the seventy. When he arrived, he stayed with Tobias son of Tobias.
When word about him spread, they informed Abgar: “An apostle of Jesus has come here, just as he wrote to you.”
Now Thaddaeus began to heal every affliction and disease by the power of God, so that everyone was amazed. . . .
And when Abgar heard of the great deeds and wonders that he was doing, and that he was healing,
he thought that this was the man about whom Jesus had written to him, saying, “When I have been taken up, I will send you one of my disciples, who will heal your illness.”
he sent and summoned Tobias, the man with whom Thaddaeus was lodging, and said to him: "I have heard that a mighty man has come and entered and is lodging in your house. Bring him up to me, then."
When Tobias came to Thaddaeus, he said to him: "King Abgar sent and summoned me and told me to bring you up to him, so that you may heal him."
And Thaddaeus said: "I will go up, for it is with power that I have been sent to him."
So Tobias rose early the next day, took Thaddaeus, and came to Abgar. When they went up, his nobles happened to be standing there.
Immediately as he entered, Abgar saw a great vision in the face of Thaddaeus the apostle.

And when Abgar saw Thaddaeus, he bowed down before him. And amazement seized all who were standing there, for they did not see that vision, which appeared to Abgar alone. And he was asking Thaddaeus . . .
"If you are truly a disciple of Jesus, the Son of God, who told me, 'I will send you one of my disciples, who will heal you and give you life'..."

And Thaddaeus answered and said: "Because you believed so greatly in the one who sent me, I was sent to you for this reason. And further, if you believe in him, the requests of your heart will be granted to you."

And Abgar said to him: "So truly have I [?believed] in him that I even wanted to lead an army against the Jews who crucified him and destroy them, had I not been held back on account of the empire of the Romans."
And Thaddaeus said: "Our Lord fulfilled the will of his Father, and having fulfilled it, he was taken up to his Father."
Abgar said to him: "I too have believed in him and in his Father."
And Thaddaeus said: "For this reason I lay my hand upon you in his name."
When he did this, Abgar was immediately healed of his illness and the pain he had. Abgar was amazed,
because, just as he had heard about Jesus, so he now saw it in deeds through his disciple Thaddaeus, who healed him without medicines or herbs.
He healed not only him but also Abdu son of Abdu, who had gout. He too had come in and fallen at his feet.
When Thaddaeus prayed over him, he was healed. He also healed many other inhabitants of their city. He performed great deeds and proclaimed the word of God.
After this, Abgar said to him, “You, Thaddaeus, are doing these things by the power of God. We too are amazed at them.
But besides all these things, I ask you to tell me about the coming of Christ: how it happened, and about his power,

. . . and by what power he was doing these things that I have heard of. And Thaddaeus said: "For now I will be silent. But since I have been sent to preach the word of God, gather for me tomorrow all the people of your city,
and before them I will preach and sow in them the word of life,
I will speak about the coming of Jesus and how it happened, and about his mission and why he was sent by his Father,
and about his power and his deeds, and about the mysteries he spoke of in the world, and by what power he performed these things, and about his new proclamation, his lowliness, and his humility,

and how he humbled himself, emptied himself, and made himself lowly, and was crucified and descended to Sheol, and broke through the barrier that had never before been broken through, and raised the dead,
and he came down alone, and went up with a great multitude to his Father. . . ."
Abgar therefore commanded that all the people of his city should gather in the morning and hear the preaching of Thaddaeus. And after that he commanded that gold and silver be given to him.
But he did not accept it, and said: "If we have left what is our own, how shall we take what belongs to others?"
These things took place in the year three hundred and forty.
These things, translated word for word from Aramaic into Greek, have been placed here at their proper point in time, not without purpose.
The first book is complete.
The Second Book of the History of the Church.
First chapter: on the conduct of the apostles after Christ was taken up. / Of the second: how Tiberius was moved when he learned about Christ.
Third: How in a short time the faith of Christ spread through the whole world. Fourth:
How, after Tiberius, Gaius set Agrippa over the Jews, after he had removed Herod from his kingdom.
Fifth: How Philo went on an embassy to Gaius on behalf of the Jews.
Sixth: How many evils overtook the Jews after their audacity against Christ ... Seventh: How Pilate killed himself.
Eighth: On the famine that took place in the years of Claudius.
Ninth: The martyrdom of James the apostle ... Tenth: How Agrippa, who is Herod, when he persecuted the apostles,
was immediately overtaken by the judgment of God.

Chapter Eleven: On Theudas the deceiver.
Chapter Twelve: On Helena, queen of Mesopotamia.
Thirteenth: On Simon the sorcerer. Fourteenth: On the preaching of Peter the apostle in Rome.
Fifteenth: On the Gospel of Mark.

Chapter Sixteen: How Mark first proclaimed the knowledge of Christ to those in Egypt.
Chapter Seventeen:

What Philo relates about the ascetics in Egypt.
Chapter Eighteen: How many writings of Philo are known to us.
Chapter Nineteen: What affliction befell the Jewish people in Jerusalem on the day of Passover.
Twentieth: What things were done in Jerusalem in the days of Nero. ...
Twenty-first: On the Egyptian whom the Acts of the Apostles also mentions.
Twenty-second: How Paul was sent bound from Judea to Rome, and when he obtained relief he was released from every charge. Twenty-third:
How James, who was called the brother of our Lord, was martyred.
Twenty-fourth: How after Mark, Annianus became the first bishop in the church of Alexandria.
Twenty-fifth: On the persecution that took place in the days of Nero, in which Paul and Peter received the crown of martyrdom in Rome for the sake of the fear of God.
Chapter Twenty-Six: How the Jews suffered countless miseries, and on their final war with the Romans.

First chapter: On the deeds of the apostles after Christ ascended. All the things that we had to set out first, in sections, before the narratives of the Church: about the divinity of our Savior, and about the antiquity of the tenets of our teaching,
and about the antiquity of the way of life of the faith of Christianity,

and not only about [?], but also about the manifestation of our Lord that took place in the last times, and about his passion, and about the choosing of his apostles: in the book before this one we have given their account in sections. Now let us also tell the things that happened after his ascension.
Some of these things we will record from the Holy Scriptures, and others from histories in secular literature, mentioning them in their proper times.
First, then, Tolmai, who was one of our Lord's disciples, as we have already said, was chosen for the apostleship in place of Judas the betrayer.
Through prayer and the laying on of the hands of the apostles, there were appointed to the service of the community

chosen men, seven in number, namely Stephen and his companions. Stephen was the first after our Lord to be stoned to death, at the hands of those who had killed their Lord, as soon as he had received the laying on of hands.
As though he had been chosen for this very purpose, he was the first to receive the crown of victory belonging to Christ’s martyrs—a crown that matched his name.
Then James, who was called the brother of our Lord, because he too was a son of Joseph,
Joseph, who was thought to be the father of Christ, to whom the Virgin Mary was betrothed, and before they came together she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit,
as the holy text of the Gospel teaches—this James was called “the Just” by the people of old because of his excellent conduct.
It is related that he was the first to receive the bishop’s throne in the church of Jerusalem. Clement writes about him as follows:
that Peter, James and John, after the ascension of our Savior,
although they were men who had been honored by our Savior himself, did not strive for glory, but chose James the Just for the episcopate of Jerusalem.
In this same treatise he also says these things about him again: that after our Lord rose from the dead, he handed on his knowledge to James the Just, to John and to Peter.
They passed it on to the rest [?] of the apostles, and those apostles to the seventy, one of whom was Barnabas.

There were two men named James. One was James the Righteous, whom they threw down from the pinnacle of the temple, and who was struck with a fuller's club and died. The other was the one who was beheaded.
Paul also mentions this James the Righteous when he writes: "I did not see any other of the apostles, except James the brother of our Lord."
Along with these things, our Savior's promise to the king of Mesopotamia was also being fulfilled.
For Thomas, as if by divine arrangement, sent Thaddaeus to Edessa to be a preacher and teacher of the doctrine of Christ, as we showed a little earlier from the documents found there.

When he reached that place, he healed Abgar by the word of Christ, and he amazed all the people of the place with the wonderful miracles he performed. Fully, through his apostles, he sent them to his works [?].
and brought them to worship Christ’s power and made them disciples of the teaching of life.
Because of him, the whole city of Edessa remains devoted to Christ’s name to this day, and great evidence of our Savior’s help is plainly visible among them.
These things have been related on the basis of the accounts of earlier generations. Let us now return to the holy Scriptures.
When the first fierce persecution of the church in Jerusalem arose from the Jews at Stephen’s martyrdom,
all the disciples except the twelve were scattered throughout Judea and Samaria, as holy Scripture says.
Some of them went down and travelled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch. But they did not dare to preach the word of God to the Gentiles; they taught it only to the Jews.
Meanwhile Paul was still full of murderous rage against the church. He went into the houses of the believers, dragged off men and women, and handed them over to prison.
Philip too, one of those chosen for service along with Stephen, was among those who had been scattered.
He went down to Samaria, full of the power of God, and was the first to preach the word of God to the people there.

The grace of God was working in him so powerfully that Simon the sorcerer and many others were won over by his words. At that time Simon was called [?] by those who had been led astray by his sorcery.
for they regarded him as the great power of God. Then he too, amazed at the wonderful miracles of God that were taking place through Philip,

He pretended to commit himself to faith in Christ, to the point of even receiving baptism. We should be amazed at this: to this day the same thing is done by those who belong to his abominable heresy. They use the cunning of their father, and it is carried among them like the disease of an evil sore.

They harm and destroy those they manage to mix with the evil poison hidden in them. But many of them were exposed for what they are, and they were driven out and thrown away. Simon himself, too, received the punishment he deserved when he was exposed by Peter the apostle. And while the gospel of life was growing and increasing every day:
As if by the providence of God, the treasurer of the queen of Ethiopia (Cush) came to Jerusalem. According to the custom of that country, a woman rules over them to this day.
He was the first of the Gentiles to receive the good news of God from Philip, through a revelation from God. He became the firstfruits of the believers from all the nations.

When he returned to his country, he proclaimed there the knowledge of the God of all and the life-giving coming of our Savior among people. Through him, that prophecy was fulfilled in fact, which says: "Ethiopia (Cush) shall hasten to stretch out her hand to God."
Along with these, Paul too, the chosen vessel, not from a man or through men, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ and of God his Father, who raised him from the dead.
through that vision and the revelation of the voice that came to him from heaven, was found worthy of the calling and became an apostle.

Second: how Tiberius was moved when he learned about Christ from Pilate. When the glorious resurrection of our Savior from the dead, and his ascension to heaven, was becoming famous and being proclaimed to many, according to an ancient custom of the rulers of the nations,

they would report anything new that happened to the one who held the authority of the empire, so that nothing that happened would escape him. The resurrection of our Savior from the dead was famous throughout Palestine.

So Pilate informed the emperor Tiberius about the signs of our Lord, and that after he rose from the dead many people believed that he was God. Then Tiberius referred this matter to the Senate. But the Senate rejected this report.
because the Senate had not examined it first, as the ancient custom required.
that among the Romans no one could be a god except by the Senate's decision and decree. It appeared that this was the reason,
but in truth it was because it was not fitting that the living teaching of God should be established by human judgment and decision.

Although the Senate rejected the matter that had been referred to it about our Savior, Tiberius kept the opinion he had held before, and he did not plan anything hostile against the teaching of Christ.
These things were said by Tertullian, a man thoroughly versed in the laws of the Romans.

For he was distinguished in other respects too, and he was one of the well-known and respected men in Rome. In the defense he wrote in Latin on behalf of the Christians, which was translated into Greek, he wrote the following: "Let us also look at the origin of these laws. You have an ancient law that no god may be established by a king unless he is approved by the Senate.
Marcus Aemilius did this with a certain idol, Alburnus.
And this happened on our account. For among you divinity is granted by the judgment of men. And so, unless God pleases man,
