he cannot be God. And so, as a result of this, it is right for man to be gracious to God.
Tiberius, then, in whose days the name of the Christians came into the world,
when they informed him from the land of Palestine about how this teaching had first begun, he in turn informed the Senate. He made it known that this teaching pleased him.

The senate, however, rejected this proposal because it had not examined the matter itself. But he held to his decision and threatened death to those who accused the Christians. It was as if this had come into his mind through the eagerness of providence from heaven, because the gospel was still at its beginning, so that the teaching of the word might run through the whole earth without hindrance.
Third: How in a short time
the gospel of Christ flourished in the whole world. So then, by power and zeal from heaven,
the gospel of life suddenly shone on the whole world like the light of the sun. And then, as the testimony of the divine scripture says,
the voice of the evangelists and apostles went out into all the earth, and their words were heard to the ends of the world.
The good news increased in every city and village, and suddenly many churches were established, like threshing floors filled with tens of thousands of people.
Those whose souls had been bound by the tradition of their ancestors and their former error in the ancient sickness of idol worship,
by the power of Christ, through his disciples, by teaching and by wondrous works, [people] were set free as if from evil masters and released from harsh bonds.
And they despised the multitude of their gods, and confessed that God alone is one, the Creator of all.
And they honored him with upright conduct in truth and with pure and holy worship, which had been sown by our Saviour among humankind.
Now when the goodness of God was being poured out also on the rest of the Gentiles, first in Caesarea of Palestine
Cornelius with all his household received faith in Christ, through a divine vision and the ministry of Peter.
And many others of the Gentiles in Antioch: those who had been scattered by the persecution that arose over Stephen preached the gospel to them, and the church in Antioch grew and multiplied.
And while many were gathered there, including the prophets who had come from Jerusalem, and with them Barnabas and Paul and a large gathering of the brothers,
The name of the Christians then first flowed from there, as from a rich spring. And Agabus, one of the prophets who were with them, prophesied about the famine that was going to come.

Paul and Barnabas, when they had completed their ministry there, were sent for the service of the brethren. Fourth: How, after Tiberius, Gaius set Agrippa over the Jews, having removed Herod from his kingdom.
Tiberius reigned for twenty-two years and died.

After him Gaius took over the government. At that very time he put a crown on Agrippa and made him king over the Jews, over the tetrarchy of Philip and of Lysanias. A short time later he also handed over to him the tetrarchy of Herod in addition to these.

And he removed Herod, together with his wife Herodias, for many reasons of wrongdoing. This Herod is the one who lived at the time of the passion of our Saviour. And the witness to these things is Josephus.
Fifth: How Philo went on an embassy to Gaius on behalf of the Jews. In the days of this man,
Philo was very famous, not only in our own learning,
but he was also a well-known man in the learning of the Hebrews. He was a Hebrew by race, and he was not inferior to the famous men who lived in Alexandria.
How much effort he devoted to the divine teaching of his fathers is evident and known from his work.
As for his learning in secular wisdom and what it was like, we do not need to speak of it, for it was trained in the teaching of Plato and Pythagoras.
People say of him that he surpassed everyone who lived in his time. He wrote down in five books what happened to the Jewish people in the days of Gaius, and handed it down to us.
He also spoke about the deficiency of mind of Gaius, who made himself a god and abused his authority at his own whim, and about the evils the Jews suffered in his days,
and about how he went to Rome on an embassy on behalf of the people of his nation who were in Alexandria.
and how he stood before Gaius in defense of the ancestral laws. Gaius laughed at him and mocked him, and he nearly met his death at his hands.
Josephus also mentions these things in the histories he wrote, in these words: “During the unrest that arose in Alexandria between the Jews living there and the Gentiles,
Three ambassadors were chosen from each of the two sides, and they went to Gaius.
One of these envoys of the Alexandrians, whose name was Apion, spoke a great deal of abuse against the Jewish people.
Among other things, he said that they also showed contempt for the honor of Caesar. For all the others who were subject to the rule of the Romans

were building altars and temples to him, and in every other way they received him as a god. Only these Jews did not count it an honor; they did not honor him with statues and did not swear by his name.
Apion said many evil things by which he hoped Gaius would be provoked, and indeed this was likely. Then Philo, who led the embassy on behalf of the Jews, a man praised in every respect,
who was the brother of Alexander the son of the Alabarch and was trained in philosophy, was well able to make a defense against these accusations.
But Gaius stopped him and drove him from his presence. Since Gaius was enraged against them, it was clear that he would do something evil to them.
Philo left his presence insulted, and said to the Jews who were with him, "We should take courage,
for Gaius is angry with us in deed, but God is reconciled to us." Josephus said these things.
How many evils overtook the Jews
after their insolence against Christ. Philo himself also, in what he wrote about his embassy, made known clearly, one by one, everything that was done to them.
I will leave out many things, and set down those that clearly show readers what suddenly befell the Jews because they acted insolently against Christ. So he relates
that first, in the days of Tiberius, in the city of Rome, Sejanus the prefect,

who had been permitted to manage great affairs on the emperor's behalf, was eager to destroy the whole Jewish people. Meanwhile, in the land of Judea, Pilate, in whose days they dared to act against our Savior,
wanted to do something in the temple in Jerusalem that was unlawful among the Jews, and he caused them great distress.
After Tiberius died and Gaius succeeded him in power, he insulted many people in many ways, but especially harassed the whole Jewish people in many ways.
We can learn a little about these things from the words of the writer, who writes about them as follows:
This, then, was how diseased Gaius's mind was toward every person, and especially toward the Jewish race, which he hated viciously. He took over the houses of prayer in other cities for himself.
He began with those in Alexandria, and he filled every place with images and statues of his own likeness. For he gladly accepted whatever others set up for him.
he was, in effect, erecting it for himself. As for the temple in the holy city, which had remained inviolate,
the emperor himself altered it and made it a temple of his own, so that it would be called the [?] temple of Gaius.” But countless calamities, difficult to recount,
This writer relates what happened to the Jewish people in Alexandria in his days, and Josephus also agrees with him.

He shows that from the days of Pilate, from the time they dared to act against our Savior, terrible afflictions began to overtake the whole people. Hear, then, how he shows these things in the second book of the Jewish War, in these words:
“When Pilate was sent by Tiberius as governor over Judea, he secretly brought images of Caesar into Jerusalem by night.
When day came, this caused a great uproar among the Jews. Those who were nearby were appalled at the sight,
because their laws had now been trampled underfoot. For they would not allow an image of anything to be placed in their city.”
When you compare these things with the book of the Gospel, you see that not long afterward they were overtaken by the cry they had raised before Pilate: "We have no king but Caesar."
Again, about another evil that befell them, this writer relates in these words: "After these things he also stirred up another disturbance.
He spent the treasure of the temple, which was called Corban, on building an aqueduct, bringing the water from three hundred stadia away. Because of this the crowd of the people was stirred up.
And when Pilate came to Jerusalem,

they surrounded him, behaving insolently and shouting. But because he had known about their unrest in advance, he mixed the Roman soldiers into the crowd of people. The soldiers were armed but had covered their armor with ordinary clothes. He forbade them to use swords, however, and ordered them to beat those who were shouting with clubs. And he gave them the signal from his tribunal.
When the Jews were being beaten, many of them died from the blows, and many others, while fleeing, were trampled by one another and perished. At the evil that happened to those who were killed

the crowd was astonished and fell silent." Along with these things he relates that very many evils happened in Jerusalem itself, and that from then on tumults, wars, and evils of every kind did not cease from the cities or from all Judea, until the final destruction, in the years of Vespasian, overtook them.
So the just judgment of God overtook the Jews for what they dared to do against Christ.
Seventh [chapter]: How Pilate killed himself. It is worth knowing that the Pilate who lived in the days of our Savior is the same one whose times, in the years of Gaius, we are speaking about.

It is said of him that he fell into severe misfortunes, so that out of great distress he became his own murderer. By his own hands he received the punishment that was fitting for him, and the just judgment of God quickly overtook him.
So the Greek writers relate about him.
Eighth: On the famine that happened in the years of Claudius. Gaius held the authority of the kingdom for less than four years, and Claudius the emperor received it after him.
It was in his days that the famine came upon the earth. Even those who are strangers to our teaching have recorded the account of this in their writings,
As Luke related in the Acts, where he spoke about the prophet Agabus,
who prophesied about the famine that was going to happen; and how the brethren in Antioch, as each of them was able, sent relief to those in Judea by means of Paul and Barnabas.
Ninth: The martyrdom of James the apostle. At that same time, which is known to have been in the years of Claudius, Herod the king laid hands on people of the church to harm them.
And he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.
Clement also related a story about this James that is worth remembering, as he had it from the tradition of those who came before him:
the man who had brought him to court was moved when he saw him bear witness, and he confessed that he too was a Christian.

Both of them were led away. As they were going along the road, he asked James to forgive him. James thought about it in his mind for a little while, then said to him, "Peace be with you," and kissed him.
Thus both of them were then beheaded together. As it says in the divine Scripture,
When Herod saw that the killing of James pleased the Jews,
he laid hands on Peter and threw him into prison, and he would have killed him too,
if it had not been for a divine vision: an angel stood over him at night in a miraculous way, and he was released from those chains and sent out to the ministry of preaching.
That was how things were arranged for Peter.

Tenth: How Agrippa, who is Herod, was immediately overtaken by the judgment of God when he persecuted the apostles. There was no delay in the punishment for the king's arrogance against the apostles. The agent of the wrath of God's judgment overtook him at once, after his arrogance against the apostles, as the Acts shows:
when he came to Caesarea and put on the splendid royal robe on a certain feast day,
sat on a raised platform, and addressed the people. All the people praised him for his words and said,

[the people cried,] "These are the voices of a god and not of a man." At once the angel of the Lord struck him, and he became infested with worms and died. We should marvel at how the account of Josephus agrees with the divine scripture in this miracle too, bearing witness to the truth. He tells it like this:
When three years of his reign over all Judea were completed, he came to the city of Caesarea, which was formerly called Strato's Tower.
There he was holding a festival of spectacles in honor of Caesar, for his welfare.

Prominent men who held great honor had gathered there from the province. On the second day of the spectacles, he put on a magnificent robe woven entirely of silver and came to the theater at the beginning of the day.
When the first rays of the sun fell on that silver, it shone and glittered wonderfully.

Fear and trembling seized those who gazed at its rays. At once flatterers cried out from every side, saying things that were not for his good. They called him a god and begged him to be gracious to them.
They said, "Even if until now we have feared you as a man, from now on we confess that you are exalted above mortal nature."
But the king did not rebuke them for these words, and he did not reject their wicked flattery.
And after a little while he looked up and saw the angel standing above his head.

Immediately he realized that this one, which had earlier been the cause of his good fortune, was the cause of his ruin. Distress seized his heart, and at once a pain sprang up in his belly and began violently.
Looking at his friends, he spoke up and said:
I, whom you were calling your god, I—

look, I am ordered to leave the world, and the fate laid upon me [?] the words of flattery you shouted at me. I, whom you called immortal, am now being led away to death. But I accept the fate that is the will of God, for I have not been treated badly.
For I have lived with the hope of lasting happiness. While he was saying these things, he was tormented by the severity of the pain.
So they brought the king in haste to his palace, and word went out to everyone that he would die shortly afterwards.

The crowd of the people, with women and children, were sitting on sackcloth, and according to the law of their fathers they were pleading with God for the king, and they were weeping and wailing. The king was lying in a high upper room.
and he looked down at them below as they fell on their faces. He himself was weeping too. And when the pain of his belly overpowered him, after five days he departed from the world miserably.
He lived fifty-four years, and he remained in the kingship seven years:
four in the reign of Gaius Caesar,
and three under the rule of Claudius Caesar. He governed the tetrarchy of Philip for three years, and in the fourth year that of Herod was also added to it.
I marvel at how Josephus agrees with the Holy Scriptures in these matters as well as in others.

And if anyone is in doubt about the name of the king, yet the time and his deeds show that it is he. For either his name was changed, as it were through the error of scribes, or he had two names, as many do.

11. On Theudas the Deceiver.

Now, since Luke again introduces in Acts the account of what Gamaliel said when they were deliberating about the apostles:

For at that time, it says, Theudas arose and said that he was someone great, speaking about himself; and he was destroyed, and all those who followed him were scattered. Let us set down something that Josephus also wrote about this.
For he relates as follows: When Fadus, it says, was procurator over Judea,
a certain deceiver named Theudas persuaded a large number of people to take their possessions and follow him to the Jordan River.
For he said of himself that he was a prophet, and that by his command he would divide the river and make an easy way for them. By saying these things he led many astray.
But Fadus did not let them enjoy their folly. He sent an army and horsemen against them.
When they were not expecting it, the soldiers attacked them and killed many of them, and took many others alive. They seized Theudas himself, cut off his head, and brought it to Jerusalem.
After these things, he also mentioned the famine that occurred during the reign of Claudius.

Twelfth: about this Helena, queen of Beth Nahrawatha. Along with these events the great famine also broke out in Judea. During it this queen bought grain from Egypt with a great deal of gold and distributed it to those in need.
You can find that these things agree with the Acts, where it is written: "to the disciples," it says, "who were in Antioch."
each of them according to his ability, set apart something to send as relief to the poor who lived in Jerusalem. And they did so, and sent it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Paul.
Of this Helena, whom this writer has mentioned, notable pillars stand to this day before the gates of Jerusalem.
It is said of her that she reigned over Mesopotamia.

Of the thirteenth: concerning Simon the sorcerer. While the faith of our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ was being brought to all people, the enemy of human life was scheming to seize the royal city first,
and he brought there Simon, the one about whom we gave an account earlier.
And through the [?] of his magical craft, he drew many of those living in Rome into his error.
Justin, who lived a short time after the apostles, reports about this.

He was renowned in the teaching of the fear of God. I will set down the things that ought to be said about him in their proper times. In the first apology that he addressed to Antoninus on behalf of our teaching, he wrote this:
“After our Lord was taken up to heaven, the demons raised up men who claimed to be gods.
"...that not only were they not persecuted by you, but you even deemed them worthy of honour: Simon, a mighty [?] Samaritan man from the village called Gitta,
He who, in the years of Claudius Caesar, through the art of the demons that was at work in him, performed signs of sorcery in Rome, the city of your empire, and was thought to be a god.
And as a god he was honored by you, with a statue that you made for him on the river named Tiber, between its two bridges. And on it was written in Latin thus: “To Simon the holy god.”

"Almost all the Samaritans, and a few among other nations, acknowledge him as the first God and worship him. They also honor a woman named Helena, who traveled around with him at that time. She had earlier been a prostitute in Tyre of Phoenicia. It is said that she is the Thought, which she had received from him beforehand [?]."

These things Justin said about him. Irenaeus also agrees with him in the first book that he composed against heresies, where he wrote about the man and about his impure and defiled teaching together. It would be superfluous for me to repeat this in the present account.
For those who wish to learn about him, and about those who after him became heads of heresies, including the beginnings of their schemes and how they conducted them in every respect,
One can learn about this from the writings of Irenaeus. So, first, as we have received it:
Simon was the head of all the heresies. From his time until now there have been people who follow his heresy.

In this sect they adopt the chastity of the Christians, which everyone knows for its purity, only in outward show. They fall back into the same error of idol worship that they thought they had left behind. With incense, sacrifices and libations they worship images and likenesses of Simon and of Helena, the woman we said was with him.
And there are things more abominable than these to speak of. As they say, whoever first hears them from the books they have is astonished and amazed.
For in truth they are full of such strangeness of mind and such madness of stupor [?].
Not only can they not be set down in writing; chaste men ought not even to repeat them with their lips.

This is because of how abominable and impure they are. For whatever abominable and filthy thing a person could think of, the filthiness of this heresy goes beyond it. Its followers make sport of wretched women laden with every kind of evil.
At that time, the power of evil raised up this Simon, the father and author of all these evils.
And the hater of good things, the adversary of the life of humankind,
as a great adversary against the great and holy apostles of our Savior.

Fourteenth: On the preaching of Peter the apostle in Rome. But the heavenly grace of God was at work through its ministers. Wherever they arrived and appeared, it quickly put out the flame kindled by the Adversary,
and through their hands it destroyed and brought low every height raised up against the knowledge of God.
For this reason neither the following of Simon nor that of any of the others who sprang up after him could stand in the times of the apostles.
For the light of truth and the divine Word, which had then shone from God on humanity, prevailed and was stronger than everything.
Its power was strong on the earth, and it dwelt in his apostles.

Then the sorcerer we mentioned, as though the eyes of his mind had been swallowed up by the glorious rays of God, fled from there to a great distance. He had earlier been rebuked by Peter the apostle in the land of Judea for the evils he had done.
And he traveled from the east to the west,

for he thought in his mind that there he would live as he pleased. And when he entered the city of Rome, the power that accompanied him greatly assisted him, and here in a short time he was so successful in his effort
so that they even set up a statue to him there, honoring him as a god.
But his plan did not succeed for long. Immediately after him, in the reign of Claudius, through the providence of God's goodness and mercy, that mighty and great one of the apostles:
the one who was the head of all his companions because of his excellent way of life—Peter, whom God's goodness chose and brought to Rome.

He came as if against this destroyer of the world, like a victorious general of God girded with God's armor. And he was bringing the precious merchandise of spiritual light from the east to those in the west.
He proclaimed to them the good news of the kingdom of heaven, saying, “This is the light and the Word that gives life to human souls.”
When the word of God reached them, Simon was immediately extinguished, and his power was dissolved.

Of the fifteenth: On the Gospel of Mark. So the light of the fear of God shone in the minds of Peter's hearers, so that the proclamation of the teaching, heard only by word of mouth, was not enough for them.
Instead, with many entreaties they persuaded Mark, the one who wrote the Gospel and who was a follower of Peter, to leave them in writing a record of the teaching they had received by word of mouth.
This had not been done by him before. So they became the cause of this book, the Gospel of Mark.
When Peter learned of this, which the Holy Spirit revealed to him, he was pleased with the zeal of these men and sent this book out for the building up of the churches.
Clement relates this in his account, and the bishop of Hierapolis, whose name is Papias, also bears witness with him.
Peter mentions this Mark in his first epistle, which he wrote from Rome.
where he refers to the city figuratively, calling it Babylon, and says, “The chosen church in Babylon, chosen like you, sends you greetings, as does my son Mark.”
Chapter Sixteen: How Mark first preached the knowledge of Christ to those in Egypt. It is said of this Mark
that he was the first to go to Egypt and preach there the Gospel that he also committed to writing. He was also the first to establish a church in Alexandria.

Of the seventeenth: What Philo relates about the ascetics in Egypt. In this way an assembly of believers, men and women, was established there from the very beginning in the perfect practice of wisdom.
So Philo even wrote a book about them: about their dwellings, their assemblies, their common life, and the rest of their way of life. It is said about this Philo
that in the years of Claudius, while Peter was preaching in Rome, Philo spoke with him there. And this is likely,
because this book that we are speaking about,

which he worked on and composed after a long time, clearly shows the order of the liturgy that is kept in the Church to this day. It also describes accurately the way of life of the solitaries among us, just as it is. And he did not merely know about them; he also approved of them and admired them.
He praises those men, disciples of the apostles, who lived in his days. They were of Hebrew origin, and they still kept most of the ancient customs in the Jewish manner.
First, he affirms that he has added nothing beyond the truth out of his own inclination in what he recounts in the treatise he wrote about the way of life of the solitaries.
He said of them that they were called Therapeutae, and the women who were with them Therapeutrides. He also gave the reason for the name they were called by:
either because, like physicians, they gave relief to the souls of those who came to them and healed them from the suffering caused by evils,
or because they gave rest to God through their pure and holy service,
or because he himself gave them this name as one that suited their outlook.

Or perhaps the ancients properly called them this, because the name "Christians" had not yet become known everywhere. First, he testifies that they gave up their possessions, saying: "When they begin," he says, "the solitary life,
they separate themselves from their possessions and from all the cares of the world, and then they go out beyond the city wall."

They live in enclosures and gardens, because they considered the company of those who do not share their way of life harmful and disturbing." They did these things out of the fervor of the love of faith,
and they were eager to live in the ways of life of the prophets.
The Acts of the Apostles also shows that all those who became disciples of the apostles sold everything they owned and distributed to each person whatever he lacked,
so that there would be no one among them who lacked anything. For, as the text says, those who owned fields and houses sold them and brought the proceeds.
and laid them at the apostles’ feet, so that each person could be given whatever they needed. Philo testifies to similar things about these people,
He speaks in his own words as follows: "In every place, indeed in the whole world, this order of disciples exists.
For it was fitting that Greeks and barbarians also should receive a share of the perfect good.
There are many of them in Egypt, in every city,
and especially in Alexandria. The best of them from every place go, as if to a city where the solitaries settle, to one place that suits them.
which is above the lake called Mareotis, and is set on a hill for safety and because the air is temperate.

After this he describes what their life was like, comparing it to the churches everywhere. "For this reason," he says, "they have there a holy house called the house of the chastity of solitude, where they spend time alone. In it they perform the mysteries of the chaste way of life, and they bring nothing into it."
no food and no drink, and none of the things required for the needs of the body,
but only the laws and words set down by the prophets, and praise, and all the things by which wisdom and the fear of God are increased and perfected."
And a little later he said:
“From morning until evening they spend the whole day in their work. As they read the holy Scriptures,

"They train themselves in the wisdom of the fathers and interpret the allegories recorded in it. For the words that are stated are only the outward form of the writing, and they contemplate the hidden meanings of the allegories that these words signify. They also have the writings of ancient men who were the leaders of their school, who left them a record of their way of interpreting.
They hold fast to these as if to a mirror, and imitate the pattern of their thought." It seems, then, that this man said these things
after hearing them discuss the holy scriptures.
And when he said that they have the writings of the ancients,

He says this about the Gospels and the writings of the apostles, and about the accounts of the early interpretations of the prophets. Perhaps he also means the Epistle to the Hebrews and Paul's other epistles.
He also writes this about the hymns and songs of praise they compose themselves as new works: "that they not only contemplate the Scriptures
but they also compose their own songs and praises to God, in every metre and in solemn melodies." He also said many other things about them. But it seemed to me
necessary to choose and set down the useful passages, which reflect the way of life of the churches.
But someone may think that what has been said does not describe the way of life taught by the Gospel and could also apply to others. Let such a person be persuaded by the words he wrote next,

from which anyone with discernment will accept testimony that cannot be disputed. For he writes this: "They lay self-control in their souls as a foundation, and on it they build the rest of the excellent practices.
None of them tastes food or drink before the sun sets.
For they judge that the pursuit of wisdom belongs to the light, while the body's needs belong to darkness. For this reason they set aside the daytime for wisdom,

They give the body only a small portion for its needs, at night. Some of them remember to eat only after three days. These are the ones in whom love for the labour of wisdom is deeply rooted. Others are so delighted and so well fed on the abundance of wisdom that they barely taste anything even after six days, because they have grown used to that abundant food."
These words of Philo clearly and beyond dispute apply to our way of life.
But if, after this, anyone still argues and is not persuaded, let him too put aside his doubt when he receives clear proofs,
These practices, which follow the teaching of the Gospel, are found only among Christians.
For he also said about them that there were women with them, many of whom grew old as virgins. They kept themselves pure not under compulsion, as some among the pagans do, but of their own free will.
out of zeal and love for the wisdom of reverence for God, in which they strive to share. For this reason they have rejected bodily desires.

"They long not for mortal offspring but for the offspring that does not die, which only the soul that loves God can bring forth for itself." A little later, as he goes on with his account, he wrote this plainly:

"For," he says, "the interpretation of the holy Scriptures is laid down for them as something spoken in riddles. To these men the whole law seems like a human being, and they compare the words that are spoken, the outward form of the writing, to the body."
but, in the soul, to the hidden meaning that is concealed in them.

Whoever has undertaken to look into this way of life more closely, since in these plain words, as if in a vision, they see the wonderful beauties of its meaning: what need is there for us to add anything more, and to say something further about their assemblies, held of their own will,
in which they separate the men by themselves, and likewise the women? Concerning this practice, then, which is followed among us to this day, the writer said
that on the day of the feast of our Savior's Passion we are accustomed to spend it in fasting, in vigil and in the reading of the holy Scriptures.
This same pattern was made known in his book by this man of whom we spoke before, when he tells of the vigil of the great feast that we keep,
and of its service and the praises that we sing in it,
and that one person sings as if in an ordered sequence, while the others listen to him in silence and respond at the end of the verse.

He also wrote how, on certain known days, they behave with humility and lie low on the ground. As he wrote in his words, they never taste wine at all, and they do not eat anything that has blood in it. Their drink is water.
Their food is bread and salt with hyssop.
Along with these things, he wrote about the orders of those who preside and are entrusted with the work of the church, the ministry of the deacons, and the exalted rank of the episcopate.
Anyone who wishes to learn the precise details of these things should learn them from this man’s own account.

18. How many treatises of Philo we know. Philo reached back to the first proclamations of the teaching of the Gospel and to the customs handed down by the apostles, and wrote about these things. This is known to anyone who wishes to know it. He was rich in his speech, excellent in his thought,
and lofty and exalted in his understanding of the Scriptures of God. He also wrote interpretations of the words of the Scriptures, setting them out clearly in all their kinds.

In sequence, one passage after another, he wrote an interpretation of the book of Genesis, and on it he wrote an interpretation of the allegories of the holy laws. He also went through, one by one [?], the points that are examined in the holy Scriptures, and gave the solution to each point concerning them. He also wrote on the questions found in the book of Exodus and their solution.
He wrote on these just as he had written on the book of Genesis. He also has treatises that stand on their own: two on agriculture, and two on drunkenness.

He also has other works that he wrote separately. For this reason they refer to him by the treatise he wrote on what the mind desires and curses when it is awake [?]. There are also treatises on the confusion of tongues and on flight and division [?].
He also wrote on the gathering for the sake of learning, on who is the heir of the things that belong to God, and an interpretation of things that are equal and things that are opposite.
He also wrote on the three virtues, which Moses wrote about along with others.
And also on the changes of names found in the Scriptures and why they were changed; and, in the same work, also on the two covenants.
He also has a work on sojourning, and on the lives of wise men perfected in righteousness, or unwritten laws.
And also on giants, and on the fact that God does not change; and another five on Moses’ statement that dreams were seen as coming from God.
These are all the works we know that he composed on the book of Genesis.

On Exodus, we know that he composed five books on its problems and their solutions, one on the tabernacle, and one on the Ten Commandments. He also wrote four on the things stated in the Law that complete those Ten Commandments.
He also wrote on the animals from which offerings used to be offered.

He wrote on which animals are offered as sacrifices. He also wrote on what is set down in the Law: blessings for the good, and punishments and curses for the wicked. Along with all these are other writings attributed to him, one by one.
such as the one he wrote on providence, and those on the Jews, on ways of life, and on Alexander,
He also wrote on whether dumb animals have speech.

Along with these, he wrote that every wicked person is a slave, and in the same work, that every diligent person is free. Along with these is the work attributed to him on the way of life of the solitaries.
We repeated material from it when we discussed the way of life of the disciples of the apostles.
The interpretation of the Hebrew names found among the peoples [?] in the Law and in the Prophets is also said to be his.
This man went to Rome in the years of Gaius, and he wrote about the wickedness of Gaius.

He wrote about Gaius mockingly, under the title 'On the Virtues', so to speak, of Gaius. It is said that this book was read before the whole Senate of Rome in the years of Claudius. It was praised and placed in the library there.

Nineteenth [chapter]: What calamity happened to the Jewish people in Jerusalem on the day of Passover... In these times Paul the apostle fully preached the gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome.
Aquila and Priscilla escaped from Rome with other Jews and came to Asia. There they lived with Paul.
At that time Paul was still laying the foundations of the church there and strengthening them. The book of Acts tells about these things.
While Claudius was still governing the empire, there was a tumult and disturbance in Jerusalem on the day of the feast of Passover. As the people were crowding through the gates of the temple,
thirty thousand Jews were trampled by one another and died.
And the feast was turned into mourning for the whole people, and there was wailing in every house. These things Josephus says.
Claudius made Agrippa, the son of Agrippa, king over the Jews. And he sent Felix as procurator over the whole land of Samaria and Galilee, and of the region called 'Across' (Peraea).
After ruling the kingdom for thirteen years and eight months, he left Nero to succeed him in power and died.

20. The things that took place in Jerusalem in the days of Nero. In the days of Nero, while Felix was procurator over Judea, Josephus again tells of the strife and disturbances that arose among the priests, one against another.
In his histories he wrote as follows: "Strife," he says, "was kindled between the high priests on one side and the priests and the leaders of the people of Jerusalem on the other."
Each of them formed a band of bold and disorderly men and became their leader. As they quarreled with one another,

'They spoke evil words against one another and threw stones, and there was no one among them to restrain them. Instead, as in a city that has no governor, these things went on in it without any check. The chief priests came to such a degree of insolence and audacity'
that they even sent their servants to the threshing floors and took the tithes that were due to the priests.
"It came about that one would see priests perishing from want. In this way the violence of those agitators overpowered all justice."
The same writer also relates that in those very times a kind of robber appeared in Jerusalem who would kill the people they met in broad daylight, in the middle of the city.

Above all at the festivals they would mingle with the crowd, hiding swords under their clothing, and with these they would stab prominent men. When their victims fell, the killers themselves would join those who were crying out in anger against the murderers.
Because of their outward appearance, they were not recognized. The first to be killed was Jonathan the high priest.
After him many were killed every day. The fear was worse than the suffering itself, for at every moment, as if in war, each man expected his death.
21. On the Egyptian, whom the Acts of the Apostles also mentions. After these things, among other matters, Josephus also says this:

"But the Egyptian false prophet," he says, "did the Jews harm with a greater blow than these. For this deceiver came into the country and took for himself the name of prophet. He gathered to himself about thirty thousand people, and they were led astray after him. After leading them around, he brought them out of the wilderness to the mountain called the Mount of Olives."
'From there he wanted to enter Jerusalem by force,'
'and once he had seized the Roman garrison, he would rule the people as a tyrant, together with the armed men who were with him.'

'But Felix forestalled his attack and went out to meet him with the Roman soldiers, and the whole people also joined them in the retaliation. When the battle took place, that Egyptian fled with a few men.'
'But many of those who were with him were captured and killed.'
These things Josephus said in the second book of his history. It is right for us to compare what is said here about this Egyptian with what is said in the Acts of the Apostles:
where that military commander spoke to Paul when the crowd of Jews in Jerusalem was rioting against him in the time of Felix.
'Are you not that Egyptian who some time ago stirred up and led out into the wilderness four thousand men, evildoers?' These things happened in the time of Felix.

Twenty-second [chapter]: How Paul was sent bound from Judea to Rome, and, after he made his defence, was acquitted of every charge. Festus was sent by Nero to replace Felix. When Paul had pleaded his case, he was sent bound to Rome.
Aristarchus was with him, with Paul,

which is why Paul calls him in one place 'my fellow prisoner.' Luke too, who wrote the Acts of the Apostles, ended his history at this point, saying of Paul that he spent two years in Rome, free [?] from his bonds,

and preaching the word of God there without hindrance. It is said of the apostle that after he had made his defence, he went out again at that time to the ministry of preaching, and when he came to that city a second time, he was then perfected in martyrdom.
That while he was a prisoner there he wrote the second epistle to Timothy, in which he describes both the first defense he made and his end that came afterward.

Accept, then, as evidence for these things his own testimony, in which he said: "At my first defense," he says, "none of the brethren stood by me [?], but they all abandoned me. May it not be held against them."
'But my Lord alone stood by me and gave me strength, so that through me the preaching might be fully accomplished and all the nations might hear; and I was rescued from the mouth of the lion.'

He shows clearly in these words that in that first defense he was delivered from the mouth of the lion so that his preaching might be completed. By the lion he means Nero, whom he called a lion because of the harshness of his anger. And because he saw in the Spirit that the time of his perfection had not yet come, he added to the words "I was delivered from the mouth of the lion":
"And the Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will save me in his kingdom in heaven."

He was pointing to his martyrdom, which was to come soon afterward and which he spoke about plainly in this same letter: "For I am now near the time of being offered up, and the time of my departure has come upon me." In this second letter to Timothy,
which he wrote then, he shows that Luke alone was with him.
At the first defense, then, not even that one [?]. From this it is clear that Luke ended his history in the Acts of the Apostles at the time when he was with Paul. These things that we have said
show that Paul's martyrdom was not completed at the time when he went to Rome, which is when Luke [?] was writing. It seems, rather, that at the beginning Nero was not harsh toward this disciple.
For this reason Paul's first defense was readily accepted. But when Nero grew bolder in his audacity, along with other things he also attacked the apostles. .܀. .܀. .܀.

Twenty-three: How James, who is called the brother of our Lord, was martyred. When Paul appealed to Caesar and was sent to Rome by Festus, the Jews, having failed in that plan, [turned against] James the brother of our Lord,
who had received the throne of the episcopate in Jerusalem from the apostles.
Their audacity against him was like this: they set him in the middle and wanted him to deny faith in Christ in front of all the people.
But contrary to what all of them wanted and expected, he declared openly in a loud voice, in front of all the people, that our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, is the Son of God.

Everyone believed that James was righteous because of the perfection of his wise way of life and his fear of God. So when they could not endure his testimony, they seized a moment of power, because they had no governor at the time.
For at that time Festus had died in Judea, and the administration there was without leaders or governors.
We have already explained earlier, from Clement's accounts, how James died: they threw him from the pinnacle of the temple, and he was beaten to death with a club.
But the most accurate account of him is given in the fifth book of the narratives by the man who received the tradition first from the apostles.
He tells his story as follows: “James, our Lord's brother, received charge of the church from the apostles, and down to our own time.
[He is called the brother of our Lord] because many were called James.
This man was holy from his mother's womb. He did not drink wine or strong drink,
and he did not eat anything that has life in it. No razor came upon his head, and he did not anoint himself with oil.
And he did not use the bath. He alone was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies, for he did not even wear wool, but only linen.
And he alone used to enter the temple.

They would find him kneeling on his knees and asking forgiveness for the people, until his knees became hard like a camel's, because he was constantly kneeling, worshipping God, and asking forgiveness for the people.
Because of his outstanding righteousness, he was called ‘the Righteous One,’ and ‘the people's bulwark and their righteousness,’ as the prophets say about him.
So some men from the seven heresies among the people, which I described earlier in these narratives, were asking him, "What is the door of Jesus?" And he told them that Jesus is the Savior.
And some of them believed that Jesus is the Christ.
But the heresies we mentioned before did not believe that he rose from the dead, nor that he is coming to repay everyone according to his works. Those who did believe, believed because of James.
When many, even among the people's leaders, were coming to believe, there was an uproar among the Jews, the scribes, and the Pharisees, who said,

"The whole people is being pushed to look for Jesus as the Christ." So they gathered and said to James, "We ask you to restrain the people, because they have gone astray after Jesus, thinking that he is the Christ.
We ask you to persuade all those who have come for the day of Passover about Jesus.
For we are all persuaded by you. We and all the people bear you witness that you are righteous and do not show partiality to anyone.
So persuade this crowd not to go astray about Jesus, for the whole people and all of us are persuaded by you. Stand, then, on the pinnacle of the temple, so that you can be seen from up high.
and your words may be heard by all the people.’ For all the tribes, together with the Gentiles, had come for Passover.
So those scribes and Pharisees we spoke of before set him on the pinnacle of the temple. They cried out and said to him: "Righteous one, whom we all ought to obey,
since the people are going astray after Jesus, the one who was crucified, tell us what the door of Jesus is."
He answered in a loud voice and said: "Why do you ask me about the Son of Man?"
He is seated in heaven at the right hand of the great Power, and he will come on the clouds of heaven.”
Many were convinced and gave glory because of James's testimony, saying, "Hosanna to the Son of David." Then those same scribes and Pharisees said to one another:

"We did wrong in giving Jesus such a testimony. Let us go up and throw him down, so that they will be afraid and not believe him." They cried out, saying: "Oh, oh, even the Righteous one has gone astray!" And they fulfilled what is written in Isaiah:
"Let us throw down the righteous one, because he is of no use to us. Therefore they shall eat the work of their hands."
So they went up and threw down the Righteous one, and they said to one another: "Let us stone James the Righteous."
They began to stone him, because when he fell he did not die. Instead he turned over, knelt down, and said:
"I beg you, Lord God, Father of all, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing."

While they were stoning him in this way, one of the priests of the sons of Rechab son of the Rechabites, of whom Jeremiah the prophet bears witness, cried out and said: "Stop! What are you doing? The Righteous one is praying for you."
Then one of them, a fuller, took the club he used to wring out clothes and struck the Righteous one on the head. And so he was martyred.
They buried him on the spot, beside the temple.
To this day his monument stands beside the temple. He was therefore a true witness [?] to Jews and Gentiles that Jesus is the Messiah.
Immediately afterward Vespasian took them captive. Clement related these things at length. Hegesippus also gave an account agreeing with them.
So admirable was James to everyone, and so famous for righteousness, that even those among the Jews who had understanding held this view:
that this was the reason Jerusalem was captured immediately after his martyrdom. It happened to them for no other reason than that they had dared to act against him.
Josephus too did not hesitate to bear witness to this in his writings, in these words: "These things happened to the Jews in vengeance for James the Righteous."
who was the brother of Jesus who is called the Messiah, because, although he was a righteous man, the Jews killed him.”
He himself also describes his death in these words: “When Caesar heard of the death of Festus, he sent Albinus as governor over Judea.
Now Ananus [?] the younger, who we said had received the high priesthood, was harsh and extremely bold.
He belonged to the sect of the Sadducees, who are harsher in judgment than all the other Jews, as we have said before.
Since Ananus was this kind of man, he thought he had found a suitable opportunity, because Festus had died
Albinus was still on his way. Meanwhile Ananus convened the council of judges and brought before it the brother of Jesus who was called the Christ, whose name was James, along with some other people.
He accused them of breaking the law and handed them over to be put to death. But this act displeased all the fair-minded people in the city who kept the laws strictly.
They sent secretly to the king and asked him to send word to Ananus that he should no longer do things like this, since even before this he had not acted rightly.
Some of them, when Albinus came from Alexandria,

They told him and informed him about Ananus: that he had no authority to convene an assembly of judges without your command. He was persuaded by them, and he wrote to Ananus in anger and threatened to punish him.
King Agrippa also removed him from the high priesthood for this reason, after he had held it for three months, and appointed Jesus son of Dammaeus in his place.
These things are said about James, to whom the first of the catholic epistles is said to belong.
But we should know that it is not accepted. For not many of the ancients mentioned it, nor the one called the epistle of Jude.
For that one too is one of these seven catholic epistles. Nevertheless, we know that these too, along with the others, are read in many churches.

Twenty-fourth chapter. That after Mark, Annianus was the first to stand at the head of the church of Alexandria. In the eighth year of the reign of King Nero, Annianus received the ministry of the church of Alexandria after Mark the evangelist.

Twenty-fifth chapter. On the persecution that took place in the years of Nero, in which Paul and Peter received the crown of martyrdom at Rome for the sake of reverence for God. When Nero had grown strong in his rule, he gave himself over to evil deeds and armed himself against reverence for God.

We do not have the time now to write how great his wickedness was. Many have given accurate accounts of him, so that anyone who wishes can learn from them about the madness of this man. Without a second thought he destroyed tens of thousands of people, and he came to such a lust for killing
that he did not hold back even from murdering members of his own household and his friends.
For he killed his mother, his brothers, his wives, and many of his relatives by every kind of death, as though they were enemies and foes.
It was fitting, then, that along with all these things this too should be written about him: that he proved to be the first emperor to persecute reverence for God. This man, moreover, [?]
Tertullian the Roman mentions him in this way, saying:
"Read your own records, and there you will find that Nero was the first to persecute this teaching in Rome. He was cruel to everyone after he had subjugated the whole East.

And we take pride in having such a man as the leader of our killers. For anyone who knows that period can see that it was something greatly good for us to be condemned by Nero." This man, then, above all who were adversaries, was proclaimed to be the first adversary of God,
so that he was carried away into killing the apostles.
Paul, then, was beheaded in Rome itself, and Peter too was crucified upside down, as is related in the histories.
The account is confirmed by the name of Peter and Paul, which has remained attached to the cemeteries there to this day. And not only this,
but also a churchman named Gaius, who lived in the days of Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome.
while debating with Proclus, who championed the teaching of the Phrygians,
He said the following about the places where the holy bodies of the apostles we spoke of earlier are laid: "But I can show you the trophies of the apostles.
For if you choose to go to the Vatican or to the Ostian Way, you will find the trophies of those who founded this church."
That both of them were martyred at the same time is shown by Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, writing to the Romans, in these words:
"So you too, by your teaching, have joined together the planting that Peter and Paul planted in Rome and in Corinth. For both of them planted together in Corinth and taught.
In the same way they also taught together in Italy and were martyred at the same time."

Twenty-sixth chapter. On the many evils the Jews suffered, and on the last war they waged with the Romans... To make the account even more credible: Josephus again relates the many evils that overtook the Jewish people. Among many other things, he shows in his words that many of those held in honor among the Jews were tortured with scourging in Jerusalem
and crucified upside down at the hands of Florus, who was governor of Judea,
when the war first broke out, in the twelfth year of Nero's administration.
And throughout all Syria, because of the revolt the Jews had made,

a bitter oppression came upon the people everywhere at the hands of the inhabitants of the cities, so that they were destroyed without mercy, as in war. One could see cities full of unburied corpses, with children, old men, and women thrown together, so that not even their nakedness was covered [?]. The whole province was full of countless afflictions. Yet the threat of torments was more severe even than the outrages committed every day.
These things Josephus said in his words. These things happened to the Jews.
The second book of the Ecclesiastical History is finished.
The third book of the Ecclesiastical History.

/ Thirty-third [chapter]: How Trajan forbade that the Christians be hunted down.

Chapter 1. In which lands the apostles proclaimed Christ. The holy apostles and disciples of our Savior had gone out into the whole world.
As tradition shows, Parthia fell to Thomas as the region in which to preach, Scythia to Andrew, and Asia to John, who lived among them, and the end of his life came at Ephesus.
And Peter [preached] in Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia and Asia.
At the end he went to Rome and was crucified head downward, for he had asked for this.
And what shall we say about Paul, who from [?] and at the end was martyred in Rome in the years of Nero?
These things are stated by Origen word for word.
Second [chapter]: Who first stood at the head of the church of Rome.
After the martyrdom of Paul and Peter, Linus was chosen as the first bishop over the church of Rome.
Paul mentions him when he writes to Timothy from Rome, at the end of the letter.
Chapter 3. On the letters of the apostles. There is one accepted letter of Peter, the one called the first.
The ancient elders also made use of this letter in their writings, without dispute.
As for the second letter, we have not received it as belonging with the holy scriptures. Even so, many have found it useful, and they have studied it along with the other scriptures.
But the Acts and the Gospel,

and what is called the Preaching, with the elders [?] the Revelation called his: we do not know that these have been handed down to us from the elders of the church. For none of the ancients, nor in our own days any of the writers who have been in the church, has used them as testimony for the word. As we proceed with the history, along with the succession [of bishops], we will make known which of the church's writers in their times used which of the writings whose status is disputed, and how they used them.
And [we will show] what they said about the holy scriptures that the church acknowledges without dispute, and about those that are not so.
Of the letters named as Peter's, we know only one to be genuine, which our fathers, the ancient elders, also acknowledge.
And of Paul's, fourteen.
These are clearly known. But it is right for us to know that certain people of the church of Rome rejected the letter to the Hebrews and said that it was not Paul's.

About this letter too, we will set down at the proper time what was said by people who lived before us. As for the so-called Acts of Paul, as we have received [them], their status is disputed. And since Paul himself, in that final greeting of the letter to the Romans, mentioned Hermas among others, the one to whom they say the book called the Shepherd belongs, it is right for us to know that some of the ancients did not accept it.

Because of them it is not placed among those [books] that the church acknowledges. But others judge that it is very [?], that it is especially [?] for those. But these judge that it is very [?], that it is especially [?] for those who are entering into instruction. For this reason it is also read in many churches.
And we have found that some of the earliest writers used it.
These, then, are the things I said I would show about the divine Scriptures: which of them are accepted without dispute, and which are those that not everyone acknowledges.

That I should inquire into the first succession of the apostles. Paul preached to the Gentiles, and from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum he laid the foundations of churches. This is known from his own words and from what Luke related in the Acts.

And from the words of Peter, from that epistle which we said is accepted in the Church, it is clearly known in how many regions he preached Christ to those of the circumcision and delivered to them the word of the New Covenant.
that is, to those Hebrews who were scattered in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.

But who of these were their genuine followers, and were chosen to shepherd the churches that had been established, it is not easy for us to say now, unless perhaps someone is able to gather it from the words of Paul. For he had many helpers,
and, as he calls them, they were his fellow workers in the gospel. He deemed many of them worthy of an unforgettable remembrance.
and he constantly counted them in his epistles, bearing testimony about them.
Not only he, however, but Luke also in the Acts mentions by name those of them who were well known.
Of Timothy they relate that he was the first bishop of Ephesus, just as Titus was of the churches that were in Crete.
Luke came from a family of Antioch and was a physician by profession. He spent most of his time with Paul, and he also kept close company with the other apostles.
He showed what power he had gained from them for healing souls in the two books that he wrote by the Spirit of God.
in the Gospel, where he testified in writing that it was according to what had been handed down to him by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word,

[The first is the Gospel, written from] the things he said he had followed [?] for them. The second is the book of the Acts of the Apostles, in which he wrote what he had seen with his own eyes, not what he had heard about or learned from reports.
So they say that Paul was in the habit of speaking of the Gospel of Luke as his own, whenever he said, "As it is written in my gospel." And the others who had been Paul's companions…
Concerning Crescens, Paul himself testifies that he went to Galatia. And Linus is the one whom he mentions in the Second Epistle to Timothy as being with him in Rome.
we have already stated that he was the first after Peter to receive the bishopric of the church of Rome.
And concerning Clement, who became the third bishop in Rome, Paul himself testifies that he was his helper and fellow worker.
Also concerning Dionysius, the one of whom he says in the Acts that he was the first from the Areopagus to believe when Paul taught there, another Dionysius relates,
who was bishop of the church of Corinth, that he was the first bishop in Athens.
As we proceed with this history, we will speak about those who received the succession from the apostles, each in their own time. But now let us return to the historical account.

Chapter Five. Concerning the final captivity of the Jews after Christ.

After Nero had reigned for thirteen years, and after him Galba and Otho for a year and a half,
while Vespasian was winning the war against the Jews in Judea itself, the Roman army stationed there proclaimed him emperor.
He immediately handed over the war against the Jews to his son Titus and went off to Rome himself. After our Savior's ascension,
the Jews boldly turned against him, and they also devised many plots against the apostles.
First they stoned Stephen to death. After him they beheaded James the son of Zebedee, the brother of John.
Besides these, as we said earlier, they also killed the other James, who had received the throne of the episcopate there after our Savior's ascension. And against the rest of the apostles
they made many schemes to put them to death, and they drove them out of the land of Judea.
But they were sent by our Lord among the nations to proclaim the good news in his name. The people of the church in Jerusalem also, through a revelation given to the distinguished men among them,
Before the war, they were ordered to leave the city and go and live across [?]
in a city called Pella. All the people in Jerusalem who believed in Christ were to leave, so that every holy person would be gone from the city. Then God's judgment of vengeance would come upon it:
upon the royal city of the Jews and upon the whole land of Judea,
because of what they had dared to do against Christ and his apostles, so that he might wipe out that generation of wicked people from that land.
What calamities befell the whole people everywhere, and how the inhabitants of Judea in particular were tormented with terrible sufferings;
how many tens of thousands fell together by the sword and famine, dying in many different ways, and how many cities of Judea were taken captive;
also what terrible calamities were experienced in Jerusalem itself by those who had fled there to take refuge in it as a fortified city;

As for the outcome of the whole war, and everything that happened in it at each point, and how at last the sign of the abomination of desolation stood, as was said in the prophet, over that renowned temple which from of old had been God's, and how it was utterly destroyed by fire — whoever wishes to learn these things accurately
can learn them from the history that Josephus wrote. But how this Josephus shows

that they had gathered from all Judea in the days of the feast of Passover, and went into Jerusalem and were shut up there as in a prison, about three million souls — this it is fitting for us to make known.
For it was fitting that on those very days when they had assembled and dared to act against our Savior and the benefactor of all, Christ the Son of God,
they should be confined as though in a prison, and destruction should overtake them through God's righteous judgment.
because of the wickedness that held the Jews in its grip. I will pass over the many ways in which [?] the Jews were struck down by the sword and by other means.

I will speak only of the bitter sufferings that the famine brought on them. In this way, even from a brief account, the readers of this book may know that God quickly punished them for their arrogance against Christ.
Take, then, the fifth book of the history of Josephus and read what happened at that time, where he says this:

"For those who had possessions, it was all the same whether they stayed or perished. For on the pretext of accusing a man of wanting to desert to the Romans, he would be killed for the sake of his possessions.

Along with the famine, the audacity of the rioters also grew strong, and every day these two evils were kindled. Grain was nowhere to be seen openly. For they would burst in and enter, searching houses.
And if they found anything on people [?] who had denied it, they would beat them. And if they did not find anything, they would torture them as people who had hidden it because of the distress.
The proof of whether a person had something or not was the appearance of the bodies of the wretched.
Those of them whose bodies were still sturdy were thought to have plenty of provisions. But to kill those who were close to dying of hunger was considered pointless.
Many people secretly exchanged their possessions for a single measure of wheat, if they were rich, and those of them who were poorer, for barley.

And they would hide themselves in the innermost parts of their houses. Some of them, out of great need, ate the wheat just as it was, without grinding it. Others baked it as necessity required, and no table at all was set anywhere.
They snatched the food straight from the fire and ate it before it was cooked. That meal was a source of suffering.
The sight of it was worthy of tears. Those who were stronger snatched food from their companions, and those who were sick wailed.
Famine is harsher than all sufferings, and nothing destroys shame as it does. For things that at another time are worthy of reverence are despised in it.
Wives snatched food from their husbands' mouths, children from their fathers', and worst of all, mothers from their infants'. Even as their loved ones were wasting away in their arms,
they did not hold back from taking the last drops. In their arms they were wasting away. They did not hold back from taking the last drops of their life.

Even when they ate in this way, they could not hide. The rebels showed up everywhere and seized whatever food people had grabbed. Whenever they saw a house with its door shut, they took it as a sign that the people inside were eating some food.
They would immediately break down the doors, jump in, and enter.
And they would squeeze it out of their throats and bring it out. The old men who clung tightly to their provisions they would [?], and the hair of women who hid any food was torn out.
And there was no pity for grey hairs or for infants. For they would lift up the infants

and hang them up by the food and dash them on the ground. As for those who had got ahead of them and eaten the food before they came in, so that they had not caught them, they grew bitter like people who had been wronged — had been wronged — and they devised ways to find evil kinds of torture for searching out provisions.
For they stopped up the private parts of the wretched with vetch, and drove sharp rods into their seats. It was terrible even to hear what a person suffered to make him confess to a single loaf
and for a handful of barley meal.
Their torturers were not even hungry. They considered it a small act of cruelty to snatch things out of necessity.
Rather, they practiced cruelty and prepared provisions for themselves in advance for the days to come.

Those who crept out by night to the Roman guard posts to gather wild herbs and grass, they would meet; and just when these thought they had got away [?] from their enemies, they would snatch from them whatever they had brought.
And many times they begged them and adjured them by the fearful name of God to give them a small portion of what they had risked their lives and suffered for and brought.
But they gave them nothing of it. And they counted it a kindness that they did not perish along with being robbed.
After these things, along with other matters, he adds and says that for the Jews, together with their way out, the hope of their life was cut off.

The famine prevailed in every house and in every family and devoured the people. For the roofs were filled with women and infants who were fainting and lying cast down, and the alleys with dead old men.
Boys and young women wandered about, moving through the streets like shadows. They would fall wherever suffering overtook any one of them.
Those who were suffering could not bury their loved ones. Anyone who still had the strength grew weary because of the great number of the dead.
And no one knew what would befall him. For many of them fell and died on top of those they were burying, and many died before they reached the grave.
And in these bitter distresses there was no lamentation or weeping, for the famine overpowered all feelings.
And with dried-up eyes, those being strangled toward death gazed at those who had gone before them in death.
A deep silence surrounded the city, and a night full of death. And worse than all these were the robbers. For they plundered the dead in their houses and stripped off the coverings of their bodies.
And they came out of there laughing, and tested the edge of their swords on the [?] bodies.

And they would pass them along [?] among those who had been cast out while they were still alive. But those who begged them to lend them a right hand and a sword, so that they might be delivered from the famine, they disdainfully neglected, and those died.

Each one of them breathed his last gazing toward the Temple, because he was leaving the rebels alive. At first the rebels ordered the dead to be buried from the public treasury, because they could not bear the foul smell.
But when they could no longer bury them,
they threw them from the wall into the ravines.” When Titus passed by those ravines and saw that they were full of dead bodies, with fluid flowing from the corpses,
he groaned, raised his hands toward heaven, and called God as his witness, saying, “This deed is not mine.” After Josephus had said a little more,
he added these words: “I will not hold back from saying what grief commands me to say. I believe

for if the Romans had delayed coming against these wicked men, either the city would have been swallowed up by a chasm, or it would have perished in a flood, or the fire of Sodom would have been sent down upon it. For God bore with this generation, which is godless, more than with those who suffered these things.

For through the recklessness of these men the whole people also perished with them. And again, in the sixth book, he wrote as follows: Of those who were being destroyed by famine in the city, a countless multitude fell.
Their sufferings cannot be told. For in every house where even the shadow of food appeared, there was war. Even the dearest came against one another and snatched away the wretched provisions of life.
But no one believed they were in need, not even when they were dying.
Rather, those robbers even searched the very ones who were dying, in case one of them had something in his bosom when death overtook him.

Others, because of their need, roamed about with their mouths gaping like dogs, broken, staggering against the doors and reeling like drunkards. In the distress that surrounded them, they would burst into the same houses two or three times in a single hour. Necessity was bringing everything to serve as food.
And things that not even foul animals eat, they would gather and eat.

For they did not even keep away from the belt that binds the loins, or from the shoes put on the feet. And they would strip off the hides laid over shields and chew them. For straw became food for some people, and a small weight of it was sold for four asses. But what need is there for us to say that they were tormented by famine in things that are without life?
For I have to show a deed
the like of which is not told to have been done either among the Greeks or among the barbarians.

For it is a horror to tell, and hard for the hearing to believe. But do not suppose that I am introducing on my own account a new marvel for people. I would gladly have passed over this calamity and let it go, if it did not have countless witnesses.
Besides, I would be doing my countrymen [?] a poor kindness if I neglected to tell what was actually done in deed. A woman, one of those who lived beyond the Jordan,
whose name was Mary, the daughter of Eleazar, from a village called Beth-Hazor [?],
which means “house of hyssop.” She was a woman distinguished by her family and wealth. She fled with many others to take refuge in Jerusalem and was trapped there.

Now the possessions of this woman, which she had brought with her to the city from beyond the river, those tyrants had seized. And the rest that was left to her of her household goods, and any food that might be found with her, those armed men would rush in, enter and seize from her.
But she was bitterly enraged, and many times she would revile and curse those plunderers, so that she might provoke them against her to kill her.

But when none of them, either out of anger or out of pity, would kill her, and even if she did find some food, she was toiling for others, and from every side even the possibility of finding anything was cut off from her — famine, and the rage of one who was being robbed [?] — then this woman
took counsel from wrath and from necessity, and set upon nature.
She seized the son she had, who was still a nursing infant, and said: "Wretched child, in war, in famine and in sedition, for whom shall I keep you?
"Even if we live, there is slavery to the Romans; but famine has come before slavery.
And more bitter than both of these are those rebels. Come, then, be food for me, a fury to those rebels, and a byword to the whole world, which alone is lacking from the calamities of the Jews."
When she had said these things, she killed her son, roasted him, and ate half of him.
The rest she covered up and kept. At once the rebels caught the smell of this abominable defilement. They drew their swords and threatened to kill her,
but showed them the thing she had cooked. Then she said to them at once, "I have kept a good portion for you too from what I left of my son."
She uncovered it and showed them. At once trembling seized them, and they were struck and froze at the sight. Then she said, "This is my own son, and the deed is mine. Take, eat."
"For I too have eaten. Do not be weaker than a woman, or more compassionate than a mother. But if you are righteous,
and you refuse my sacrifice, I have eaten until now."
and I have kept what remains for myself.” After this they left that place in fear and trembling, scarcely bringing themselves to leave even this food for the woman.
Immediately the whole city was filled with this dreadful report. Everyone pictured this suffering before his eyes,

Each one shuddered at it as though he had done the deed himself. Those who were being strangled by this famine became eager to die. And those who had died before were counted blessed, because they had not lived to hear and see such evils.
Seventh: Concerning what Christ had prophesied beforehand. Such, then, was the retribution that came upon the Jews

for their iniquity and wickedness which they committed against the Christ of God. It is right, then, that we compare with these things the prophecy of our Saviour, which did not prove false, in which he said: "Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse in those days."
Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath. For there will be great distress,
such as has not occurred from the day the world came into being until now, and never will occur again.” Now this same historian

This writer gathered up the number of those who perished by famine and by the sword, and said that it came to one hundred and twenty myriads. And the rest, those rebels and robbers, were killed after its destruction, for they were informing on one another.
But those who were young, tall in stature, and excelled in beauty of body were kept to be shown in the triumph.

The rest of the people, from seventeen years old and up, were bound and sent to Egypt for forced labor. Many were distributed among the provinces to perish in the spectacles by swords and wild beasts.
Those seventeen years old and under were taken captive and sold. Their number was nine myriads.
These things happened in this way in the second year of the reign of Vespasian, in accordance with the foreknowledge of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ,
who by divine power foresaw these things and prophesied what was going to happen, just as it did happen. He wept over the city, as is written in the holy Gospel,
for he spoke to Jerusalem in this way:
“If only you knew the things that make for your peace, even on this day of yours! But they are hidden from your eyes.
"Days will come upon you when your enemies will surround you and press you on all your sides, and will overthrow you and your children within you." And again he said concerning the people:
"For there will be great distress upon the land and severe wrath upon this people.
And they will fall by the edge of the sword and be taken captive to all the nations, and Jerusalem will be trodden down by the nations until the times of the nations are fulfilled."
And again he said: "When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then you will know that its destruction has drawn near."

So when someone compares the words of our Saviour with the narratives of this historian, which he told about the whole war, how will he not marvel that the foreknowledge of our Saviour is glorious in the highest degree, and confess that it is truly of God? Now concerning the things that happened to the whole people of the Hebrews after the passion of our Saviour:
and those cries of the whole assembly of the Jews, who were shouting and demanding that the robber and murderer be released and handed over to them,

and pleading that the Prince of Life be taken away from them, we do not need to add anything to these accounts. But it is right for us to add the things that show his compassion and the [?] of his goodness:
that for forty full years after their outrage against Christ he put off their destruction,
During those years, many of the apostles and disciples, and James, who was called our Lord’s brother and was the first bishop,
while they were still alive and going about in Jerusalem itself,
and they dwelt in the place like a strong wall. For the visitation of God was still being patient with them, so that perhaps at some time they might repent and be sorry for what they had done,
and there might be forgiveness and life for them.
Eighth: Concerning the signs that occurred before the war. Along with all this patience, wondrous signs were also given to them of what was going to happen to them unless they repented.
This writer, whom we mentioned before, also recorded these signs in his accounts. There is no hindrance
