to our setting these down as well as we go through the book. So take and read what is said in his sixth book, where he speaks as follows: "At that time the wretched people were persuaded by those deceivers who bore false witness about God, so that they would neither pay attention to nor believe the clear signs that showed in advance the destruction that was going to come."
But like people whose minds had been taken from them, who had neither eyes nor soul, they ignored the proclamation of God. First, then:
a star that looked like a sword stood above the city, and it stayed there, standing upright, for one hour.
And again, before they rebelled and the war was stirred up against them, when the people were gathered on the day of the feast of Unleavened Bread,
on the eighth of Nisan, at the ninth hour of the night, a light shone over the altar and over the temple, so bright that one would have thought it was day.

And it lasted there for half an hour. The unlearned thought this was a good sign, but those who knew the holy scriptures understood beforehand that these things were about to happen. And at this same feast a man brought a cow to the sacrifice.
and it gave birth to a lamb in the middle of the temple. Again, the eastern gate of the inner court, which was made of bronze and was heavy,
And in the evening twenty men could barely shut it, and it was secured with iron bars,
and below it had deep bolts. At the sixth hour of the night it was found open by itself.
And a few days after the feast, on the twenty-first of Iyyar, an apparition appeared, which would have been thought hard to believe
if those who saw it had not told about it, and if their sufferings had not also shown that the signs were worthy of belief,
For before sunset, chariots were seen overhead throughout the whole region, and an armed army high up in the clouds, rushing about and encircling the city.
Again, at night during the feast called Pentecost, the priests entered the temple to perform their service, as was their custom.
And first, they say that they heard a sound of commotion and clattering.

And after that, suddenly, a voice saying: "Let us depart from here." And things more fearful than these… Now a certain man, a villager from among the common people, whose name was Jesus son of Ananias, four years before the war, when the city was at peace and abundantly full of everything,
he came to the feast at which they customarily made shelters for God. Suddenly he began shouting in the temple:
"A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds; a voice against Jerusalem and against the temple; a voice against the bridegrooms and the brides;
a voice against the whole people." And he went around crying this out all day and all night in all the streets,
until some prominent men of the people became angry at this evil report. They seized this man and beat him severely. But he did not even answer a word on his own behalf to those standing there,
nor did he say anything of his own; he only kept crying out those same earlier cries, as was his habit.
The rulers concluded that this man's agitation came from a demon, and they brought him up to the governor of the Romans.

There they tore him with scourges down to his bones. But he did not plead with them, and he did not even weep. Instead, as was especially his way, at every blow they struck him he would intone this cry with groans, saying: "Woe, woe, Jerusalem." This writer also relates other wonders.
For a word of prophecy was found in Jerusalem, in which it was written that at that time someone from their land would arise and rule over the whole world.
which they thought had been fulfilled in Vespasian.
But he did not rule over the whole world, only over the Romans. Therefore this should be understood as referring to Christ,
to whom the Father said, “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possessions.”
For at that very time the good news of the holy apostles went out throughout the whole earth, and their word was heard at the ends of the world.

Ninth [chapter]: On Josephus and the books he left behind. Along with all these things, it is right for us to know also about Josephus himself, who passed on to us the full account of all these narratives in these books: where he came from and what his lineage was. He himself tells us this too, saying:
“Josephus, son of Matthias, a priest from Jerusalem, who at first [?] with the Romans and finally, under compulsion, fell into their hands.”
At that time he was known not only among the Jews, his own people, but was also renowned among the Romans.
And they honoured him by setting up a statue of him in the city of Rome.

And the books that he diligently wrote were judged worthy to be placed in the library. He set out the whole ancient history of the Jews in twenty books, and the account of the Roman war that took place in his own days in seven.
He wrote it not only in Greek but also in the language of his ancestors, as he himself testifies. And on account of his other writings, he deserves to be believed.
There are also two other books, which he wrote with care, on the antiquity of the Jews.
In them he also argued against Apion the grammarian, who wrote against the Jews at that time, and against others who wanted to slander the Jewish people. .:. .:.

Tenth [chapter]: How Josephus mentions the holy scriptures. In his first treatise he gives this number for the books of the covenant called the Old, which among the Hebrews are undisputed, as handed down from the first tradition. In his words he teaches as follows: The books of the covenant called the Old, which among the Hebrews are undisputed, as handed down from a [?] tradition. In these words he teaches as follows: "We do not have many books that disagree with one another and contradict each other.

There are twenty-two books which are rightly believed to be from God, and which contain the record of all time. Five of these are by Moses. They contain the laws and the tradition from the birth of humankind down to his own death.
This period is a little less than three thousand years. From the death of Moses until Artaxerxes, king of the Persians,
The prophets who came after Moses wrote down what happened in their own times in thirteen books.

The other four contain hymns. Everything that has happened from then up to this time in which we live has been written down. But these writings do not deserve to be believed like the earlier ones, because there was no exact succession of prophets.

In practice it is well known how we approach the books of the prophets. For in all the time that has passed, no one has dared to add [?] to them, or to take anything away from them, or to change anything.

For this is instilled in the whole Jewish people from their earliest birth: that they believe these are the commandments of God, that they hold to them, and that, if it is required, they die gladly for their sake.
It was right to set down here these things that this writer said. He also wrote another treatise, on reason that is master of its own house,

Concerning the contest of those described in the book called the Book of the Maccabees: the Hebrews who prevailed because of the fear of God. At the end of the twenty histories that he wrote, he also mentions [?]
that he wished to write four books and to set out the opinion of the fathers of the Jews
about God and his being, and about the laws: why some things are permitted to be done and others [?].
He also has other works, as he himself mentions in his writings.
Along with these, it is fitting for us also to quote the words he placed at the end of his history, to confirm the testimonies we take from it. He was an opponent of Justus of Tiberias.
who, like him, had wanted to relate what happened in those times, saying that he did not write truthfully. He also brings other charges against this man, in these words:

"I did not hide my writings as you did. Instead, I presented my books to the kings themselves while the events were still witnessed by those who had seen them. For I was convinced in my own mind that I had kept to the truth of the history.
And because I expected to receive testimony about it, I was not mistaken in anything. I also presented this history to many others, many of whom had been present in the war itself,
So were King Agrippa and some men of [?]. For the emperor Titus wished that knowledge of his deeds should be passed on to people from these accounts alone.
He wished to write on them with his own hands and send them out, and he ordered that they be read before everyone. But King Agrippa...
wrote sixty-two letters bearing witness to the truth of this account."
Of these letters he included two in the work he relates. Up to this point we have reported about him.
Of the eleventh [chapter].
That after James, Simeon stood in the church of Jerusalem.

Let us now come to what followed. After the martyrdom of James and the destruction of Jerusalem that happened at that time, it is said that the apostles and disciples of our Lord who were still left in the world at that time gathered together from every side with the kinsmen of our Lord according to the flesh, for many of them were also still alive at that time. They took counsel about who was worthy to take the place of James.
With one mind they all judged that Simeon son of Clopas was worthy of the throne of the church there,
the one mentioned in the book of the Gospel. As they say, he was a cousin of our Savior, for Hegesippus relates
that Clopas was the brother of Joseph.

Twelfth: How Vespasian ordered a search for those who were of the seed of David. Along with these events, after the destruction of Jerusalem, Vespasian ordered a search for all who were of the family of David, so that no one of the royal family would be left among the Jews. For this reason a great persecution came upon the Jewish people.
When Vespasian had reigned for ten years, his son, the emperor Titus, succeeded him.
In the second year of his reign, Linus, bishop of Rome, handed the ministry over to Anencletus, after holding it for twelve years.
After Titus had reigned for two years and two months, his brother Domitian succeeded him.

Thirteenth: That Abilius became the second bishop of the church of Alexandria [?]. In the fourth year of King Domitian, Annianus, the first bishop of the church of Alexandria, departed from the world after completing twenty-two years, and Abilius became the second after him.
Fourteenth: That Anencletus became the second bishop in Rome. In the twelfth year of the same reign, after Anencletus had led the church of Rome for twelve years, Clement succeeded him.

Fifteenth: About Clement, who was the third after [?]... About Clement, the apostle Paul, writing to the Philippians, teaches that he was his helper in the gospel, saying: "With Clement and with the rest of my helpers, whose names are written in the book of life."

Sixteenth: On the letter of Paul. Now this man has one great and wonderful letter, which the Church acknowledges. He wrote it as from the church of Rome to the church of Corinth, because of a disturbance that had arisen there in Corinth at that time.
We know that this letter has been read publicly before all the people in many churches from ancient times down to the present.
That a disturbance arose in Corinth in his days is attested by a trustworthy witness, Hegesippus.
Seventeenth: On the persecution that took place in the years of Domitian. Domitian the emperor treated many people very harshly. In Rome itself, not a few men of high birth

and a great number of notable men he put to death without just judgment. Countless other famous men he banished beyond the frontiers, and their property was seized unjustly. In the end he took over from Nero the role of being, after him, an enemy of God. For after Nero he stirred up a second persecution against us.
His father Vespasian, however, had not even considered doing anything harmful to us...

Eighteenth: On John the apostle and that Revelation. It is reported that John, the apostle and evangelist, was still living in the world at this time. Because of his testimony to the word of God, he was banished to live on an island called Patmos.
Now Irenaeus, when writing about the numerical value of the deceiver’s name, which is written in the Revelation called John’s,

He said these things about John in the fifth book, which he wrote against heresies. He spoke as follows: "If it had been necessary for his name to be openly proclaimed at this time, it would have been stated by the one to whom the revelation was shown.
For it was not seen long ago, but almost in our own generation, at the end of Domitian's reign." At that time the teaching of our faith shone so brightly
that even writers who were outside our teaching did not hesitate to record in their histories the persecution and the martyrs of that time. They also stated the date exactly, saying
that in the fifteenth year of Domitian, along with many others, they also told about Flavia Domitilla,
who was the daughter of the sister of Flavius Clemens, one of the consuls in Rome at that time. Because of her testimony to Christ, she was banished as a penalty [?] to an island called Pontia.

Nineteenth: How Domitian ordered that those of the family of David be put to death. This Domitian ordered that those who were of the family of David be put to death. There is an old account that certain heretics brought accusations against the sons of Jude,
who was the brother of our Lord according to the flesh, as being men of the lineage of David and of the family of Christ.
Hegesippus relates these things as follows.
Twentieth: On those who were of the family of our Savior. Hegesippus says that those of the family of our Lord were still living in the world:

the sons of Jude, who is called his brother according to the flesh. They had been denounced as being sons of David. The evocatus brought them to Domitian Caesar, because, like Herod, he feared the coming of Christ. He asked them whether they were of the family of David.
And they acknowledged it. Then he asked them again how much property they had and how much gold they possessed. They said:
…that the two of them together had only about nine thousand denarii,
half of which belonged to each of them. And they did not have this in denarii. It was the value of thirty-nine plethra of land, which was all they had.
On this land they also paid taxes. And with their hands as evidence: that they worked with their hands, the toughness of their bodies, and their hands, which had become hardened by constant labor.
When they were asked about Christ and his kingdom, what it is like, where it is, and when it will appear, they answered that it is not of this world
and would not be on earth, but is above heaven, over the angels.
It would be revealed at the end of the world, when he came in glory to judge the dead and the living and repay everyone according to their deeds.
Domitian did not condemn them for these things. Instead he despised them as lowly people and released them as free men. He also issued an order to stop the persecution against the churches.

When these men had been released, they led the churches, since they were witnesses and since they were of the family of our Lord. There was peace, and they remained alive until the reign of King Trajan.
Hegesippus said these things. But he is not the only one. Tertullian also mentions Domitian, in these words:
“At one time Domitian too wanted to act as that man had, since he shared in Nero’s cruelty.
But, as I think, because he had a little understanding, he soon stopped and even brought back those whom he had persecuted.”
After Domitian, who had held power for fifteen years, Nerva succeeded him, and all the honors of Domitian were abolished.

All those whom he had unjustly persecuted returned to their homes, and their property was given back to them, as by decree of the Senate of Rome. These things are related by men who recorded in writing what happened in those times.
Then John the apostle also returned from the island to which he had been banished and came to Ephesus. He lived there, as the account of the earlier generations has handed down to us.

Twenty-first: that Cerdo was the third bishop in the church of Alexandria. When Nerva had reigned for one year, more or less, Trajan succeeded him. In his first year, when Abilius had governed the church in Alexandria for thirteen years, Cerdo succeeded him.
He was the third to be appointed there, after Annianus, the first. At this time Clement was still governing the church of Rome.
He too held the third place among the bishops who had been there after Paul and Peter: Linus was first, and after him Anencletus.
Twenty-second: that Ignatius was the second bishop in Antioch. In Antioch too, after Evodius, who was the first bishop there, Ignatius was known in these times as the second bishop.
Likewise Simeon, the second bishop of the church of Jerusalem after James, the brother of our Savior, held the ministry at this time.
Of the twenty-third [chapter]. An account concerning John the apostle...

In those times the one whom Jesus loved, John the apostle and evangelist, was still alive in Asia and governed the church there. He had returned from the island to which he had been banished, after Domitian's death. Two trustworthy witnesses are enough to prove that he was still alive in those times, and these were teachers of the true faith of the church.
namely Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria.
For Irenaeus, in the second book that he composed against heresies, wrote this: "All the elders who were in Asia, who associated with John the disciple of our Lord,
testify that he handed it down to them. For he remained with them until the times of Trajan." And in the third book of this same work he shows the same things.
"But the church of Ephesus too, which was founded by Paul,

and where John remained with them until the time of Trajan, is also a true witness of the tradition of the apostles." Clement also indicates the time, and adds a story that is very useful to those who love to hear things that are fine and profitable.
He adds it in the treatise that he composed and wrote on which rich man is saved. Take and read it in his book, which runs as follows:
"Hear a parable, though it is not a parable but an account that has been handed down and preserved in memory about John the apostle. For after that tyrant had died,
he returned from the island of Patmos and came to Ephesus. And when they asked him, he would go to the regions of the Gentiles as well.

In some places he would appoint bishops; in others churches would be built; and in others he would lay hands on someone for one of the orders of the churches, those whom the Holy Spirit made known to him.
He also came to a city a short distance away—some people even give its name—and attended to all the brothers’ needs.
In the course of all this, he saw a young man who was physically strong, handsome in appearance, and ardent in spirit.
He looked at the bishop who was standing there and said to him, ‘I entrust this young man to you with all earnestness, before the church and with Christ as witness.’
The bishop accepted the charge and made many promises. John again said the very same things to him and solemnly charged him.

Afterwards he went to Ephesus. The presbyter took the young man who had been entrusted to him into his house and brought him up. He was patient [?] with him and tender toward him, and afterwards baptized him. After this he slackened, through much negligence [?], in his care and watchfulness,
as if he had set the seal of the Lord on him as a perfect guard.
But once the young man had gained this freedom, companions of his own age attached themselves to him. They were idle and corrupt, and practiced in evil deeds.
At first they took him to expensive banquets. Afterwards they also went out at night, robbed people, and took him along with them. Then they persuaded him to do even worse things with them.

Little by little he grew used to it. Then, through the force of his nature, he ran wild. Like a horse with an unbridled mouth that bites its bit on the straight road, he hurled himself arrogantly into the chasms.

Once he had completely given up hope of being saved in God, he no longer thought of doing anything small. Since he was already lost for good, he set his mind on something greater than all, and he persuaded himself to become like his companions. So he took them and formed a band of robbers. He readily became the robbers' chief and led them with violence: a murderer, wicked and defiled. Meanwhile, time passed.
Then they summoned John to that city.
When he had settled the matter for which he had come, he said to the bishop: 'Return to us the deposit that Christ and I entrusted to you, before the witness of this church over which you preside.'
At first the bishop was astonished, thinking he was being falsely accused over money he had not received. He could not believe in something that he did not have, nor could he doubt John.
When he said to him, "It is that young man I am asking for, the soul of that brother," the elder sighed bitterly and wept, and said, "He is dead." But he said,
"How, and by what death?" He said, "He is dead to God."

For he went out wicked and depraved, and in the end took to banditry. And now, instead of the church, he holds out on the mountain with others like himself.” The apostle tore his clothes, and with great lamentation he struck his face.
And he said, "A fine guardian you left for that young man's soul! Quickly, bring me a horse, and a man to show me the way."

So he set out from the church just as he was, and went. When he reached that place, the robbers' guard seized him. He neither fled nor pleaded. Instead he cried out and said, "This is why I have come. Take me to your chief."

That young man was waiting for the moment, armed. But when John came near and he recognized him, he was ashamed and began to run away. John, however, chased after him with all his strength, forgetting even his old age.
And he was crying out and saying:
“Why are you running away, my son, from your old, unarmed father? Have pity on me, my son! Do not be afraid. You still have hope of life.
I will answer to Christ for you. If I must die in your place, I will gladly endure it, just as our Lord did for us.
I give my own life for you. Stop, be still, and believe me. Christ sent me.” When the young man heard this,

At first the young man stood still and looked down at the ground. Then he threw down his weapons. And, trembling, he wept bitterly. When the apostle came near and embraced him, that young man poured out his feelings as well as he could with many tears, and was baptized a second time with tears. Only his right hand he kept hidden. The apostle gave him his pledge on this and swore to him
“that I am asking forgiveness for you from our Saviour, and you are pardoned.”

He kept pressing and kissing the young man's right hand, as if it had been cleansed by repentance. He took him and brought him back to the church. With abundant prayers he offered on his behalf, with continual fasts he endured together with him,

and with persuasive words of every kind, he comforted his mind. He did not leave until he had restored him to the church. So he gave an example of true repentance and a great proof of being born anew,
and a trophy of a resurrection that can be seen. These are the accounts of Clement, recorded for the benefit of those who hear them. ...
Chapter Twenty-Four. How the Gospels Were Composed. Let us now set out the writings of this apostle about which there is no dispute.
Now, as for his Gospel, which was known in all the churches under heaven:
let it be acknowledged first. And by the ancients it was, with good reason [?], counted fourth in number, with those three placed before it.
Now let us describe Christ’s holy apostles, who were truly worthy of God and whose conduct was entirely pure.

Their souls were adorned with every virtue and every glorious quality, but in speech they were unlearned. They relied on the wonderful and divine power that had been given to them by our Saviour, [and did not try] to proclaim the teaching of their Master through persuasiveness and skill with words.
They neither knew how to do this, nor did they devote themselves to it.
Instead, they relied solely on the demonstration of God’s Spirit, which was active in them, and on the power of Christ’s miracles, which were accomplished through their hands.
They proclaimed the knowledge of the kingdom of heaven throughout the world, but gave little attention to setting their words down in writing.
They did this because the ministry they performed was beyond human capacity.
For Paul, who was the most powerful of them all in excellence of speech and who also surpassed them in understanding, did not commit to writing more than these short letters,

although he had countless unspoken things to say, as a man who had attained to the vision of the third heaven, had been caught up even to that glorious paradise, and had been found worthy to hear there words that a human being is not permitted to speak. Nor, indeed, were the rest of our Saviour's disciples lacking in these things.
For there were twelve apostles, seventy other disciples, and many others besides these.
Yet of all our Lord's apostles, only Matthew and John left us accounts in writing, and even they, as the record shows, wrote because it became necessary for them.
For Matthew, having first preached to the Hebrews and being about to go to other places, delivered his Gospel to them in the Hebrew language,
so that, in his place, he might supply them in writing with the good news he had been preaching.
We have already spoken about Mark and Luke and the handing down of their Gospels. As for John, according to what is said about him,
he had been preaching the good news all along without writing, and finally came to write for this reason:

When those three Gospels that had been written had been brought to everyone, and had also reached him, as the record shows, he accepted them and testified that they had written the truth. Only this was lacking in them: an account of what was done from the beginning of Christ's teaching. This statement is true. So we can learn
that these three evangelists wrote only what was done by our Lord in one year, after John the Baptist had been put in prison.
They made this very point clear at the beginning of their accounts: after the forty days during which our Lord fasted and was tempted,
they began their accounts at that time. For Matthew explains it this way: “When he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew from Judea to Galilee.”
Mark likewise says: “After John was handed over, Jesus came to Galilee.”
Luke, too, before he begins the accounts of our Lord's deeds, likewise took note of this and said that Herod, on top of all the evils he had done, also added this: he shut John up in prison.
So let us ask John the apostle about these things: that this [?] which the first evangelists had left out,

and what our Savior did during it, he completed in his own book. This means what was done before John the Baptist was handed over to prison. He made this known when he said, "This is the first sign that Jesus did, and he showed his glory."
At one point he mentions John the Baptist among the deeds of Jesus, saying that he was still baptizing at Aenon near Salim. He shows this clearly when he says:
"For John had not yet been cast into prison."
So John, in his Gospel, wrote the things that our Lord did before John the Baptist was handed over to prison.

The other three evangelists, however, record the things that were done after John was handed over. So once we are convinced of this, it becomes clear to us that the Gospels do not disagree with one another.
because John’s Gospel contains accounts of Christ’s earlier deeds, while the others contain accounts of what he did in the later period.

It seems, then, that this is why John said nothing about the record of the bodily genealogy of our Savior: Matthew and Luke had already written about it. He began instead to write about his divinity, as though the Spirit of God had reserved this for him as the more excellent apostle.
We have said these things about the writing of John’s Gospel. We have also previously explained the circumstances that gave rise to Mark’s Gospel.
Luke too, when he began his book,

first set out the reason why he wrote. Many others had wanted to write a careless account of the things of which he himself was fully convinced. So, to keep us from holding the doubtful opinions of others, he handed down to us the truth of the things that he had received and been assured of
through his close association and constant companionship with Paul and his dealings with the rest of the apostles.
He wrote these things in his Gospel. These are the things we have said; we will also make known, at the appropriate points, the tradition of the early writers concerning them.
On the writings of John: besides the Gospel that he wrote,
his first epistle too

has been accepted without dispute by both earlier and later writers. But the other two that are said to be his are disputed. As for his Revelation, to this day many people's opinion is divided, some leaning one way and some the other. On this too we will show, in their proper places, the opinions held about it, drawing on the testimony of the ancients.
Chapter twenty-five. On the writings: which are accepted and which are not. Now that we have reached this point,
it is fitting to list again the writings of the New Testament that we have already discussed. Let us place the holy Gospels first,

After them comes the book of the Acts of the Apostles. After these we should place the epistles of Paul, and after them the first epistle of John. In the same way we should also count the first epistle of Peter.
After these comes the Revelation of John too, if that seems proper.

We will set out in their proper time the opinions that many have held about it. These books are to be placed among those that the church acknowledges. Among the books that are disputed but are still accepted by many
are the second epistle of Peter, and the second and third epistles that are called John's,

whether they belong to the evangelist or to another man of the same name. Among the disputed books we should also place the books of the Acts of Paul, the work called the Shepherd, and the Revelation of Peter. Along with these come the epistle of Barnabas and the work called the Teaching of the Apostles.

Again, as I said before, the Revelation of John belongs here too, if it seems that it also falls in this class. Some people reject it, while others place it among the genuine books that the church acknowledges. Others again place the Gospel of the Hebrews among these books as well,
the Gospel that the Hebrews who have accepted Christ especially delight in. All of these should be counted among the disputed books. So it was necessary for us to arrange them in order
so that we can distinguish the genuine books, in which nothing has been mixed, and which the church [?]
from the books about which there is disagreement and dispute. These are not placed in the church's canon, though many members of the church use them. We should also know
that from the writings that the heretics put out under the names of the apostles —
namely, gospels attributed to Peter, Thomas, Bartholomew, or others, or Acts of Andrew, John, and the other apostles.

No one at all from the members of the church who came in succession thought them worthy of mention in his writings. The style of their language differs greatly from that of the apostles. The purpose and intent written in them are very far removed from the true faith. For heretical men fabricated them from their own minds,
and this the books themselves clearly show. For this reason they should not even be placed among the disputed books,
but should be rejected as foreign and abominable.

Twenty-sixth: On Menander the sorcerer... Let us now come to the account that follows. Menander received his teaching from Simon the sorcerer. He showed himself to be a second instrument of Satan's working, worse than the first. He too was a Samaritan. When he had become as accomplished in sorcery as his master,
he boasted with great, arrogant words. He said of himself that he was the savior sent from above, from the invisible aeons, for the salvation of human beings.
He taught that no one could overcome the angels who made this world in any other way, unless he first came to the instruction in sorcery that Menander delivered,
and to the baptism given by his hands.

Those who are found worthy of it, he said, receive eternal life in this world and remain in it without growing old and without dying. These things can be clearly learned from the words of Irenaeus. Justin too, where he mentioned Simon, also wrote an account of this man, and said:

"Menander, who was himself also a Samaritan, from a village called Capparetaea, was a disciple of Simon. He too was driven mad by the working of demons. He came to Antioch and led many astray by the art of his sorcery."
He persuaded those who followed him to believe that they would not die. Even now there are people belonging to his school who profess this.
This was the work of Satan: through these sorcerers who put on the name of Christ, he was eager to slander by sorcery the great mystery of the fear of God,
so that by their hands the life of the soul, which does not die, and the resurrection from the dead, which are the foundations of the church, would be mocked.
But those who had inscribed their masters as saviours for themselves fell away from the hope of truth.

Twenty-seventh: On the heresy of the Ebionites. But the evil demon, who could not shake those who love the Christ of God, found others who could be taken hold of from among these and led them astray after himself.

The first ones fittingly called them Ebionites, because they held poor and low views of Christ. For they considered him a plain man, like anyone else, who was justified by progress in his habitual conduct,
and who was born from the union of a man and Mary.

They also say that they are required to observe the law, because they do not believe they can live by faith in Christ alone and by the way of life he taught. There are others, too, who are called by this same name,
who escape the great audacity of those I have just spoken about.
For they do not deny that our Lord was born of a virgin and of the Holy Spirit. But they do not confess, as we do, that he already existed beforehand as God the Word and Wisdom.
Still, they became partners in the wickedness of the first group. In particular, they too are eager, like those others, to keep the bodily observance of the law.
These people, however, entirely reject all the letters of Paul,
and they call him an apostate from the Law. They use only the Gospel called that of the Hebrews, and they held the others in little account.
They keep the Sabbath and the rest of the practices of Judaism, like the others. But they also observe the first days of the week, as we do, in memory of the resurrection of our Saviour.
Because of the way they thought, they received the name Ebion, which shows the poverty of their thinking.
For this is what a poor man is called in the Hebrew language...
Chapter Twenty-Eight: Cerinthus, the Leader of a Heresy. We have received the tradition that in those same times Cerinthus became the leader of another heresy.
Gaius, whose words we quoted earlier, wrote about him as follows in his discussion:
"But Cerinthus too, who introduced a written account of absurd statements through revelations, as though he were a great apostle, falsely claimed, 'We learned these things from angels.'
He said that after the resurrection Christ's kingdom would be on earth, and that we would again serve bodily desires in Jerusalem.
Because he was an enemy of God's Scriptures, he wished to lead people astray by saying that there would be a wedding celebration lasting a thousand years."
Dionysius too, who was bishop of the church of Alexandria,
In the second treatise "On the Beginning" [?], he says some things about the Revelation of John, as though from the tradition of earlier times.

And he mentions this man in these words: "Cerinthus, the one who founded the heresy called Cerinthian, wanted to put a name worthy of belief on the error he had fashioned. For this was the teaching he used to give:
that the kingdom of Christ would be on earth.

He was very carnal and loved pleasures, so the things he longed for were what he dreamed it would consist of: filling the belly, that is, eating, drinking, and marriage. He also included the things he thought would make these respectable:
feasts, sacrifices, and the slaughter of animals."

This is what Dionysius said about him. Irenaeus also set out some of this man's more secret ideas in the first book Against Heresies. In his book he also recorded an account worth remembering, as from the tradition of Polycarp, who said:
“John the apostle once entered a bathhouse to bathe. But when he learned that Cerinthus was inside, he sprang from his place and fled to the door,
because he could not bear to be under the same roof as him. He urged those who were with him to do the same, saying, ‘Let us flee,
lest the bathhouse itself collapse, since Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, is inside it.’”
Twenty-ninth: On Nicolaus and on those named after him. Along with these, the heresy called that of the Nicolaitans also arose for a short time. The Revelation of John also mentions it.
These people boasted of Nicolaus, who was one of those chosen with Stephen to serve the needy.
Clement of Alexandria, in his narrative of these three [?], says this about him:

"This man had a wife who was beautiful to look at. After the ascension of our Lord he was reproached by the apostles for being jealous over her. But he brought his wife out into their midst and allowed anyone who wished to marry her. Those who have gone astray say that this act agrees with the saying they teach, that one must give the body over to be used in its pleasures. And [?] this thing that was done and the thing that was said, shamelessly and naively.
And for this reason those who are named after his heresy commit fornication without shame.
But I have learned about Nicolaus that he had no relations with any other woman

But [he had relations] only with the one woman he had married. And again, concerning his children: the daughters born to him grew old as virgins, and his son remained uncorrupted. Since this is so, it is clear that the act of giving up his wife, which took place in front of the apostles because of jealousy, was a renunciation of passion and a restraint from the eagerness of desire. For others, however, it became a pretext for indulging in the pleasures of the body.

For, as I think, he did not want to serve two masters, lust and our Lord, contrary to the command of our Saviour. They also say that Tolmai taught the same thing: that one should fight against the body and subdue it, and grant it nothing for its pleasure, but nourish the soul with faith and knowledge. These things, then, we have said about those who at that time tried to pervert the truth, and who were snuffed out quickly, as the saying goes.
Chapter 30: On the apostles who were married in the world...
Clement, whose words we have just quoted,
after the things we have already quoted, next turns to the people who reject marriage. He lists the apostles who were married in the world, and he says this: "Or do they reject even the apostles?"
For Peter and Philip had children.

Philip also gave his daughters to husbands. And Paul did not hesitate to greet his wife in one of his letters, but he did not take her around with him, so that his ministry might remain modest." Since we have mentioned these things, it is not a burden to us to also include this story by the same writer, which is worth repeating.

In the seventh book of his narratives he wrote this: "They say that when the blessed Peter saw his wife being led away to die, he rejoiced [?] at her call to grace and at her being escorted to go to the house of truth.
He spoke to her, urging and comforting her. He called her by name and said, 'Remember our Lord.'"
Such was the marriage of the blessed, and the perfect love of those dear to one another.” These things were appropriate to the subject before us,
This is how things were arranged in their times.
As for the departure of Peter and Paul from the world, when it happened, and where their bodies were laid after their departure [?], we have already spoken about these things.

Chapter 31: On the departure of John and of Philip. We have already spoken about the time of John. The place where he was laid is known from the letter that Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, wrote to Victor, bishop of Rome:
He mentions him together with Philip the apostle and his daughters, writing as follows: “In Asia, too, great lights have fallen asleep.
"who will rise on the last day, at the coming of our Lord,
when he comes in glory from heaven and searches out all his saints: Philip, one of the twelve apostles, who lies in Hierapolis,"
along with two of his daughters who grew old as virgins. Another daughter of his, who lived under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, came to rest in Ephesus.
There is also John, who reclined against our Lord’s breast, who was a priest and wore the holy crown, and was a witness and teacher.
This man died in Ephesus.

We have said these things also about how these men died. In the dialogue of Gaius, which we mentioned a little earlier, Proclus, who was debating with him, also speaks about the deaths of Philip and his daughters, saying things that agree with what we said above:
"After this there were four prophetesses, the daughters of Philip, at Hierapolis in Asia."
Their tomb is there, as is their father’s.” This is what he said. Luke, however, in the Acts of the Apostles,
mentions the daughters of another Philip, who were with their father in Caesarea in Judea at that time and had the gift of prophecy.
He speaks of them in these words: “We came to Caesarea, entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
"He had four virgin daughters who prophesied."
These are the things we have received and learned about the apostles and their times, and about the holy scriptures they left us,

about the writings that are disputed yet accepted by many, and about those that are rejected entirely and are foreign to the true faith of the apostles. This is what we have to say about them. Now let us move on to the next part of the history.

Thirty-two: How Simeon, bishop of Jerusalem, was martyred. After Nero and Domitian, in the days of Trajan, whose times we are now describing, there is a report that a persecution was stirred up against us here and there in the cities, as if from the eagerness of the populace.
In it, we have received by tradition, Simeon son of Cleophas, of whom we said that he was appointed the second bishop in the church of Jerusalem, departed from the world by martyrdom.
Hegesippus testifies to these things,

and we have used his words in many places. While he is telling about people who came from the heresies, he reports that at this time Simeon was accused by some of them of being a Christian. For many days he was tortured with all kinds of tortures,
so that the judge himself and those around him were amazed at his endurance. In the end his death was completed in the likeness of our Lord's suffering on the cross.
But nothing prevents us from hearing these things, which are told in this way, from the writer himself: that it was by some of those heretics that Simeon son of Cleophas was accused.
[He was accused] of being from the house of David and of being a Christian. He was martyred in the years of Trajan Caesar and of Atticus the consul. He was a hundred and twenty years old.

This same Hegesippus also says that at that time people descended from the royal family of the Jews were being hunted down, and so the very men who had accused Simeon were also destroyed, as being members of that family.
If one also considers the matter carefully, one finds that this Simeon was one of those who saw our Lord and heard him, taking as proof the [?] length of his life.
and because the Gospel mentions Mary the daughter of [?]. The account has already explained that he too was his son. This same writer
also indicates that other descendants of Judas, who was called our Lord’s brother, were alive during this reign.
And after the account of their first martyrdom for faith in Christ, which took place in the days of Domitian the king,
he wrote as follows: that they came and led all the churches, as martyrs and as people of the family of our Lord.
And when there was great peace in all the churches,
they lived on until Trajan Caesar, until the time when Simeon son of Clopas was denounced by heretics like those already mentioned.

in the years of Atticus the consul, after being tortured for many days, he was martyred, so that everyone was amazed, the consul himself included, at how he endured all this when he was a hundred and twenty years old. And he ordered that he be crucified. In addition to these things, this man, while giving an account of them, went on to say:
that up to that time the church remained a pure and uncorrupted virgin,
since until that time they were hiding, as if in darkness,

if there were people who wished to corrupt the sound rule of the teaching of life. But when that company of the holy apostles had departed from the whole world, and that whole generation had passed away which was counted worthy to hear the wisdom of God with its own ears,
then godless error began to establish itself through the deception of those who were altering the teaching of the truth.
Since none of the apostles remained at that time, they sought openly and boldly to proclaim falsely named knowledge in opposition to the proclamation of the truth.
At that time the persecution against us spread so widely in many places that even Pliny Secundus, a famous governor, was disturbed when he saw the great number of martyrs,
and he informed the king about the great number of people who were being killed on account of the faith.
Along with this he informed him that they had not been caught doing anything hateful or contrary to law, apart from rising at dawn and praising Christ as God.
They themselves rejected adultery, murder, and other evil offenses like these, and everything they did was in accordance with the law.

In response to this, Trajan issued a decree to this effect: that the Christian community should not be hunted down, but if they were encountered, they should be punished. By this the great force of the war of persecution that had been raised up was largely extinguished.
Yet those who wished to devise ways to harm us did not lack pretexts. Sometimes it was people from the populace,

But at times some of the judges in the provinces contrived to plot against us, so that persecution was kindled in various places without a decree of the king, and many of the faithful were martyred in contests of every kind.
[Chapter] thirty-three: How Trajan forbade that Christians be hunted down. We have taken this account from the Apology of Tertullian, whom we mentioned earlier, who wrote in Latin.
Its translation runs as follows: "Yet we have found that the search for us was prohibited.

For Pliny Secundus, governor of the province, condemned some of the Christians and removed them from their rank. He was disturbed by the great number of martyrs there were, and because he did not know what he should do,
he informed Trajan the king, saying: 'Apart from the fact that they do not wish to worship idols, I have found nothing hateful in them.'
He also informed him of this: that the Christians rise early at dawn and praise Christ as God,
and that in their teaching they command that one should refrain from murder and adultery, from fraud and robbery, and from things like these.
In response, Trajan wrote that the Christian people were not to be sought out, but if they were accused, they were to be tried.” Such, then, were these events.

Chapter thirty-four: That Evarestus became the fourth bishop in the church of Rome. In the third year of Trajan, Clement, bishop of Rome, having completed nine years in his ministry and in teaching the word of God, departed from the world and handed over his ministry to Evarestus.

Chapter thirty-five: That Justus was the third bishop in the church of Jerusalem. After Simeon too had been perfected [in martyrdom], as we said before, Justus received after him the throne of the episcopate of the church of Jerusalem.
He was one of the Jews who had believed in Christ. For at that time there were tens of thousands from among the circumcised who had believed.
In these times Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, was renowned in Asia.
He was a man who had associated with the apostles and had received his office as bishop from those who had seen and served our Lord.
In his days the bishop of the church of Hierapolis was well known. His proper name was Papias.
Chapter thirty-six: On Ignatius and his letters. Ignatius, who is famous among many to this day, was the second bishop in the church of Antioch after Peter. A story is told about him.
He was sent from Syria to the city of Rome and was devoured by wild beasts because of his testimony for Christ.
While he was travelling through Asia, he was guarded very closely by the guards who held him. In the cities he entered, he strengthened the people with words of comfort and encouragement.
Above all, he urged them first of all to be on their guard against heresies, because these had already become numerous by that time.

He asked them not to depart from the tradition of the apostles, and he thought it necessary, as a strong warning, to testify to them in writing as well. And when he came to Smyrna, where Polycarp was,
he wrote a letter to the church in Ephesus, mentioning that Onesimus was their shepherd.

and another letter to Magnesia, the city that lies beside the river Maeander, in which he also mentions that there was a bishop there named Damas; and another again to the city of Tralles, and he wrote that there was a leader there named Polybius.

Along with these he also wrote to the church of Rome. In it he pleaded with them not to ask that he be spared his martyrdom and so rob him of the hope he longed for. It is fitting that we set down a few passages from it to show what has been said.
He wrote in his own words as follows: "From Syria all the way to Rome I am fighting with beasts, on sea and on land, by night and by day."
"While I am in bonds with ten leopards, who are a band of soldiers, who, when we do them good, only do more harm."
"And by their harm I am all the more being taught."
"Yet not because of this am I justified. ... I greet the beasts that are prepared for me, and I pray that they may be found ready for me quickly, and I will coax them to devour me quickly."
"Not as with others, whom they feared and did not approach. Even if they hold back and do not want to approach me, I will go at them by force. Know this of me, from my own self:"
"I know what is good for me. Now I am beginning to be a disciple."

"Let nothing among things seen and things unseen begrudge me attaining to Jesus Christ. Fire and cross, and packs of beasts, and scattering of bones, and cutting off of limbs, and destruction of the whole body, and the torture of Satan: let them all come upon me,"
"if only I may attain to Jesus Christ." He wrote these letters from the city we have mentioned to the churches we have listed.
When they had passed beyond Smyrna, he wrote again from Troas to those in Philadelphia and to the church of Smyrna,
and in particular to Polycarp, the bishop there, whom he knew to be an apostolic man.
As a good and true shepherd, he entrusted to him his flock in Antioch and urged him to take diligent care of it. And when he wrote to those in Smyrna, he used these words, from where I do not know:
He spoke this way about Christ: “Even after his resurrection, I know him in the flesh, and I testify and believe that he is so.
And when he came to Peter and his companions, he said to them, ‘Come, touch me and see that I am not a bodiless spirit.’

"And they came at me all at once," and they believed [?]. Irenaeus also knew of his martyrdom. He mentions his letters and says this: "As one of ours said, who was condemned to be thrown to the beasts because of his witness to God:"
"I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of beasts so that I may be found pure bread."
Polycarp also mentions these things in the letter he wrote to the Philippians, in these words:
"I ask all of you to be persuaded and to stand firm in all the endurance that you saw with your own eyes, not only in the blessed Ignatius, Rufus and Zosimus,
but also in others who came from among you, and in Paul himself and the rest of the apostles, being convinced that all these did not run in vain."
but in faith and righteousness. And now they are in the place that was their due, with our Lord, with whom they suffered.
For they did not love this, but Jesus, who died for us and rose from the dead for our sake.” And afterward he said:
“You and Ignatius wrote to me that if anyone goes to Syria, he should also take your letters.
I will do this if I have a suitable opportunity, either myself or through someone whom I send to serve as a messenger on your behalf as well.
The letters sent to us by Ignatius, and the other letters that we have here with us, we have sent to you, as you instructed us.
They are appended below to this letter, and you can benefit greatly from them.
For they contain faith, endurance, and every kind of instruction needed for reverence toward our Lord.”
Such were the events concerning Ignatius. After him, Heros assumed the bishopric of Antioch.

Chapter thirty-seven: On the evangelists who were prominent up to that time. Among those who were prominent in the days of these men was Quadratus, together with the daughters of Philip, of whom it is said that they had the gift of prophecy.
There were also many others who were well known in those days, who held the first rank in the succession from the apostles.
Such, then, were these disciples who were worthy of God. They were building on the foundations that had been laid by the apostles in every place, and they were greatly increasing the preaching.
And the seed of life of the kingdom of heaven throughout the whole world

they were sowing abundantly. For many of the disciples of that time, through the abundance of their love and fear of Christ, were raising up their souls by the word of God. And first they were fulfilling the commandment of our Savior,
and were distributing their possessions to the needy, and afterwards they travelled through the countries.
And they carried out the work of evangelists, preaching the word of faith, and they handed over to them the holy books of the Gospel. These foundations of faith they were laying in distant countries.
and appointed others as shepherds, entrusting them with the care of those who had first become disciples.
Then they would turn to other countries and peoples, with the grace and help of God, because even at that time the Spirit of God was working wondrous powers through their hands.
so that, from their very first hearing, great numbers of people suddenly received the fear of God anew into their souls.
But since it is not possible for us to list by name all those who received the first succession from the apostles, who became shepherds and evangelists in all the churches throughout the whole world,
we record by name in writing only those whose tradition of the teaching of the apostles has come down to us until now through their writings,
such as Ignatius, in the letters that we have listed.
Thirty-eighth [chapter]: On the letters of Clement, and on the books that are falsely said to be his. And of Clement, in the letter that he wrote, which everyone acknowledges,
which he wrote as from the church of Rome to the church of Corinth. In it he included many thoughts of understanding from the Letter to the Hebrews.
Moreover, he also wrote words in the same form in which they are stated in it,
He clearly showed that this Letter to the Hebrews had not been written recently. For this reason it was rightly counted among the apostle’s other letters.
For the apostle wrote to the Hebrews and addressed them in their ancestral language. Some say that Luke the evangelist translated it,
And some say that it was this Clement.

This seems to be true, because this Letter to the Hebrews and his own letter share the same style of language, and the ideas in the two are not far from each other. It should also be known that a second letter is said to be Clement's. We do not, however, simply decide that it is his, as we do with the first, because we do not know that even the ancients used it.
Recently, some people have also brought forward another very lengthy book as though it were his. It contains a debate between Peter and Apion.
Not one of the ancients mentions it at all, for it does not even resemble the pure and true teaching of the apostles.
The writing of Clement that everyone accepts is well known. We have also spoken of the writings of Ignatius and of Polycarp...
Chapter Thirty-Nine. On the treatises of Papias. Papias has five treatises, bearing the title “Exposition of the Sayings of Our Lord.”
Irenaeus mentions these, saying that he wrote only these, and he spoke thus: "These things also Papias said, who had heard from John himself,
and who was a companion of Polycarp and was an ancient man. And he testifies in writing at the beginning [?] of his books."
For five books are attributed to him. These things Irenaeus said about him.
But Papias himself, at the beginning of his account, did not indicate that he had heard the holy apostles or seen them.
That he received the substance [?] of the faith from those who knew the apostles, he teaches in these words that he said:
"I will not hesitate," he says, "to set down for you, along with these interpretations, also the things that I learned well from the elders,
and that I remember well, and I testify to their truth. For I did not take pleasure, as the many do, in those who say many things, but in those who teach the truth.
nor in those who recount the commands of outsiders, but in those who handed down what was given by our Lord for faith
and was conveyed and came from the truth itself. And whenever anyone came who had followed the elders, I would inquire into the elders’ words: what Andrew said,
or what Peter said, or what Philip, Thomas, James, John, or Matthew said,
Or one of the other disciples of our Lord, or what Aristion or John the Elder [say].
For I did not suppose that I could profit as much from their books as from a living and abiding voice."
Here we need to observe that he counts the name of John twice. He reckons the first with Peter, James, Matthew, and the rest of the apostles, clearly indicating the Evangelist.

But the other John he distinguishes in his account and places him separately from that number of the apostles, and he places Aristion before him and plainly calls him an elder, so that from these things he might show concerning the account that it is true, that of those who said [?]
...that there were two men in Asia who were called by the same name. Their tombs are in Ephesus, and to this day both are called John. We should keep this in mind.
As for the Revelation that is called John's: if anyone does not accept that it is by John the Evangelist, it is likely that it was seen by this other John.

This Papias, about whom we are now informing you, admits that he received the words of the apostles from those who had followed them, and from Aristion and from John the Elder. For he says that he heard them himself.
He mentions them by name many times, and in his writings he set down the tradition he received from them.
We have not said these things to no purpose.
But it is fitting to add to these words of Papias that we have quoted other words of his, in which wonders are related, along with other things that he received from tradition.
We have already made known that Philip lived in Hierapolis with his daughters.
Now we explain that Papias himself lived in their days and mentions accounts of miracles that he received from Philip’s daughters.
For he relates that a dead person rose in his days. He also relates another miracle concerning Justus, who was called Bar-Shealt [?]:
They say that he drank a deadly poison, but because of the grace of our Lord nothing harmful happened to him.
After our Savior's ascension, they put this Justus forward, together with Matthias, to take Judas's place in his ministry. The Acts of the Apostles tells it this way:
"They put forward two."
Joseph, who was called Bar Sha'lat [?], who was surnamed Justus, and Tolmai; and they prayed.
This man also wrote other things that he received as if from unwritten tradition: certain strange parables of our Saviour and his teaching, and also other tales.
Among these he also says that there will be a thousand years after [?] the earth.
But I think that the narratives of the apostles that he received, which they had spoken figuratively, in mysteries,
I think he took these things the wrong way, because he did not look into them according to their meaning. Judging from his own words, he seems to have been a man of very limited understanding.
Even so, for those who came after him, a great many members of the church, he became the reason they held this opinion.
since they respected his antiquity, as Irenaeus did,

and anyone else who holds such an opinion. In his book he also set down other interpretations by Aristion of the words of our Lord, as well as the tradition of John the Elder. To his words we will add the tradition that he wrote about Mark the evangelist, in which he set down these things [?]: 'The Elder used to say this:'
'Mark,' he says, 'became Peter's interpreter.'

'He wrote down accurately what he remembered of the things spoken or done by our Lord, but not in order. For he neither heard our Lord nor followed him. Later, however, as I said, he followed Peter, who used to give his teaching as the need arose.'
"But he did not set out our Lord's words in order. So Mark made no mistake in writing some things as he remembered them, for he had only one concern:"
"to leave out nothing of what he had heard and not to falsify any of it." This is what Papias reported about Mark. About Matthew he said this:
'Matthew,' he says, 'wrote a gospel in the Hebrew language, and each person translated it as well as he could.'
This Papias also used testimonies from the epistles of John and of Peter. He also wrote a story about a woman
who had been accused of many sins at the time when our Lord was in the world. This story is written in the Gospel of the Hebrews.
It was necessary to set down these things together with those we mentioned earlier.
The third book of the History of the Church is finished.
The fourth book of the History of the Church.
Chapter One. Who the bishops in Rome and Alexandria were during Trajan’s reign.
/ Second: what the Jews suffered in the days of Trajan.
/ Third: which men 'went out in spirit' [?] on behalf of the faith in the days of Hadrian.
Fourth: On the bishops who were in Rome and also in Alexandria in the days of Hadrian.
Fifth: On the bishops who were in Jerusalem from our Lord up to these times.
Sixth: On the last destruction of the Jews, which took place in the years of Hadrian.
Seventh: Who were, in those early times, the leaders of the teaching of false knowledge.
Eighth: Which writers there were among the children of the church.
Chapter 9: Hadrian’s letter, which he wrote ordering that Christians should not be persecuted without a trial.
Chapter 10: Who were bishops in Rome and Alexandria during the reign of Antoninus.
Chapter 11: On the leaders of heresy who lived in those days. Chapter 12: On the defense that Justin wrote to Antoninus.
Thirteenth: On the letter of Antoninus which he wrote to all Asia concerning our teaching.
Fourteenth: How there is a record of the acquaintances of the apostle.
Fifteenth: How in the years of Verus Polycarp was martyred, together with others, in the city of Smyrna.
Sixteenth: How Justin the philosopher was martyred while proclaiming the word of Christ in Rome.
/ Seventeenth: On the martyrs whom Justin mentions in his treatise.
/ Eighteenth: On the treatises of Justin that have come down to us. / Nineteenth: On the bishops who held office in Rome and Alexandria in the days of Verus...
Chapter 20: Who were bishops in Antioch.
Chapter 21: On the writers belonging to the church who were renowned in those times. Chapter 22: On Hegesippus and the people he mentions.
Twenty-third:
On Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, and on the letters that he wrote.
Twenty-fourth: On Theophilus, bishop of Antioch,
and on Philip, and on Modestus,
and on Melito, and on those whom he mentioned;
and on Apollinaris, and on Musanus. / Twenty-fifth: On the heresy of Tatian. / Twenty-sixth.
On Bardaisan the Syrian and his writings.
Chapter one: Which bishops were in Rome and in Alexandria in the reign of Trajan.
In the twelfth year of Trajan's reign, Cerdo, bishop of the church of Alexandria, of whom we spoke a little earlier, departed this world.
Primus took over the ministry there. He was the fourth bishop in succession from the apostles.
At this time, when Evaristus had completed eight years as bishop of Rome, Alexander, the fifth in succession from Peter and Paul, took office after him.

Second: What the Jews suffered in the days of Trajan. The growth of the teaching of our Savior and of his church was increasing and growing strong every day. The oppression of the Jews by evils of every kind was also growing stronger. For when the emperor reached his eighteenth year,
the disturbance of the Jews was stirred up again, and a great multitude of them perished. For in Alexandria and in all Egypt and in Cyrene, as though driven by an evil spirit of sedition,

And they rose up in fury against the gentiles who lived among them. They stirred up a great riot, and the next year they fought a major war. At that time Lupus was governor of all Egypt. In the first battle they fought, they happened to defeat the gentiles, who fled and took refuge in Alexandria.
These seized all the Jews who were in the city and killed them. But when the Jews in the region of Cyrene lost the help of these...
they pursued the Gentiles in Egypt and undermined its laws. Their leader was Lucuas.
The emperor sent Marcius the tribune with a force of infantry in ships, and also some cavalry.
For a long time he engaged in many battles in the war against them, and killed many tens of thousands of Jews,
not only those from Cyrene, but also those in Egypt who were supporting Lucuas their king. The emperor, however, supposed
that the Jews there in Mesopotamia were likewise rising against the inhabitants of the country, and ordered Lusius Quietus
[?] to destroy them from that province. He then attacked them and killed a great multitude of them. And because of this victory that he achieved, the emperor appointed him governor over Judea.
The writers among the Gentiles who lived at that time also recorded these things in their writings.
Third: On the men who made defences of the faith in the days of Hadrian. Trajan held the empire for six months short of twenty years, and Aelius Hadrian succeeded him.

Quadratus wrote a discourse of defence to this man and presented it to him on behalf of our faith, because certain wicked men were trying to trouble our people. This discourse is still in the hands of many of the brethren to this day, and in ours as well.
From it we can see clear proofs of this man's understanding and of the straightforwardness of the faith of the apostles.
He also shows how early he lived, in these words, which run as follows:
"The works of our Saviour were always present, for they were real: those who were healed and those who rose from the dead. Not only were they seen being healed and being raised [?],

but they were also always present. This was true not only while our Saviour was in the world. Even after he departed from the world they were present for a long time, so that some of them have lived on even to our own times." This is what he said.
Aristides too, a faithful man of our teaching, made a defence on behalf of the faith as Quadratus did, and presented it to Hadrian.
His writing also is still found today in the hands of many.

Fourth: On the bishops who were in Rome and in Alexandria in the days of Hadrian. In the third year of Hadrian's reign, Alexander, bishop of Rome, died after completing ten years in his office, and Xystus succeeded him.
In the church of Alexandria, Primus departed from the world after completing twelve years, and Justus succeeded him as bishop.

Fifth: On the bishops who were in Jerusalem from our Lord until these times. As for the bishops who were in Jerusalem, I have not found the dates of their years [?] in writing. It is said, however, that each of them held office for a very short time.
But I have learned this from written sources: until the last destruction, which took place in the days of Hadrian, there was a succession of fifteen bishops there.

All of them were Hebrews, who from the beginning had sincerely received the knowledge of Christ. Those of them who were worthy of the office of bishop were chosen by people who were able to judge such matters.

At that time the whole church there was made up of Hebrew believers. This was so from the days of the apostles until the last destruction, when the Jews rebelled against the Romans and were destroyed in great battles. Because the bishops from the circumcision came to an end at that time,
And it is fitting [?] that we should now list them in order, starting from that first one.

Now there was James, who was called the brother of our Lord... the second, Simeon; the third, Justus; the fourth, Zacchaeus; the fifth, Tobias; the sixth, Benjamin;... the seventh, John;... the eighth, Matthew.
The ninth was Philip... The tenth was Seneca. The eleventh was Justus. The twelfth was Levi. The thirteenth was Ephraim. The fourteenth was Joseph.
And the last of them all, the fifteenth, was Judas. All these were bishops in the church of Jerusalem from the apostles down to this time, and all of them were from among the circumcised.
In the twelfth year of Hadrian's reign, after Xystus had completed ten years as bishop of Rome, Telesphorus succeeded him. Telesphorus was the seventh in the succession from the apostles.
A year and a few months later, Eumenes became the sixth bishop of the church of Alexandria, after his predecessor had completed eleven years.

Sixth: On the last destruction of the Jews in the years of Hadrian. When the Jews' rebellion became great and strong, Rufus, the governor of Judea, together with the army the emperor had sent to help him,
dealt with their reckless defiance by merciless punishment. He destroyed tens of thousands of men, women and children alike, and under the law of war he seized their lands.
At that time the Jews had a leader called Bar Kokhba ("son of the star"). In other respects he was a murderer and a bandit.
He boasted on account of his name, as though a saviour had shone forth for them from heaven,
as for the oppressed and the captives. When the war grew fierce in the eighteenth year of his reign, there was a small city near the land [?], and it was very strongly fortified.
not very far from Jerusalem, and the Jews rebelled there. The war surrounded it from outside for a long time, and those rebels perished from hunger and thirst.
The man who had caused them to rebel received the punishment he deserved. Because of this, the entire Jewish people were barred altogether from setting foot in the area around Jerusalem,
As if by a law and command, Hadrian ordered that they should not even look upon the land of their fathers from a distant mountain. Aristo of the city of Pella has recorded these things.
Jerusalem was completely emptied of all the Jews who had lived there before. It was rebuilt as a different city by the Romans and was settled by foreign peoples:
In honour of the man who held the kingship, Aelius Hadrian, the city was called Aelia. The church there was also gathered from the Gentiles, after those bishops who had been of the circumcision.
The first to receive the bishopric there was Mark. [?]
For these seven were, in those times, the leaders of the teaching of the knowledge of the truth. Now while the churches throughout the whole world were shining like bright stars,
and faith in our Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, was flourishing among the whole race of humankind, Satan, who hates what is good and is the enemy of the truth,
and who is at all times the adversary of human life, was scheming against the church in every place.
For through every change of fortune in former times, he had armed himself against it by means of persecution through foreigners.

But when he was cut off from these, he made use of wicked men and sorcerers as instruments that destroy souls and as ministers of perdition. He armed himself with other crafts and tried by every means,
that sorcerers and deceivers too should take on the name of Christianity, and that those of the believers who came to resemble them
would be drawn down into the pit of destruction, and that those who had not yet come to the faith would be turned back by their wicked conduct, so that they would not come near the word of life.
Now Menander, of whom we said a little earlier that he succeeded Simon, first appeared as an alien power in the form of a serpent with two heads [?], through two leaders of two heresies who arose.
Saturninus, who was an Antiochene by race, and Basilides the Alexandrian, one in Syria and the other in Egypt, established the teaching of a heresy hateful to God.

Saturninus, like Menander, spoke lies in many things, as Irenaeus showed. But Basilides, under the pretext of something ineffable, stretched his devices out without limit, for he invented impious and foolish fables for his heresy.

At that time there were many men among the members of the church who were contending for the truth, and who were wisely fighting on behalf of the faith that the apostles had established in the church.
Many also left warnings in writing, for those who came after them, against these heresies we have spoken of.

We ourselves have seen a powerful refuting discourse against them, which Agrippa Castor, one of the well-known writers of that time, composed against Basilides, exposing the wickedness of his error. When he revealed his secrets, he said of him
that he had written twenty-four books against the Gospel, and that he named for himself the prophets Barcabbas and Barcoph
and other barbarous names that do not exist, so as to astonish those who are swayed by such things.

He taught that they should eat what had been sacrificed without making any distinction, and that in time of persecution they should deny the faith without scruple. And like the Pythagoreans, he commanded those who came to him to keep silent for five hours [?]. He said other things like these about him, about Basilides. Irenaeus too fully and openly exposed this heresy.
Irenaeus also writes about another heresy, which was called that of the Gnostics,

saying that these people did not conceal the sorcery of Simon the way he had, but practised it openly. They boasted, as if of something great, of the things they did by sorcery to produce love charms.
dream visions, the constant presence of demons with them, and other similar things.
And so they teach that those who are initiated into their mysteries must commit every abomination, that is, by means of their own foulness,
for otherwise, as they say, they cannot escape from the archons of the world

unless they have paid them their dues through foul and unspeakable acts. Satan, who delights in evil, made use of these servants of evil. Those who were led astray by them were miserably taken captive to destruction, and the Gentiles who had not yet believed were taken captive as well.
Because of these people, the Gentiles who had not yet believed were given great occasion to blaspheme the word of God,
since these people went about under the name of Christianity. Because of these apostles of falsehood, it happened that a godless suspicion grew strong against us:
that we have unlawful intercourse with our mothers and our sisters, as if married to them, and that we defile ourselves with unclean foods. But these things were not allowed to go on for long.
For the truth itself stood firm and showed its light after a short time. The schemes of the enemies were exposed by their own deeds, and they were quickly extinguished.
for the heresies kept changing and being renewed,

while the earlier ones were coming to an end, and from time to time they were corrupted into every form and every likeness. But the glory of the truth of the church grew and became truly strong, continuing without change. It alone everywhere lives in chastity, purity and freedom.
and for the purity and holiness of its way of life and of the wisdom of God. It was shining over the whole race of humankind, among Greeks and barbarians.
In time, that slander against the whole Christian people also died away, and our teaching endured, alone victorious and acknowledged by everyone
as glorious in the commandments of chastity and holiness of the wisdom of God. No one dared to say a filthy word against our faith
or to be suspected of slandering any of our people. .:. .:. .:.
so that [?] those who had been slanderers from the members [?] of the church. But in those same times the truth brought forward many who contended on its behalf.
They refuted those heresies and contended against them,
not only with unwritten arguments but also with written demonstrations.
Among these people in those times, Hegesippus was well known. We have already made much use of his words, and we have set down from his tradition a few things about the apostles.
In five books, then, he recorded in simple words the unerring tradition of the apostles' preaching.
He gave information about those who had been set up as idols in earlier times and in his own time. He wrote as follows: "Those for whom they made tombs and temples, as they still do even to this day.
One of them is Antinous, the slave of Hadrian Caesar, in whose honour games are also held. This Antinous lived in our own days.
For Hadrian also built a city named after him, Antino[?]."
In his days there also lived Justin, a lover of true wisdom, who at that time was still occupied with the philosophy of the Greeks.

At this time he also gives information about him in the apology that he wrote to Antoninus. He wrote as follows: "It is not out of place," he says, "to mention along with these things Antinous as well, who lived recently."
This man, whom everyone is eager to worship with reverence as God, although they know who he is and where he comes from.
This same writer also mentions the Jewish war at that time and writes as follows: “Also in the war involving the Jews,
