"For Bar Kokhba," he says, "who was the leader of the Jewish revolt, ordered that Christians be brought to bitter punishments [?] if they would not deny and blaspheme Jesus Christ." He also spoke about himself:
how he turned from the wisdom of the Greeks to the fear of our Lord, and how he did this with reflection and judgment. To show this, he wrote:
"For I too," he says, "used to delight in the teaching of Plato. I heard the Christians being slandered,
but I saw that they did not fear death, nor anything that is thought to be fearful.

So I reasoned in my mind that it was impossible for them to be living in wickedness and lusts. For who is there that loves lusts and lacks [?] self-restraint, or who accepts the eating of human flesh,

and could still consider death a good thing, when death deprives him of his lusts? Rather, such a person would try by every means to go on living in this world always, supporting himself, and to escape the notice of the judges. He would not give himself up so that they could kill him..."
Chapter Nine. The letter Hadrian wrote ordering that Christians should not be persecuted without a trial. Justin himself also relates
that Hadrian received a letter about the Christians from the distinguished governor Serennius Granianus, who had written to him
"...It was not just that, without any charge, someone should do favours to please the clamour of the people and put them to death unjustly." In response to these things the king wrote
to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia. He ordered that no one should be put to death without a charge and a just prosecution.
He included a copy of this letter, writing it in the Latin language as it originally stood.
Before it he says the following: “On the basis of the letters of the great and renowned emperor Hadrian, your father,

We could have demanded of you, as we are asking, that you order a trial to take place. We do not ask this on the grounds that Hadrian ordered it. Rather, we are convinced from this that our request is just. We have also set down a copy of Hadrian's letter.

so that from it you too may know that we are speaking the truth." This man included the letter in Latin, as its copy stood. We have rendered it into the Greek language as well as we could. It reads as follows:
"To Minucius Fundanus. I have received a letter written to me by Serennius Granianus, a most distinguished man, whom you have succeeded.
Therefore I do not wish the matter to be left uninvestigated, so that people are not troubled either.

Nor should an opening for mischief be given to the informers. So, plainly, regarding this petition with which the people of the provinces petition that the Christians be put to death: if they are able to show a deed against them that deserves death, let them be heard on this ground alone.
But let him not listen to petitions or to mere outcries alone.
For it is entirely right that, if anyone wishes to accuse them, you should judge the case.
But if anyone accuses them and shows that they are acting contrary to the law, issue your ruling according to the seriousness of the offense.
And I charge you by Hercules: if anyone does this maliciously, take care to judge the matter and turn the penalty for his wickedness back upon him...
Chapter Ten. Who were the bishops in Rome and Alexandria during the reign of Antoninus.
After Hadrian had ruled the empire for twenty-one years and died, Antoninus, who was called Pius, received the empire of the Romans after him. And in the first year of his reign,
Telesphorus, having completed eleven years in his ministry, departed from the world, and Hyginus received the bishopric of Rome after him.
Irenaeus relates about Telesphorus that his departure from the world was made glorious by martyrdom.
Eleventh: On the leaders of the heresies that existed in those days. Irenaeus also reports that in the days of Hyginus, the bishop of Rome of whom we have spoken, Valentinus introduced his heresy.
And Cerdon was the founder of the error of Marcion's followers. Both of them became known in Rome at that time. He writes as follows:
"Valentinus came to Rome in the days of Hyginus, and his error grew strong in the days of Pius.

And he remained until the days of Anicetus. Cerdon, who came before Marcion, also came to the church in the days of Hyginus, who was the ninth bishop, and confessed that he had gone astray. And he kept doing this continually: at times he taught in secret, and at other times he confessed his error again; and at times he was rebuked for the things he wickedly taught and was separated from the assembly of the brethren.
He said these things in the third book Against Heresies.
And in the first book he also said this about Cerdon: "Cerdon," he says, "who took his starting points from those of the school of Simon, came to Rome in the years of Hyginus.
who was the ninth bishop in the succession from the apostles. He taught
that the God proclaimed by the Law and the Prophets is not the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
For the former, he said, is known, but the latter is unknown; and the former is [?], but the latter is good.

And Marcion received this teaching from him and enlarged it, and he blasphemed shamelessly." This same Irenaeus, with great vigor of spirit, exposed the unfathomable depth of the error of Valentinus, which was lurking and hidden in its holes like a venomous reptile.
And along with these he also spoke of another, named Marcus, who he said lived among them in those times and was trained in the art of sorcery.
He also wrote about and exposed the deeds of their impious mysteries in these [?].

For some of them, he says, prepare a bridal chamber, and perform the mysteries of their rites with words that they recite over them, over those [being initiated], and they call the thing they perform a spiritual marriage.
in the manner of those mixers mentioned above.

And others bring them to the water and baptize them, and say over them as follows: "In the name of the Father of all, who is unknown; and in the name of Truth, the Mother of all; and in the name of him who descended upon Jesus."
Others pronounce Hebrew names, in order to greatly astonish those who are being initiated into their mysteries."
After Hyginus had completed four years in the bishopric, Pius received the ministry of the bishopric of Rome.
In Alexandria Mark became shepherd, after Eumenes had completed thirteen years.
And when Mark had completed ten years in his ministry and gone to his rest, Celadion received the ministry of the church of Alexandria after him. And again, in the church of Rome:
after fifteen years of his bishopric, Pius departed from the world, and Anicetus was appointed there.
In his days, Hegesippus relates, he came to Rome and stayed there until the bishopric of Eleutherus.

Twelfth: On the defense that Justin wrote to Antoninus. Justin was especially strong in those times. While he wore the garb of philosophy, he preached the word of God, and in the treatises he wrote he fought on behalf of the faith.
In the work he wrote against Marcion, he mentions that Marcion himself was still alive at the time he composed it.

And he said this: "And Marcion of Pontus, who is still living even now, teaches those who are persuaded by him to believe that there is a God greater than the Creator. And this man, in every place [?]"
With the help of the demons who were assisting him, he persuaded many people to speak blasphemy and to deny
that the Maker of all is the Father of Christ, and to confess that there is another who is greater than he.

And all who have come from these are, as I said, called Christians, in the same way that the name of philosophy is shared by the philosophers even though their teachings do not agree with one another. And after these things he adds and says:
"We have," he says, "treatises against all the heresies that have existed.
If you wish to read them, we will give them to you." Now this Justin

He also earnestly wrote a treatise against the pagans. And again, other [writings], in which he speaks with boldness of spirit on behalf of our faith, to the emperor Antoninus, who was called [?]. He also wrote to the senate of Rome, for he was living in Rome. And in the boldness of spirit with which he wrote, he shows who he is and where he comes from, in these words: "To the Emperor Titus
Aelius Hadrian
Antoninus Pius Caesar Augustus, and to Verissimus his son, the philosopher, and to Lucius, the son of Caesar, and to the whole senate.
and to the whole Roman people, on behalf of those from every race of humanity who are unjustly hated and wronged:
I, Justin, son of Priscus, son of Bacchius, from Neapolis in Palestine, present this petition and supplication to you.”

Chapter thirteen: The letter of Antoninus that he wrote to all Asia concerning our teaching. When others also brought petitions to the emperor Antoninus, saying that throughout Asia the Christians were being oppressed by the people of the towns with every kind of contempt, he issued the following edict throughout all Asia:
"The Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, to all Asia, greeting.
I know that the gods also take care that people like these do not escape notice.
For they punish those who do not wish to worship them much more than you do.
For by stirring up disturbances against them, you confirm the opinion they hold, when you accuse them of having no God.
But because of the very thing they are accused of, they choose to die for their God rather than to live.
Therefore they also win, since they give up their lives

rather than submit to what you are trying to persuade them to do. As for the earthquakes that have happened and are still happening, it is right that we remind you, since you are dismayed whenever they happen, to compare our conduct with theirs. They have more confidence before God than we do. But you, for the whole time that you are in error,
also despise the other gods and neglect the worship of the Immortal One, so that you drive out the Christians who worship him and persecute them even to death.
Many governors in the provinces also wrote to my father about these matters.

He wrote back to them that no one should trouble such people in any way, unless they are found to be attempting something against the rule of the Romans. Many have also informed me about these matters.
I too have written in agreement with my father's opinion.
But if anyone persists in this intention and brings any of these people to court, saying that this person is such, then let the accused be released from blame,
even if he turns out to be what he is said to be, and let the one who accuses him be held guilty." This edict was published throughout all Asia.
Melito, who was bishop of the church in the city of Sardis, testifies that these things happened in this way.
He was well known at that time for the defense he addressed to Emperor Verus on behalf of our faith.
Chapter fourteen: How there is a record of the disciples of the apostle. In the days of this Anicetus, who we said was bishop of the church of Rome, Irenaeus relates
that Polycarp was still alive in the world and came to Rome, because he had a question to discuss with Anicetus about the day of Passover.
And Irenaeus also gives another account about Polycarp, which it is also fitting to add to what is said about him.
It is written as follows in the third book that Irenaeus composed against heresies:
“Polycarp,” he says, “was not only taught by apostles and associated with many who had seen our Lord,
but was also appointed by the apostles themselves as bishop of the church in Smyrna in Asia. We too saw him in our youth.

He remained in the world for a very long time and lived to a great age. He was martyred gloriously and famously, and so departed from the world. He constantly taught these things, which alone are true.
All the churches in Asia bear witness to these things, as do those who to this day have held the succession from Polycarp. For he was far superior, a faithful witness to the truth,

And further, against Valentinus and Marcion and the rest of the corrupters of minds. And when he came to Rome in the days of Anicetus, he turned many of these heretics we have spoken about to the church of God.
And he taught and proclaimed that this was the only truth he had received from the apostles.
the truth that the church hands down. Some people heard him say that John, the disciple of our Lord, once went to bathe in Ephesus
and saw Cerinthus inside. He leapt out of the bathhouse without bathing and said, "Let us flee, or even the bathhouse may fall on us, because Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, is inside it."
Marcion himself also once came face to face with Polycarp and said to him, "Recognize us." Polycarp replied, "I recognize you: you are the firstborn of Satan."
The apostles and their disciples were this careful. They would not share so much as a word with anyone who perverted the truth.

As Paul also said: "As for a man whose mind is divided by another teaching, after one warning and a second, have nothing more to do with him. You know that such a person is perverse and sins, and condemns himself to guilt."

There is also a well-known letter of Polycarp, which he wrote to the Philippians. Those of us who want to, and who care about our life, can learn from it the pattern of the faith and the preaching of the truth. Irenaeus said these things.
Polycarp himself, in this letter that he wrote to the Philippians, which survives to this day, drew testimony from the first letter of Peter.

Fifteenth [chapter]: How Polycarp was martyred, along with others, in the city of Smyrna in the years of Verus. Antoninus, who was called Eusebes (Pius), ruled the empire for twenty-two years. After him his son Marcus Aurelius Verus Antoninus, together with his brother Lucius, succeeded to it.

At this time there was a great disturbance of persecution in Asia, and Polycarp was crowned with martyrdom. It is fitting that we include in the record of this history the written account of his martyrdom, which has been preserved to this day. It is written,
that document, as if in the person of the church he governed, to the churches in Pontus, and it reports these things in the following words:
The church of God, to those in Philomelium and to all the congregations of the holy church in every place:
May grace, peace and love from God the Father and from our Lord Jesus Christ be multiplied.
Brothers, we are writing to you about those who were martyred, and also about the blessed Polycarp, who by his martyrdom put a seal on the persecution and brought it to an end.
After these things, before the account of Polycarp, they tell about other martyrs and have recorded in writing what endurance they showed in their sufferings.
so that those who stood around and watched them were amazed, because at times they were torn by scourgings down to the inner veins.
so that even their internal organs could be seen. At other times, sharp sea shells were spread beneath them,
And they subjected them to every kind of torture and scourging,

and in the end they were given as food to the wild beasts. They tell that the most excellent Germanicus was especially victorious. For he was strengthened by the grace of God and overcame the fear of death that is natural to the body. And when the proconsul wished to persuade him:
and put his age before him, saying to him, "You are a youth, a young man; have pity on yourself."

But he did not falter. Instead, he gladly brought the beast toward himself, not only by provoking it but also by force, so that he might be released quickly from this world of injustice and wickedness.
The whole crowd was amazed at his glorious death and at the courage of this martyr, beloved of God,
and at the steadfastness of the whole Christian people. The crowd had been silent, but now they began to shout, "Away with the godless! Let Polycarp be sought!"
While there was a great uproar at their shouting, a man named Quintus, a Phrygian by birth, who had recently come from Phrygia,
When he stood and saw the beasts and how fierce they were, he was afraid and lost heart.

And in the end he gave way for the sake of his life. This writing shows the matter: this man had been rash, and it was not out of the fear of our Lord that he threw himself into the trial with the others.
But when this man was lost, he left everyone a plain lesson: no one should rashly throw himself into such things without the fear of our Lord. And the outcome of these things was as follows.
When the admirable Polycarp first heard about this, he remained untroubled and kept his mind steady and unshaken.
He wanted to remain in the city itself. But when those who were with him asked him to go out to a farm a short distance from the city, he agreed.
He was there with a few people, and he did nothing else, by night or by day, except persist in prayers to our Lord. In them he asked and pleaded,
and he prayed that there would be peace for all the churches throughout the whole world.

For he faithfully kept this practice. And while he was praying, three days before he was handed over, he saw a vision in the night: the pillow under his head suddenly caught fire, and the fire consumed it.
When he woke from this, he immediately interpreted the vision, and he plainly foretold to those who were with him what was about to happen:

"For the sake of Christ I will depart from the world by fire." Since those who were looking for him were pressing hard with great eagerness, the brothers, out of love, again urged him to move to another farm.
A little later, those who were searching for him caught up with him there. The love of the brothers again compelled him to move to another farm.

After a little while his pursuers overtook him there. They seized two boys from there and beat one of them, and they took them and stationed them at Polycarp's lodging. When they overtook him there in the evening, they found him lying down in an upper room.
Although he could have moved from there to another house, he did not want to. Instead, he said, “Let God’s will be done.”

When he learned that they had arrived, as the saying goes, he went down to them and spoke with them with a calm and cheerful face. To those who did not know him, it seemed that they were seeing a wonder
as they looked at his great age and at the modesty and composure of his face, and they wondered whether there was any need to be so eager to arrest such an old man.
But he immediately ordered that a table be set for them and prepared plenty of food for them. He asked them for one hour so that he could pray in peace. When they allowed him,
He stood and prayed, filled with the grace of our Lord, so that those who had come were amazed.
And they heard him as he prayed, and many of them were grieved in their souls that such a man was about to die,

an old man, chaste and pleasing to God. Along with these things, the written account of his story further shows the following: that after he had remembered everyone in his prayer, even those whom he had never known,
small and great, honored and lowly, and the whole church throughout the world, and then he finished his prayer.
When the time came for them to leave, they set him on a donkey and brought him into the city. It was a great Sabbath.
Herod the irenarch and his father Nicetes met him. They had him sit with them in the carriage.
As they sat with him, they tried to persuade him, saying, “What harm is there in saying, ‘Caesar is my lord,’ and offering sacrifice and staying alive?”
At first he did not answer them a word. But when they kept pressing him, he said to them,
"I will not do what you advise me." When they saw that they could not persuade him, they spoke abusive words to him and suddenly threw him from the carriage.
As he got down, his shin was injured. But he did not turn back. As if nothing had happened to him, he went on gladly and eagerly, and they brought him to the stadium.
There was a great uproar in the stadium, so that many people could not even hear that Polycarp had entered it. As he was entering, a voice came from heaven: "Be strong and be courageous, Polycarp!"
But no one saw the one who said this.

Many of our people heard the voice. When they brought him forward, there was a great commotion, because people heard that Polycarp had been arrested. When he came near, the proconsul asked him whether he was Polycarp.

When he confirmed it, the proconsul tried to persuade him to deny Christ, saying to him, "Have respect for your old age," along with other such things that they usually say. He said to him, "Swear by the fortune of Caesar, and repent.
Say, 'Away with the godless!'"
But Polycarp, with a stern [?] face, looked at all the people in the stadium and waved his hand at them. He sighed, looked up to heaven, and said, "Away with the godless!"
When the judge pressed him and said to him, "Swear, and I will release you; revile Christ," Polycarp said to him:
"For eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong in anything. How can I blaspheme my King, who saved me?"
When he pressed him again and said to him, "Swear by the fortune of Caesar," Polycarp said to him, "You are surely mocking when you say to me, 'Swear by the fortune of Caesar,'
and you pretend that you do not know who I am. Hear it plainly, then: I am a Christian.
If you wish to learn the teaching of Christianity, set a day and listen."
The proconsul said to him, "Persuade the people." And Polycarp said to him, "You I have thought worthy of an answer, for we have been taught
to give rulers and authorities appointed by God the honor that is due to them, so far as it does not harm us. But those people I do not consider worthy of a defense from me."
The proconsul said to him, "I have wild beasts, and I will throw you to them unless you repent."
He said, "Call them. For we cannot repent and change from good to evil. But it is good for a person to turn from evil to good."
Again he said to him, “If you scorn the wild beasts, I will torment you with fire unless you repent.”
But Polycarp said to him, “You threaten me with fire that blazes for an hour and goes out after a little while.
"For you do not know the fire of the coming judgment and the eternal torment that is kept for the wicked. But why are you delaying, then? Bring whatever you wish."
He was saying these things and more besides, filled with courage and joy, and his face was full of grace.
Not only was he not saddened or troubled by what was being said to him, but quite the opposite, so that even the proconsul himself was amazed.
He sent a herald, who proclaimed three times in the middle of the stadium, “Polycarp has confessed that he is a Christian.”
When the herald had announced this, the whole crowd of Gentiles and Jews who live in Smyrna cried out with uncontrollable fury and in a loud voice:
"This is the teacher of Asia, the father of the Christians, the destroyer of our gods, who teaches many not to sacrifice to them or worship them."
When they had said these things, they cried out and asked Philip the Asiarch to let a lion loose on Polycarp.

But he said that he did not have the authority, because the animal games were over. Then they decided to cry out together that Polycarp should be burned alive. For the vision he had seen about the pillow under his head had to be fulfilled,
when he had seen it burning while he was praying.

He had turned and said prophetically to the believers who were with him, "I must be burned with fire." And these things were carried out quickly, the moment they were said: the crowds gathered and brought logs and kindling [?] from the shops and from the baths.
The Jews were especially eager, rejoicing and busying themselves with such things, as was their custom. When the fire was ready,
he took off all his clothes and loosened the belt around his waist. He also wanted to untie what was on his feet,
though he had not done this before, because the believers used to compete over which of them would be the first to attend to his clothing.
For he was adorned with every kind of good conduct, even before his old age. Immediately, then, the equipment prepared for the fire was put in place.
When they were about to fasten him with nails, he said to them, “Leave me as I am. For the one who gives me strength to endure the fire
"He who has granted me to endure the fire will also grant me to stay in it without being shaken [?] and without being fastened by nails." So they did not nail him; instead they bound him.
For he put his hands behind his back and was bound like a choice ram taken from a great flock, an offering acceptable to God, a whole burnt offering [?]. And he prayed and said:
"Father of Jesus Christ, your beloved and blessed Son, through whom we have received knowledge of you,
God of angels and powers and of all creation, and of the whole race of the righteous who live in your presence: I bless you because you have counted me worthy of this day and this hour,
to take a share among the number of the martyrs in the cup of Christ, for the resurrection to eternal life of soul and body in the incorruptibility of the Holy Spirit.
Among them may I be offered before you today as a rich and acceptable sacrifice, just as you prepared it beforehand and revealed it and are now fulfilling it, God of truth.
For this reason, and for everything, I praise you and bless you through the eternal high priest Jesus Christ, your beloved Son, through whom be glory to you, with him and with the Holy Spirit,
from now and to the ages of ages." And when he had finished the prayer and said "Amen,"

those men in charge of the fire lit the fire. And when the flame grew strong, we saw a wonder, we to whom it was given to see it, who were preserved in order to tell others what happened. For the fire took the shape of a vault, like a ship's sail filled by the wind,
and it encircled the martyr's body all around.
And he was in the midst of it, not like flesh that is burning, but like gold and silver being refined in a furnace.
And such a sweet fragrance came to us, like the fragrance of frankincense,
or like one of the precious spices. At last, when those wicked men saw that the fire could not burn his body, they ordered an executioner to come near and pierce him with a sword.
And when he did this, a great quantity of blood came out of him and quenched the fire, and the whole crowd was amazed

that there is such a difference between those who do not believe and the elect of God. This blessed and wonderful man was one of them; in our own times he was a teacher of the apostles and of the prophets [i.e., an apostolic and prophetic teacher],
bishop of the church of Smyrna. Every word that came out of his mouth has been fulfilled and is being fulfilled.

But the adversary, the evil, jealous and envious one, who stands against the race of the righteous, when he saw the greatness of his martyrdom and his conduct, which had been blameless from the beginning,
and that he had been crowned with the crown of incorruption and had received the victory beyond dispute,
schemed to prevent even his body from being given to us, although many longed to obtain it and to have a share in his holy body.
So people urged Nicetes, the father of Herod and brother of Alce, to approach the governor so that he would not give us his body.
“Otherwise,” they said, “they may abandon the one who was crucified and begin worshiping this man.”
They urged this, and the Jews also helped them [?]. These were the very people who had kept watch on us when we were preparing to take him out of the fire.
For they did not know that we can never forsake Christ, who suffered for the life of the world, that is, for those who wish to live; nor do we worship others.

For we worship Christ, who is the Son of God; but the martyrs we love, as is fitting, because they are teachers of our Lord's martyrdom, on account of the excellent and surpassing devotion that they have toward our King and our Teacher,
so that we too may be worthy to become their disciples and companions.
But when the centurion saw the contention of the Jews,

he set him in the middle, as is their custom, and burned him. And then afterward we gathered his bones, which are more valuable than precious stones of great price and more choice than refined gold, and we laid them where the Lord granted us, so that we may gather there in joy and gladness and keep the day of the commemoration of his martyrdom,
both in remembrance of those who have already been victorious, and for the preparation of those who are going to be trained by them. Such were the things that befell the blessed Polycarp,
together with those twelve from Philadelphia who were martyred in Smyrna.
His memory alone is far more celebrated than that of all the others, so that he is spoken of even among the Gentiles.
Such, then, was the end of the wonderful Polycarp, disciple of the apostles. The brethren in the church of Smyrna wrote this account of him in this letter, which we have quoted in this very book.
Together with the martyrdom of Polycarp, they also wrote about other martyrs who were martyred in Smyrna at this same time.
And along with these they also tell about Metrodorus, who was regarded as a presbyter of the error of the house of Marcion,

he who had no hope of [?], as if out of zeal for the martyrs of God, was himself also delivered to the fire and died. Among the famous martyrs of that time, one of them was well known: Pionius. [Recorded are] his confessions on many occasions, and the frankness of his speech, and the boldness of his spirit on behalf of the faith before the people and before the judges, and his teaching before the eyes of everyone, and the welcome with which he received those who had fallen in the trial of persecution;

and the encouragement with which he comforted the brethren who came in to him in prison. Along with these, also the tortures he endured and his sufferings, and the driving in of nails, and his endurance in the fire, and his death, fully in every respect.
are recorded in the accounts about him. For those who are eager and wish to learn, these things are written in the records of the martyrs that we have already collected.

There are also in the memoirs the accounts of those who were martyred in Pergamum, a city of Asia: of Carpus, of Papylus, and of a woman named Agathonice, who were crowned with a glorious and renowned confession.

Sixteenth: That Justin the philosopher was martyred while preaching the word of Christ in Rome. At these times Justin too, of whom we spoke a little earlier, was crowned with martyrdom after he had presented to these kings a second defense on behalf of our teaching.

For Crescens the philosopher, who was a Cynic, that is, a 'dog,' and who in mind and in deed strove to live up to [?] his name, since Justin had many times defeated him in debate before the eyes of the hearers who were present,
In the end, however, a plot was laid against him, and he was crowned with martyrdom for the sake of the truth that he had been preaching.
This very thing this philosopher of the truth also stated plainly in the apology he had written.
He made known beforehand, in these words, what was going to happen to him:
"I too, then, expect to be betrayed by one of those who have been named, or by Crescens the philosopher, who has shown himself [?] a lover of boasting, and to be fastened to the stake.
For it is not fitting for us to call him a philosopher: a man who publicly testifies, before the eyes of the people, about something he does not know,

saying that the Christians are godless and wicked. He was doing this as if to do a favour and a pleasure to the many who are in error. For if he has not read the teaching of Christ, and dares to say these false things against us, it is clear that he is an evil man, and much worse than the unlearned,
who already keep themselves either to teach or to bear witness openly about something of which they are not persuaded.

But if he has read [them] and has not understood the greatness in them, or if he has understood but does these things so that he will not be suspected [of being a Christian], he is found to be all the more weak and wicked, a slave to vulgar ignorance, foolish glory, and fear.
And [know] that I asked him questions such as these, and learned from him and refuted him, [showing] that in truth he knows nothing.
I want you to know that I am speaking the truth: that if these words of the debate have not reached your knowledge,
I am ready for these questions to be set before your eyes as well; for this too is a royal task. But if you have known my questions and his words,
this is clear to you: that he is not persuaded of anything of ours; or, if he was persuaded, he did not dare to say so because of those who were listening, as I said before.
he has shown himself to be no philosopher but a lover of empty glory. He does not even honor the teaching of Socrates, which deserves to be loved.
These things Justin said.

Now what he had said beforehand, that the slander by which Justin was crowned would come upon him through Crescens, is recounted by Tatian, a man who in his early career was a sophist in the learning of the Greeks,
who gained no small renown in it and left behind records of many treatises.
In the work of his that is called Against the Greeks, he recounts as follows: "Justin too, the admirable, rightly said that those of whom we spoke above are like robbers."

After saying a little about the philosophers, he went on to say: "Crescens, who recently came into the great city of Rome, surpassed everyone in his love of corrupting boys, and was very much given to the love of money.

And though he advised people to despise death, he himself was afraid of death, so much so that he schemed to bring death upon Justin as though it were a great evil, because Justin was proclaiming the truth."
and rebuked the philosophers for being gluttons and deceivers.” This, then, was the cause of Justin’s martyrdom.

Of the seventeenth [chapter]: Of the martyrs whom Justin mentions in his treatise. Before his own martyrdom, Justin mentions others who were martyred before him, in the first apology that he wrote to the emperors, because it was relevant to the subject in hand. He writes as follows:
"A certain woman," he says, "was married to a dissolute man, and she herself had formerly been dissolute too.
But when she came to know the teaching of Christ, she became chaste, and she tried to persuade her husband to become chaste as she was.

She kept reminding him of the teaching and telling him about the fire of eternal torment that awaits those who do not live chastely and do not conduct themselves with right thinking. But he went on in his licentiousness, and through his filthy deeds
he estranged his wife.

For this woman considered it impious to remain the partner of a man who wanted to pursue, by every possible means, pleasures that went against the law of nature and against what is right, so she wished to separate from her partnership with him.
But she was held back by her relatives, who urged her to wait with him a while longer in the hope that her partner would change in time. So she forced herself and stayed with him.
But since he later went to Alexandria, and it was reported of him that he was doing evil deeds,
So that she would not share in his wrongdoing and wickedness by remaining with him in marriage, living with him, and sharing his bed, she gave him a certificate of divorce and separated from him.
But this depraved and wicked husband of hers ought to have rejoiced that she had withdrawn from what she had previously done without restraint with her servants and hired workers,

and she had rejoiced in drunkenness and in every kind of wickedness but had given up all these deeds, and she wanted him also to give up the things he was doing. Because she separated from him, he brought an accusation against her that she was, he said, a Christian. She then approached the king, the emperor, and persuaded him to let her first put her affairs in order, and afterwards to make her defence against the charge brought against her, once she had put her affairs in order. And he granted her this.
But the man who had formerly been her husband, because he could bring no charge against her, turned against Ptolemy,
who had been this woman's teacher in Christian doctrine, and whom Urbicius put to death.

In this way the centurion threw Ptolemaeus into prison, because he was a friend of her husband. For her husband had persuaded him to arrest him on a charge and to ask him only this: whether he was a Christian.

But Ptolemaeus, because he loved the truth and was not a deceiver or a liar, confessed this, that he was a Christian. At once that centurion threw him into prison and tormented him there for a long time.
Finally, when this man was brought before Urbicus, he was asked only this: whether he was a Christian.
But because he was convinced of the truth of Christ, he openly confessed this glorious teaching of God.
For whoever denies and turns back, or wavers in his faith, or regards this teaching as something fiery [?] and shrinks from confessing it—
Neither of these is found among true Christians.
When Urbicius ordered him to be put to death, Lucius, who was also a Christian, saw that this judgment had been made without thought,
and said to Urbicius, “What is the reason for this? Although he has not been proved to be an adulterer or sexually immoral,
or a murderer, robber, or plunderer, or to have committed any of these crimes, you have condemned him merely because he acknowledged that he is a Christian.
this is not fitting for the Emperor Pius (Eusebes), nor for the philosopher, Caesar's son, nor for the glorious senate, O [?] Urbicius.
When he gave him no answer about these things, he said to Lucius: "You also seem to me to be a Christian."
Lucius said: "Yes, truly." Then he ordered that this man also be put to death. Lucius gave thanks and said that it was a great kindness to him to be delivered from evil masters.
and was going to the King and good Father, God. Then another, a third man, came forward, and he too received the sentence of death.
To these accounts Justin added the words we quoted earlier, saying: "I too expect to be betrayed by one of those who have been named, and of the rest [?]."

Eighteenth: Which discourses of Justin we have received. … This Justin left us many discourses that are full of great profit. They show that he had a well-trained mind, devoted to the teaching of God. Those who love learning should study them closely.
We record the ones that have reached us, for their usefulness.
He also has a work written to King Antoninus, who was called Pius (Eusebes), and to his sons and to the senate of Rome: a petition on behalf of our teaching.

There is another that contains a defence of our faith, which he addressed to Antoninus Verus, who succeeded the first one and whose times we are now describing. There is another against the pagans, in which he deals with the many questions that lie between us and the Greek philosophers. And there is another in which he undertook to speak about the nature of the demons.
We do not need to set these out now. There is also another against the pagans, which he wrote as a refutation. And there is yet another
showing that God alone is the One who exists, which he proves not only from our scriptures
but also from the books of the Greek wise men. And again another, titled "The Psalmist." And again another, on the soul,

in which he set out explicit questions about this lofty subject. In it he presented the opinions that the wise men outside the Church held in their teaching, and he promised to argue against them, and to set out fully the views he held in other treatises. There is also a dialogue that he composed against the Jews, which he held at Ephesus against Trypho, a well-known man among the Hebrews at that time.
In it he explains how the grace of God brought him to the message of faith,
how devoted he had previously been to the study of philosophy, and how he had searched for the truth with his whole soul.
In it he also tells how the Jews plotted against the teaching of Christ, speaking to Trypho as follows:

"For you did not merely fail to repent of the evil things you did. You also chose well-known men from Jerusalem at that time and sent them throughout the whole earth to say that a godless heresy had appeared, that of the Christians,
and they spoke evil things against us, which all who do not know us repeat to this day. So you are a cause of harm not only to yourselves,
but also to all people." He also wrote and showed
that even up to his own days the gift of prophecy existed in the church.
He also mentions the Revelation of John, and says plainly that it is the apostle's.
And he mentions some passages from the prophets, and reproached Trypho that the Jews had cut them out of the Scriptures.

Many. For thus the ancients regarded the treatises of this man, which are full of diligence. Irenaeus also cites a quotation from his words in the fourth book that he composed against heresies. He cites from his words thus:
"Well did Justin say in the treatise that he composed against Marcion: 'I would not have believed even our Lord, if he had proclaimed that there is another God besides the Creator.'"

Again, in another treatise, his fifth on this subject, he says this: "Justin spoke well when he said that before our Lord's coming Satan never dared to blaspheme God, because he did not yet know his own condemnation."
These things have rightly been said to encourage those who love learning to study his treatises diligently. This was his story.
Chapter Nineteen: Which bishops served in Rome and Alexandria in the days of Verus.
In the eighth year of the reign of Antoninus Verus, when Anicetus, bishop of Rome, had completed eleven years, Soter succeeded him.
And again in the church of Alexandria, when Celadion had held office for fourteen years, Agrippinus succeeded him.
Chapter Twenty: Which bishops served in Antioch. In the church of Antioch, Theophilus was known as the sixth bishop after the apostles.
After Heron, Cornelius had been the fourth bishop there. After him, Eros received the office of bishop as the fifth.

Twenty-first [chapter]: On the church writers who were renowned in those times. Now there was renowned in the church in those times Hegesippus, whom we have learned was one of the early ones; also Dionysius, bishop of Corinth,
and Pinytus, who was bishop in Crete; and with these also Philip and Apollinaris, and Melito and Musanus,
and Modestus and Irenaeus, through whose writings the faith of the truth of the apostolic tradition has been brought down to us.
Twenty-two: About Hegesippus and the people he mentions. Hegesippus, in the five treatises of our teaching that he composed,
left a full record of his own opinion. In them he tells that he met with many bishops while he was travelling on the road to Rome, and that he received this same teaching from all of them.
Let us hear what he says, after other things, about the letter of Clement that he wrote to the church of Corinth. He relates it like this:
"The church of Corinth continued in correct teaching until Primus, who was bishop in Corinth. When I was setting out for Rome,
I spent time with them, the Corinthians, and stayed with them for many days.
"And we were refreshed together in the correct teaching. And when I went to Rome, I drew up there the succession of bishops down to Anicetus, whom Soter succeeded, and after Soter, Eleutherus.

And thus it is in every succession and in all the churches, as the Law and the Prophets and our Lord proclaimed." And he himself also records here some of the founders of the heresies that existed in his days:
"For after James the Just had been martyred, as we also said,
Simeon son of Clopas, the son of his uncle, was appointed second bishop. Everyone regarded him as a cousin of our Lord.
For this reason they called the church a virgin, because it had not yet been corrupted by vain teachings. But Thebuthis first began to corrupt it there,
because he had not been made bishop. He belonged to one of the seven heresies, and it was among the people [?]. Simon came from them.
which is why they are called Simonians; Cleobius, from whom came the Cleobians; Dositheus, from whom came the Dositheans;
and Gorthaeus, from whom came the Gorthaeans and the Masbothaeans.

And from these came the Menandrians, and the Marcionites, and the Carpocratians, and the Basilidians, and the Saturnilians, each one of whom, each in his own way [?] and differently, introduced teaching according to the opinion of their own mind,
From these came false christs, false prophets and false apostles. They divided the unity of the church with the corrupt words they spoke against God and against his Christ." Hegesippus himself also

recounts the heresies that existed among the Jews in ancient times, saying: "Among the circumcision, among the children of Israel, there were different opinions held by those who opposed the tribe of Judah and Christ. They are these: the Essenes, the Galileans, and those who are baptized every day,
the Masbotheans, the Samaritans, the Sadducees, and the Pharisees.” He also wrote many other things, some of which we have included under their respective periods in this history.
And from the Gospel of the Hebrews and of the Syrians.

And from it and [?] he has set down certain things from the Hebrew language. He shows that he himself was a believer from among the Hebrews. He also mentions other things as coming from the unwritten [?] tradition of Judaism, not from scripture.

This man, Irenaeus and all the early writers used to call the Proverbs of Solomon "All-Virtuous Wisdom." He also says of the so-called gilyone [?] (apocryphal writings) that some of them were forged in his own time by heretics.

Twenty-three: On Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, and on the letters he wrote... First, then, let us speak about Dionysius, who was bishop of the church of Corinth. Because of his zeal for divine teaching,
he taught not only the people under his charge. Through the letters he wrote to the churches, he also benefited distant countries.

He wrote one letter to the Lacedaemonians about instruction in the true faith, about peace and about harmony. He wrote another to the Athenians about the awakening of faith and about living by the Gospel.

In this letter he rebukes them because their minds had fallen away and they had nearly turned away from the faith [?]. This happened after the bishop who stood at their head, named Publius, was martyred in the persecution of those times.
He mentions that Quadratus became their bishop after Publius suffered martyrdom.

He also speaks about Quadratus, saying that through his zeal they were gathered together again and their faith was revived. Along with this he reports that Dionysius the Areopagite, who believed through Paul as written in the Acts, was the first bishop of the church of Athens. He also has another letter, to the Nicomedians [?], in which he fought against the heresy of Marcion and upheld the teaching of the truth.
He also wrote a letter to the church in Gortyna and the other churches in Crete. In it he praises their bishop, Philip,
because the church under his charge is reported to have won many victories. He reminds it to guard against the perversions of the heretics.
He wrote letters to the church in Amastris and to the other churches in Pontus. He states that Bacchylides and Elpistus urged him to write them, and so he wrote.
In these letters he included interpretations of the divine scriptures. He also reports that their bishop was Palmas.
He teaches them much about marriage and about chastity. He also instructs them to receive back those who return after lapses, failings or the error of heresy.
Following these is another letter that he wrote to the people of Cnossus. In it he urges Pinytus, the bishop of the church there,

He urges that the heavy yoke of chastity not be imposed on the brethren by compulsion, but that the weakness of the many be taken into account. Pinytus wrote back to him about this, expressing admiration and praise for Dionysius.

But Pinytus asked him to nourish the people under his charge with solid food in due time, through more advanced writings, so that they would not graze on milk-like words to the end and grow old in childish ways.
This letter shows the precision of Pinytus's orthodox faith, his concern for the benefit of the people under his charge, and his eloquence and understanding in the fear of God.
Dionysius also has another letter to the Romans, addressed to the bishop at that time, whose name was Soter.

Let us take a few words from it showing how he praises the custom of the Romans, which was kept up until the persecution of our own day. He says this: "From the beginning you have had this custom of helping the brethren in every way

and of sending supplies to many churches in every city. In this way you relieve the poor in their time of need, and you meet the needs of the brethren who are in the mines [?]. You send them supplies, as has been your custom from of old.
And as if by the [?] of their fathers, the Romans keep this festival.

...that your blessed bishop Soter has not only kept it up, but has even increased the gift that was sent to the saints, and with good words he comforted the brethren who went up there, as a loving father comforts his children.
In this same letter he also mentions the letter that Clement wrote to the Corinthians, and makes known that, according to an ancient custom, it is read there before the whole church.
So he says: "Today we kept the holy Lord's Day, and on it we read your letter. It is fitting that we should always be instructed by it whenever we read it,
as we are by the earlier letter that was written to us from Clement." And he, speaking about his own letters,
because people had corrupted them, says this: "For the brethren urged me to write letters to them, and I wrote them.
"And the apostles of Satan have filled these with tares, by taking things out of them and adding things to them."

…of theirs; for these too, woe is in store for them. So it is no wonder if people have tampered even with the writings of our Lord, since they have also plotted against writings that are not of this kind.
Dionysius also has another letter, similar to these, which he wrote to Chrysophora, a faithful sister.
He gave her the nourishment of instruction that was suitable for her. These, then, are the things concerning Dionysius.

Twenty-fourth: On Theophilus, bishop of Antioch; on Philip and on Modestus; on Melito and on those whom he mentioned; and on Apollinaris and on Musanus. Now Theophilus, of whom we said that he was bishop of Antioch, has three treatises addressed to Autolycus.
And there is another written by him against the heresy of Hermogenes, in which he makes use of testimonies from the Revelation of John. And he has other books that are [?] for instruction.
Those who belonged to the teaching of heresy were even at that time spoiling the pure seed of the apostles' teaching, like tares. But the shepherds who were in the churches in every place

As if driving off wild beasts from the flock of Christ, they were pursuing them: at times by teaching and by entreaty addressed to the brethren, and at other times openly, face to face, they engaged with them in debate and refuted them.

And again, in written treatises as well, they exactly refuted and exposed their opinions. This Theophilus, together with others, engaged against them. This is known from one treatise that he composed forcefully against Marcion, which has also been preserved along with the others we have mentioned.
After him Maximinus received the episcopate of the church of Antioch. He was the seventh after the apostles.
Philip, of whom we learn from the words of Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, that he was bishop of the church of the city of Gortyna, also diligently composed a treatise against Marcion.
So did Irenaeus and Modestus, who exposed this man’s error more openly than the others,
and many others whose discourses are preserved among many of the brothers to this day.

At this time Melito, bishop of the church of Sardis, and Apollinaris, bishop of the church of Hierapolis, were also flourishing with distinction. Each of them, on his own, composed a defense on behalf of the faith, and they presented these to the emperor of the Romans who reigned at that time.
The discourses of these men that are known to us are as follows. By Melito: two works On Passover; On Conduct; and On the Prophets;

And another on the Church, and another on the Lord's Day. And again another on the faith of man, and another on his creation. And again another on the obedience of faith. And along with these, on soul and body.
And again on the birth of Christ, and on the word of his prophecy. And again on soul and body. And another on hospitality, and on Satan, and on the Revelation of John.
another On God Who Put On a Body; and another that he wrote to the emperor Antoninus.
When he wrote about the time of Passover, he began his work by reporting the following: “In the time of Servilius Paulus, proconsul of Asia, Agris [?] was martyred.
There was a great inquiry at Laodicea about Passover, a question that kept arising in those days, and these things were written.” This discourse
Clement of Alexandria mentions it in his treatise which he wrote on the Passover, and said

that he too wrote because of Melito's treatise. In the defense that Melito presented to the emperor, he relates things like these as having happened in our time: that something which had never happened before
is now happening: the race of those who fear God is being persecuted in Asia by new decrees. For shameless informers, who covet the property of others,
since they have the decree, openly plunder and rob, night and day, people who have done nothing wrong.
And after other things he says again:
For if it is you who have commanded that this be done, then it is well done; for a just king would never do anything unjustly. We too gladly bear the honour of this death.
But we bring you this one request only: that you first examine those who carry out this strife, and judge justly whether they deserve death and punishment [?], or life and rest.

But if this will and this new decree, which would not be fitting to carry out in this way even against hostile barbarians, does not come from you, then all the more we ask you not to neglect us in this public persecution." After these things he said:
"For our philosophy first flourished among the barbarians.
Then it also flourished among your people in the days of Augustus, and it became a great power for the empire of the Romans,
And above all it was a good nurture for your empire; for from that time the power of the Romans became great and increased.

That which you have received and inherited, and you will moreover strengthen it [?] together with your son, while you guard that philosophy which grew up together with your empire and began from Augustus, which your forefathers also honoured, along with the rest of the other religions.
And this is great evidence that our message sprang up for the good of the empire, together with its auspicious beginning:
since the days of Augustus, nothing bad has befallen your empire. Rather, it has become increasingly glorious and strong in every respect through the prayers of us all.
Of all the emperors who have reigned, only Nero and Domitian were persuaded by envious people and accepted slander against our teaching.
From them it came about that this false accusation against us was handed down as an unthinking custom.
But your fathers corrected the error of those people. For they often rebuked [?] in writing many who had dared to act insolently and to oppress us on this account.
Your grandfather Hadrian wrote to many about this, including Fundanus, the proconsul of Asia.
And your father wrote to the cities on our behalf that no one should harm us, at a time when you were also governing all things with him.
also to the Pharisaeans [?], to the Thessalonians, to the Athenians, and to all the peoples.

But as for you, we are persuaded that, more than they, you are well-minded about these things. And we are especially persuaded that, since you order everything with wisdom, you will command what we ask of you. These things were set down up to this point. And in the Extracts written by Melito,
as he begins them,
he recorded the number of the books of the Old Testament and showed which ones are accepted. It is right that we set them down here.

He writes as follows: "Melito to Onesimus his brother, greeting. Since you have many times urged me, out of the zeal you have for the word, to make extracts for you from the Law and from the Prophets concerning our Saviour and concerning our whole faith,

and further, since you wished to learn exactly about the ancient books, how many they are in number and what they are in order, I have been eager to do this, for I was persuaded by your zeal for the faith and for the teaching of the word,
that more than anything you are devoted to the love of God,

and that you are striving for the sake of eternal life. So when I went up to the East and came as far as the place where these things were proclaimed and done, and learned accurately about the books of the Old Testament, I wrote them down and have sent them to you. Their names are these:
Of Moses, five: Genesis and Exodus.
Numbers, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy; also Joshua son of Nun; the book of Judges; Ruth; the four books of Kings;
the two books of Chronicles; the Psalms of David; and those of Solomon—Proverbs, which is Wisdom, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs;
...and Job; and of the prophets: Isaiah and Jeremiah, and the Twelve Prophets together, and Daniel, and Ezekiel, and Ezra. From these I have also made extracts and arranged them in six books."
All these are Melito's. Of Apollinaris, too, there are many treatises preserved among many people. Those that have come to our attention are these:
One that is set forth by the Spirit [?]. That one he composed for this king of whom we spoke earlier. And Against the Pagans, five. And Against the Jews, two.

And those he composed afterwards against the heresy of the Phrygians, which had newly arisen a short time before, when Montanus, together with the women prophets of the Galatians [?] who were attached to him, was beginning to stray from the truth.

Twenty-fifth: On the heresy of Tatian. Now Musanus, who is numbered with those we have listed, has a treatise that he addressed to brethren who had inclined toward the heresy called that of the Encratites, to turn them back to the truth. This heresy had then begun to appear and to introduce into the world an opinion that was false, foreign and corrupt. It is said that Tatian was the cause of the beginning of this error.
He is the one whose words about Justin the glorious martyr we quoted a little earlier. It is related of him that he was Justin's disciple.
Irenaeus makes this known in the first book that he composed against heresies, concerning Tatian and his heresy. He writes as follows:

"After Saturninus, they say, and Marcion, those called Encratites preached and rejected marriage. They set aside God's original creation and covertly accuse the one who made male and female for the begetting of human beings.

They teach that one should abstain from eating anything that has a soul. They wrongly reject the receiving of the goodness of God, who made all things, and they oppose the salvation of the man who was first created. This has now been discovered among them: Tatian was the first to introduce this blasphemy,
he who was a disciple of Justin.

As long as he was attached to Justin, he displayed nothing of this kind. But after Justin's martyrdom, he withdrew from the church, exalted and puffed up, because he imagined himself a teacher superior to others.
He fashioned for himself a different type of teaching, and he too told stories like those of Valentinus's school, about invisible aeons, as they say.
He called marriage corruption and fornication, as Marcion and Saturninus did, and he opposed the salvation of Adam."
This is what Irenaeus said. A short time later, a man named Severus strengthened this heresy, and he became the reason why those who were taught in it are called Severians after his name.
These people use the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel, but interpret the meaning of the Scriptures according to their own ideas.
They blaspheme against Paul the apostle and reject his letters. Nor do they accept the Acts of the Apostles.
This Tatian, their first leader, collected, combined, and composed a gospel and called it the Diatessaron, that is, "of the mixed ones." It is in the hands of many to this day. It is said of him
that he dared to alter some of the apostles' words, as though correcting the composition of their speech. This man left many discourses,
one of which is well known to many: Against the Pagans. In it he mentioned those who were renowned among the pagans from ancient times,
and he showed that Moses and the prophets of the Hebrews came before all of them.
This discourse appears to be excellent and more useful than all his other discourses. These things have been said about these people.

Twenty-sixth. On Bardaisan the Aramean and the treatises he wrote. Now in the reign of Antoninus and Verus there were many heresies. In Mesopotamia, in Edessa, Bardaisan, a well-known man who was very skilled in the Aramaic language, rose up with his word against the followers of Marcion and against others who held various doctrines.
He wrote the treatise in his own language, along with many other treatises that he wrote.

He had many disciples who were powerful in speech, and they published his treatises. Among them is the dialogue On Fate, spoken by him with great power, which he wrote to Antoninus. They also say that he wrote many others
because of the persecution that took place at that time. This man had at first belonged to the school of Valentinus.

But when he examined it closely for himself and refuted many of its fables, he thought that he had of his own accord turned to the better opinion. Yet he did not entirely escape the filth of that former heresy. At this very time the bishop of the church of Rome died

Book Five of the History of the Church.
Chapter 1. How many martyrs there were in Gaul in the days of Verus, and where they endured the struggle for the sake of devotion to God.
Soter, bishop of the church of Rome, served for eight years and then departed from the world.

After him Eleutherus succeeded. He was the twelfth bishop after the apostles. It was the seventeenth year of the emperor Antoninus Verus. At that time, in various places, persecution against us was fiercely stirred up, driven by the zeal of the populace.

One can discover that there were tens of thousands of martyrs everywhere by comparing what happened among a single people, which was written down and handed on to those who came after them as a memorial never to be forgotten.

We have recorded the full account of their stories in the collection of martyrs that we gathered. It gives us not only the narrative of the story but also teaching. Now, however, we will gather and set down the things that are needed for this history we have undertaken. Other writers, who tell and write the histories of the world, record the victories won in wars against enemies, the triumphs of generals, and the bravery of soldiers,
who defiled themselves with blood and with many killings of children for the sake of a country and for the wealth of others.

But we tell the story of the way of life that comes from the fear of God. We tell of the war that is fought for the peace of the soul, and of those who triumphed in it. They fought not for a country but for the truth,

not for their loved ones but for the fear of our Lord. We record, as an everlasting memorial, the endurance of the athletes of the truth, what they suffered in their courage, and the victories they won over demons and invisible enemies.
We proclaim their crowns as an everlasting memorial. This contest of struggle, then, took place in the country of Gaul, among these martyrs of whom we speak.
Two well-known cities there are called metropolitan cities, standing above the other cities in that land: Lyon and Vienne.
The river Rhône flows past both these cities and through their entire district, with its abundant waters.
The well-known churches in the land of Gaul wrote and sent to the churches in Asia and Phrygia an account of these martyrs and of what had happened among them.

They tell this account, and I will set it down in their own words: The servants of Christ who live in Vienne and Lyons in Gaul, to the brothers in Asia and Phrygia who share the faith of our redemption and of our hope:
Peace, grace, and glory from God the Father and from Jesus Christ our Lord.

After this they say a little before the narrative, and then they begin their account like this: As for the greatness [?] of the affliction that took place here, and the rage of the Gentiles against the saints,

How much the blessed martyrs endured we are not able to tell exactly, nor can it be contained in writing. For the adversary was roused against us with all his might, and gave us beforehand a foretaste of his coming,
which is to be without restraint. And he exerted himself in every way to stir up those who are his own and to train them beforehand against the servants of God,
so that they were driving us out not only from houses and from baths and from marketplaces,
but they even decreed that none of us at all should be seen in any place. But the goodness of God stood against them: it rescued the weak and set up firm pillars,
who were able through their endurance to take upon themselves the whole onslaught of the adversary.

Together they endured every reproach and every torture. They counted many things as small, because they were eager to go to Christ. They showed that the sufferings of this time are not worth comparing with the glory that is going to be revealed in us.
First, they bravely endured what the whole mob did to them when it gathered: blows, stoning, imprisonment, and everything that ignorant people usually do

to those they hate and to their enemies. When they came to the marketplace, they were questioned before all the people by the chiliarch and by the authorities in charge of the cities. When they confessed that they were Christians,
they were shut up in prison until the governor arrived.
Afterward they were brought before the governor, who treated our people with exceptional harshness.
One of the brothers, whose name was Vettius Epagathus, was filled with love for God and for his neighbor.
He was so blameless in his conduct that, although he was young, he could be compared to Zechariah according to the testimony given about him.

For he walked blamelessly in all the commandments and righteousness of the Lord, and was tireless in every service to his neighbor. He had zeal for God and was fervent in spirit. This is the kind of man he was.
He could not bear to see the judgment that was being passed against us so thoughtlessly.

Instead he was extremely indignant and asked to be heard, so that he might bring relief [?] on behalf of the brothers, saying that nothing of impiety is done among them, as it is among those who are without God.
But all those standing around the tribunal shouted against him, for he was a well-known man. The governor did not accept the just request he was putting to him.
He only asked him whether he too was a Christian. And he confessed it openly, in a loud voice.

So he too was counted among the martyrs and became the advocate of the Christians. For the Spirit, the Paraclete, was in him even more than in Zechariah, and he showed this by the abundance of his love.
Because he was fervent in spirit on behalf of the brothers, he was willing to lay down even his own life.
For he was a true disciple of Christ,

who followed the Lamb of God wherever he went. From then on the rest were divided. The first [?] martyrs became known and showed that they were ready; with all their mind they were completing the confession of martyrdom. But those who were unready and untrained, and still weak, also became known.
They were not able to endure the force of the great contest.
About ten of them in number turned back. They caused us much distress and great grief, and they weakened the resolve of the others who had not yet been arrested.
These others were enduring every kind of mistreatment from the pagans alongside the martyrs, and did not separate themselves from them.

Then we were all greatly dismayed, because we did not yet know what would happen in the confession. It was not that we feared the tortures that were coming upon us. We were looking toward the end, and we feared that someone might turn back. Each day, however, those who were worthy were being arrested, and they filled up the number of those who had fallen, so that all the zealous from these two churches were gathered together.

These included those by whose hands above all the churches here had been established. Some pagans were also arrested, servants of the households of some of our people, because the governor had ordered publicly, in the sight of all the people, that all of us be sought out. Through the working of Satan, these servants feared the tortures
which they saw the saints enduring. The soldiers urged them to lie about us and say that we eat our children and have sexual relations with our mothers as in marriage,

and other things that we are not permitted to speak of or think of, or even to believe that anything like this was ever done among human beings. When this report went out, everyone was filled with rage against us like wild beasts,
even if there were people who had previously shown us pity because of kinship.
Then they raged greatly and gnashed their teeth at us. And the word of our Lord was fulfilled, which he had spoken: "The hour will come when everyone who kills you will think that he is serving God."

From then on the blessed martyrs endured tortures beyond words, for Satan was striving to get some blasphemy spoken by them as well. The anger of all the people, the governor and the soldiers fell most harshly on Sanctus, a deacon from Vienne.

And against Maturus, who had only recently received baptism but was a vigorous athlete; and against Attalus, whose family came from the city of Pergamum. He had always been a firm pillar for everyone in this place.
And against Blandina, through whom Christ showed that the things which people regard as lowly, ugly and contemptible…
are counted worthy of great glory with God because of love toward him, a love that is shown by power and does not boast in appearance. For while all of us were afraid,
including the woman who was her mistress in the flesh
(for she too was one of the martyrs in the contest),

and while her mistress was anxious about this servant of hers, fearing she might not be able to confess boldly because of the weakness of her body, Blandina was filled with such power that those who took turns torturing her in every way from morning until evening grew weary and exhausted.
They admitted that they were beaten and had nothing more they could do to her. They marveled that even her breath remained in her, for her whole body was torn and laid open.
They testified that a single kind of this suffering would have been enough to take her life, let alone all this torture.

But the blessed woman, like a noble athlete, was renewed in her confession. Her refreshment and rest, and her freedom from pain in all that she suffered, was this: she kept saying, "I am a Christian, and nothing evil is done among us."
Sanctus also nobly endured tortures from men, exceedingly and beyond everyone.
Those wicked men hoped that, because of the intensity and severity of the tortures, they would hear him say something improper.

He stood against them with such endurance that he did not even tell them his name, or what people he came from, or what city, or whether he was a slave or free. Instead, in answer to everything they asked him,
he replied to them in Latin: "I am a Christian." With this he answered for his name, his city, his race and everything else alike, and the pagans heard nothing else from him.

Because of this, great fury rose against him from the governor and from those who were torturing him. When there was nothing else left for them to do to him, they finally heated bronze plates and placed them on the tender parts of his body.

While his body was burning, he endured. He did not bend or weaken, but was strengthened in his confession by the heavenly fountain of living water that flowed from the side of Christ, which dripped upon him and refreshed him. His body itself was a witness to what he endured, for it was all wounds and sores. His whole appearance was crushed and ruined, so that it no longer had a human likeness.
And while she was suffering in it…
Christ was accomplishing great glory through her. He was bringing the Adversary to nothing and showing in him a likeness [?] to others.
For nothing is fearful where the love of the Father is, and nothing is painful where the glory of Christ is. But those wicked men…

after some days, tortured the martyr again. They thought that, since his body was festering and swollen, they would overcome his strength if they applied the torments to those wounds again, for it could not bear even a human hand to touch it. Or, if he died under his tortures, he would strike fear into others...

But not only did none of these things happen to him. Something that no one imagined happened instead: his body was healed and restored by the [?] (probably “tortures”) that were applied to it afterwards, and it regained its former shape and the use of its limbs. So the second torment was not torture for him,

but healing, by the grace of Christ. There was a woman named Biblis, who was among those who had denied earlier. The adversary thought she had fallen, and he also wanted to condemn her through blasphemy, so he brought her to the tortures again.
He was trying to force her to say improper things against us, so that he might see her weakness and feebleness.
But during the tortures she came to her senses and woke up as if from a deep sleep. Through these temporary tortures she was reminded of the eternal torment of Gehenna.
She answered and said to those blasphemers, "How then could they eat children, when they are not allowed to eat even the blood of animals?"
From that hour she confessed that she was a Christian, and she was added to the number of the martyrs.
When the tortures of the tyrants had been brought to nothing by Christ through the endurance of the blessed ones, the adversary devised another scheme:

he would torture them by confining them in prison, in dark and cramped places, by stretching their feet in the stocks to the fifth hole, and by the other blows that men stirred to anger are accustomed to inflict.

The adversary inflicted these assaults on those who were imprisoned, so that many of them were suffocated in the prison. These were the ones whom the Lord willed to leave the world in this way, so that he might show himself.

For those who had been tortured bitterly, so badly that people thought they could not live even if every kind of healing were applied to them, remained alive in the prison, deprived of all human care.
But they were restored and strengthened in body and soul by our Lord,
and they encouraged and comforted the others. But those who had been newly arrested, whose bodies were not yet hardened, could not endure the burden of confinement and died inside.
Now the blessed Pothinus, who had been entrusted with the ministry of the episcopate in Lyons,
was more than seventy years old and very sick in body,

and he could barely breathe because of the weakness of his body. But he was strengthened by the eagerness of his spirit, because of his desire for the martyrdom that lay before him. They dragged him too and brought him to the tribunal, though his body was failing from old age and sickness.
But his soul was kept within him, so that Christ might be glorified through it.
He was brought to the tribunal by the soldiers, and the magistrates of the city accompanied him,
while the whole crowd raised every kind of shout at him, as though he were Christ himself. But he made a good confession.
When the governor pressed him to say who the God of the Christians was, he said:
And he endured blows of every kind. Those who were near him abused him with their hands and feet in every way, and they had no respect for his old age. And those who were far from him

Each one of them threw at him whatever he happened to be holding in his hand. All of them thought to themselves: "I would be acting very foolishly and wickedly if I held back and did not treat him with contempt."
For they supposed that in this way vengeance [?]. With [barely] breath left in him, he was thrown into prison, and after two days he died.
Then God's great providence came into play, along with the boundless mercy of Christ toward those who had fallen,

so that they were not abandoned by Christ's providence. Those who had been arrested at first and had denied were also imprisoned, and they too suffered hardships, for their denial did not gain them any advantage even in this world. Those who confessed what they were, Christians, were imprisoned
with no other charge brought against them. But the deniers were now held as murderers and defiled persons, and they were tormented twice as much as the others.

For the first group, the joy of martyrdom made their burden light, along with the hope of his promise, the love of Christ, and the Spirit, the Paraclete. But those who had denied were greatly tormented by their conscience.
So everyone could recognize them in the streets by their faces. For whenever those martyrs went out, they were cheerful.
and glory and abundant grace were mingled in their faces. Their chains were like beautiful ornaments upon them,
like an adorned bride whose clothing is decorated with fine gold. And Christ's fragrance wafted from you,

so much so that some people thought they had been anointed with worldly perfumes. But the deniers were downcast, humbled, gloomy and full of every kind of shame, and the pagans mocked them as weak and feeble.
and they were accused as murderers. They had lost the name that is honored above all, glorious, and life-giving. After saying a little,
they went on to say: “After this, at their departure, their martyrdom took every form.

For they wove a crown from every kind of flower and every kind of blossom and offered it to the Father. Now it is right to speak of the mighty athletes, who endured the contest in every form and won a great victory,
and received the great, incorruptible crown.
So Maturus, Sanctus, Blandina and Attalus were brought to the beasts in front of all the people, as a merciless spectacle for the pagans,

On the day the spectacle of combat was given on our account, they brought Maturus and Sanctus into the theater again to face every torture, as if nothing had happened to them before. In fact, they had already beaten the Adversary in many bouts, and now they were in a contest for the crown.
