Again they endured running the gauntlet of whips that was customary there, and the bites of the beasts, and everything that the frenzied crowds were shouting for from one side and the other, and the crowds called for them to be tortured. After all this, they set them on the iron chair.
As their bodies were being fried, the smell of their burning reached the crowds.
But even then the crowds did not calm down. Instead they became even more frenzied,
and they wanted to break the endurance of the blessed ones. Even so, they heard nothing else from Sanctus except the word of confession

that he had been in the habit of saying from the beginning. These two endured a great contest because their souls lingered in them for a long time, but in the end they were sacrificed. Instead of the various combat shows that were held on that day, they themselves became a spectacle for the whole world.

Blandina was hung on a stake and put out as food for the beasts that were let loose on her. To look at, she hung in the shape of a cross, and her mighty prayer gave great encouragement to those who were fighting the contest.
For in their contests, through this sight, they saw with their own bodily eyes the one who had been crucified for them,
to assure all who believe in him that everyone who suffers for the glory of Christ has fellowship with the living God.
When none of these beasts came near her, they took her down from that stake and threw her back into prison.
She was kept for another contest, so that through many exercises she might defeat Satan the Adversary and bring on him a condemnation that cannot pass away;
and so that she might encourage the brethren. This small, weak and despised woman had been clothed like a great, invincible athlete, and in many rounds she defeated the Adversary.
And [?in the contest] she was crowned with the incorruptible crown.
The crowd also loudly demanded Attalus.

He was well known. Because he had a good conscience, he entered like a ready athlete, for he had been thoroughly trained in the confession of the Christian faith, and among us he had always been a witness to the truth.
As they led him around the theater, a placard went before him with this written on it in Latin: “This is Attalus the Christian.”

While the people were raging fiercely against him, the governor learned that he was a Roman. So he ordered him to be held in prison with the others who were there, about whom he had written to Caesar,
and he waited for Caesar's reply. The time in between was not idle or fruitless for them. Instead, through their endurance, the boundless grace of Christ was revealed.
For through those who were alive, even those who had died were coming back to life.
The martyrs were bringing back those who had not become martyrs. There was great joy for the Virgin Mother, because she received alive those she had cast out as dead.

For through those martyrs, many of those who had denied were conceived and born again. They were revived and learned to confess. And while they were alive and strengthened, they came forward to the tribunal.

to be questioned by the governor, through the kindness of God, who does not desire the death of the sinner but is gracious to those who turn to him. ... Now Caesar had written that those who did not deny should be put to death, and those who denied should be released. At the festival held here, for which many people from all nations gather, he brought them to the tribunal when it began to assemble. He did this to make the blessed ones a theatre and a spectacle for the whole crowd.
Because of this he questioned them again. He ordered that those who held the rank of Roman citizens should have their heads cut off.
But he sent the rest to the beasts.
Christ was greatly glorified through those who had previously denied him, for they now confessed him, contrary to the pagans’ expectations.

For these too were questioned separately, as if they were going to be released. But when they confessed, they were added to the number of the martyrs. Those who remained outside were the ones who had never had even a trace of faith,
nor any knowledge of the wedding garment, nor any thought of the fear of God,
but who even by their conduct blasphemed the way of truth. They are sons of perdition.

And all the others were added to the church. While they were being questioned, there was a man named Alexander. He was a Phrygian by race and a physician by profession, and he had lived for many years in Gaul.
He was known to everyone for his love toward God and the boldness of his speech, for he was not without a share in the apostolic gift either.

This man was standing before the tribunal and urging them by signs to confess. He was like a woman in the pains of labour, and this was plain to those who stood around the tribunal. ... But the whole crowd was angered because those who had denied had turned back and confessed.
They cried out against Alexander, as if he had caused this.
The governor had him brought and made him stand there. When he asked him who he was, he said he was a Christian.
The governor became angry and sentenced him to be thrown to the beasts. The next day he went in with Attalus.
For the governor, wishing to do the crowd a favor, had handed Attalus over as well to be thrown to the wild beasts.
After they had been put through all the instruments prepared for torture in the theater and had endured a great struggle,
they too were finally slaughtered. Alexander did not even groan, nor did he open his mouth to say anything.
Instead, he spoke with God in his heart. As for Attalus, after they seated him on the burning iron chair, when an odor began to rise from his body,
He said to the whole crowd in Latin: "This, which you are doing to us, is the eating of human beings. For we do not eat human beings, and we do not commit anything wicked."
And when they asked him what name God has, he said, "God does not have a name as a human being does." ... After all these things,
on the last day of the contests they brought in Blandina, together with a boy named Ponticus, who was about fifteen years old.
These two had been brought in every day to watch the tortures of the others, and they were being pressed to swear by the idols.
And because they had stood firm steadfastly and were scorning them,

the whole crowd was embittered against them, so that they neither pitied the boy's young age nor showed any respect for the female sex. Instead they threw them into every kind of torture and put them through every variety of torment, and they tried to force them to swear by the idols.
But they could not make them do this, for Ponticus himself was strengthened by that sister of his.
And the heathen saw that she was encouraging and strengthening him. So he bravely endured all the tortures, gave up his spirit, and departed from the world. The blessed Blandina came last of all,

like a noble mother who had encouraged her sons and sent them crowned to Christ the King. She herself had gone through all the contests of her sons, and she was hastening to go to them, full of joy and gladness, like one invited to a wedding feast. They threw her to the wild beasts.

After the scourges, the beasts and the frying pan, they finally threw her in a net, and she was cast to a bull. And while she was being tossed by it, she seemed not even to feel what was happening to her, because of her hope and her expectation of what she believed in,
and because of her converse with Christ.
And at last she too was slaughtered.

And all the heathen admitted that no woman had ever endured such great sufferings as these. But even so, their madness and cruelty toward the saints were not satisfied. For by savage beasts, that is, by Satan,
these savage and barbarous peoples had been stirred up, and they did not know how to stop. Instead they started again on another kind of outrage, against the bodies of the saints.
They were not ashamed at having been defeated, because they had no human reason. Instead their anger against us blazed up all the more, like that of wild beasts.

…and the governor; and together with all of them they equally showed their hatred of the wickedness toward us, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which said: "Let the wicked be wicked still, and the righteous be righteous still." For those who had been strangled in prison they threw to the dogs.
And they guarded them carefully night and day, so that they would not be buried by us.
And then they set out the remains that were left from the beasts and from the fire, some torn to pieces and some burned, and the heads of the others with the pieces of their remains.
For many days they kept them under the soldiers' careful guard so that they would not be buried.
And there were some of the heathen who raged and gnashed their teeth at them, and sought to take even greater vengeance on them than this. Others laughed and mocked them,
and magnified their idols and said that it was from them that these men had received these punishments. But others, who seemed to be gentle and to feel compassion for them,
reproached them and said: "Where is the God of these people, and what good has their religion done them, which they chose above their own lives?"
Such were the varied attitudes on the part of those people… But we were in great mourning,
because we were not able to bury their bodies in the earth. For not even the night helped us in this.
Nor did money persuade the guards, nor did entreaty shame them. For they guarded them by every means,

as though they would gain something great if these were not buried… After this they said, adding other things: "So the bodies of the martyrs, after they had been exposed in every manner and left in the open air for six days,

were afterwards burned by those wicked men until they became ash, and they threw them into the river Rhône, which flows there, so that not even a remnant of them might be seen on the earth any longer. And they did these things as if they were men able to overcome God,
and take away from them even the renewal of their resurrection from the dead. For these people used to say:
so that they would no longer have any hope of the resurrection in which they had trusted. "They have brought in among us a strange and new religion, and they have despised all afflictions,
and they have gone to death with joy and readiness. Now let us see whether they will rise,
and whether their God is able to help them and rescue them from our hands."

Second: How the martyrs received the mercies of God and healed those who had slipped in the persecution. The churches of Christ endured the things we have just described in the days of the emperor Verus. From these, a person can work out in his mind what happened in those times in other countries as well. It is right, however, to record some other things from this same document as well.
in which the humility and love of these martyrs, of whom we spoke above, are made known. These words are written there:
"These martyrs were such zealous followers and imitators of Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God,
that, while they were in this glory, and had borne witness not once or twice but many times, having been taken back from the beasts and being covered with burns, wounds and bruises,
they neither called themselves martyrs nor allowed us to call them by this name.

…but if it ever happened that anyone called them martyrs, either by word or by letter, they rebuked sharply the one who called them so. For they gladly yielded this name of martyrdom to Christ, him who is the faithful and true martyr, the firstborn of the dead and the beginning of life.
And they would remember the martyrs who had departed from the world and say: 'Those are martyrs,
those whom Christ, through their confession, made worthy to be guided,

and he sealed their testimony through their departure. "But we are lowly and humble confessors." And with many tears they would plead with the brethren and ask them to offer prayers earnestly on their behalf, so that they might be perfected.
And while they showed the power of martyrdom in deed, by the great boldness they had toward the heathen,
and showed their endurance in patience, without fear or trembling, they declined the name of martyrs before the brethren, because they were full of the fear of God.
And again, further on, they said that they humbled themselves under the mighty hand by which they have now been highly exalted. They gave relief to everyone,
and accused no one. They loosed everyone and bound no one.

And for those who inflicted evils on them they prayed, [saying] as [?]: "[Do not] [?] hold this sin against them." But if he prayed for those who were stoning him, how much more for the brethren?... And a little further on they said again:
For this was the whole great struggle they had with Satan:
Because love was perfect, so that the evil serpent might be choked, and that those whom they had thought had fallen might be restored while still alive.
For they did not boast over those who had fallen. Rather, out of what they themselves had in abundance they supplied the need of others.
For they had compassion on them like a mother for her children, and they poured out many tears to the Father on their behalf.
They asked him for life, and he gave it to them, and they shared it with their neighbors.
In everything they clothed themselves in victory and went to God. They always loved peace and entrusted peace to us, and in peace they reached God.
They left no sorrow for their mother, nor turmoil and conflict for their brothers, but joy and peace, harmony and love.”
These things were said about the love of those blessed people toward the brothers who had fallen, and have been placed here for our benefit,
because of the attitude of those who are without compassion or mercy and who attack the members of Christ without pity.
Third: Of the visions that Attalus the martyr saw in his dream. This same book about the martyrs we spoke of earlier also contains another story worth remembering.
Nothing prevents us from setting it before our readers. It goes like this...
One of them, named Alcibiades, followed a very austere way of life. Before this he had eaten and drunk nothing but bread and water.
He wanted to conduct himself the same way in prison too. But after the first contest that Attalus had endured, it was revealed to him
that Alcibiades was not doing well in refusing to make use of God's creatures, and that he was leaving others an example that would make them stumble.
Alcibiades was persuaded by them all. He took food and gave thanks to God.
For they were not left without the working of God's grace, but the Holy Spirit was their teacher.” Let this suffice concerning these matters.
Fourth: How the martyrs commended Irenaeus in their letters. Now the followers of Montanus, Alcibiades and Theodotus in Phrygia

first gained a reputation among many people for prophecy. For until that time the glorious signs of God's grace were being performed in many churches, and for this reason many people also believed about these men
that they too prophesied. But there was division over them. .܀. .܀. The brothers in Gaul, in the fear of God and in true faith, also wrote their judgment about these men.

They also addressed various letters from the martyrs who had been perfected among them, which they wrote while they were in prison, to the brethren who were in Asia and Phrygia. Not only to these, however,
but also to Eleutherus, who was bishop of Rome at that time, they made appeals concerning the peace of the church. And these, then, were those martyrs.
also Irenaeus, who was at that time a presbyter in the church of Lyons,
they commended him to Eleutherus, bishop of Rome, and gave much testimony about him, as their own words show, which read: "May you rejoice in God again [?].
We pray for you continually, our father Eleutherus.

We have written these letters earlier so that our brother and companion Irenaeus might bring them to you. We ask you to receive him, and we commend him to you, for he is zealous for the covenant of Christ."

But why do we need to give the list of names of the martyrs recorded in this book, of them and for them [?]: those whose heads were cut off and who were crowned, and those who fell as food for wild beasts?
and also those who died in prison, and the number of confessors who were still alive?
Whoever wishes can easily learn about them in full by taking up their book,
which we have also included with the collection of martyrs that we gathered.

Fifth: How God brought down rain from heaven through the prayers of the Christians for Marcus Aurelius Caesar. The events that took place in the years of Antoninus were the ones we have described above.

Now the story is told that the brother of this Marcus Aurelius Caesar, while he was drawing up for battle against the Germans and Sarmatians, found his army suffering from thirst for water, and he had no means of doing anything about it.

But the soldiers of the legion called Melitene, which from that time until now has been made up of believers, while they were drawn up facing their enemies, knelt on the ground, as is our custom when we pray, and made supplication to God. And this sight seemed something of a wonder to their enemies.
And while they were amazed, a wonder greater than this followed, namely a violent crash of thunder,
and it pursued their enemies and drove them to destruction. And with the rain it refreshed the whole army, because of those who had entreated God,

for the whole army was close to perishing from thirst. This story is found even among those writers who are far from our teaching, among whom this event took place. Some of our own people have also made it known. But the writers of histories who are outside, being strangers to the faith, recorded the wonder,
but they did not acknowledge that it happened through our prayers.
Our own writers, however, being lovers of the truth, recorded what took place plainly and accurately.

One of them is Apollinarius, who said about this legion that this wonder happened through its prayers, and that from that time it received from the king a name in the Roman language that suited what had happened.
A trustworthy witness to these things is Tertullian, who wrote in Latin an impassioned defense of our faith addressed to the Senate.
We have already mentioned this man. He confirms this account with substantial evidence that it actually happened.
He too writes and says as follows: “… Letters of Marcus, the wise emperor, still exist to this day, in which he testifies
that in Germany his army was close to perishing for lack of water, and that they were saved through the prayers of the Christians.
And he said about him that he even threatened with death those who wanted to accuse our people.
And after these things this man also said: "What kind of laws, then, are these laws of wickedness, injustice and cruelty, which are enforced against us alone,
which not even Vespasian kept, though he had conquered the Jews? Trajan even partly annulled them by forbidding that Christians be hunted down."
Hadrian too dismissed them, although he investigated everything. Nor did Antoninus, who was called Pius, observe them.
Sixth: The bishops who were in Rome. Let us now come to the order of the narrative.
When Pothinus had completed all the years of his life, ninety years, and had been perfected with those martyrs of Gaul, Irenaeus succeeded him in the episcopate of the church of Lyons.
In his youth he had been a disciple of Polycarp.

He wrote down the succession of the bishops who were in Rome in the third book that he composed against heresies, and he counted them up to Eleutherus, in whose days he had undertaken the labor of those books of his.
He speaks about them and sets them in order as follows: "The blessed apostles laid the foundations of the church and built it, and appointed Linus as bishop in it.
Paul the apostle mentions this Linus in the epistle to Timothy.
Anacletus succeeded him. After him, Clement received the bishopric, the third after the apostles.
This one saw the blessed apostles and associated with them, and the preaching of the apostles was still firm in him, and their tradition was before his eyes. He was not the only one, however;

many were still left at that time who had been taught by the apostles. In the days of Clement there was great dissension among the brothers in Corinth, and the church of Rome sent a letter to Corinth to bring them to peace
and to renew their faith and the tradition that they had recently received from the apostles."
A little further on he says again: "After this Clement, Evaristus received [the office]; after Evaristus, Alexander; and then Xystus was appointed, the sixth after the apostles.
After him came Telesphorus, who suffered martyrdom gloriously. After him came Hyginus, and after Hyginus, Pius.
And again after him, Anicetus. Soter received [it] from Anicetus, and after him Eleutherus received it, the twelfth after the apostles. In this same order and in this same teaching they handed down
the tradition that the church received from the apostles, and the preaching of the truth has reached down to us." Irenaeus said these things, in agreement with the accounts we have given earlier.

Seventh: That up to those times glorious signs were taking place through believers... In the treatises that Irenaeus wrote, which are five in number, on the refutation and overthrow of the knowledge falsely so called,

in his second treatise he wrote this account: that even in his days the demonstration of the power of miracles was preserved in the churches. He makes this known in these words: "that they are not much lacking in this, namely raising the dead as our Lord raised them,"
and the apostles by their prayers; and many times in the brotherhood too, when it was necessary, the church in our regions, place by place [?], asked it of God with fasting and much supplication.
Then the spirit of the dead man returned, and the man was given back in answer to the prayers of the saints.

And after these things he says again: "If they say that our Lord too did such things in mere appearance, we will bring them to the prophets and show them from them that everything concerning him was foretold and spoken beforehand, and was truly accomplished,
and that he alone is the Son of God.

And for this reason those who are truly his disciples, in his name and by the gift they received from him, do such things for the help of the rest of mankind, each according to the gift he received from him.
For some of them drive out demons faithfully and truly, so that many times, after people were cleansed of evil spirits, they believed and joined the church.
Others again have foreknowledge of things that are to come, and visions and words of prophecy. Still others heal the sick by the laying on of hands and restore them to health.
And indeed, as we said before, even the dead have been raised and have remained with us for many years.
But why should we say these things? For there is no counting the gifts that the church throughout the whole world has received from our Lord.
And in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified in the years of Pontius Pilate, it brings help to the nations every day, while it deceives no one.
And it does not give the gift for money; for just as it received freely from God, so it also gives freely."
Elsewhere, the same writer writes: We have heard of many brothers in the church who have the gift of prophecy,
who speak in all languages through the Holy Spirit and bring people's hidden things to light for their benefit,
and who recount the mysteries of God. We have said these things to show that, down to those prophets, various gifts continued among those who were worthy.

Eighth [chapter]: How Irenaeus mentions the divine scriptures. … Since, when we began this history, we promised to set down some of what the ancient presbyters and writers of the churches said in their times about the accepted books,
according to the tradition they received and handed down in their writings, and since Irenaeus is one of them, let us now set down his words, and first what he said about the holy Gospel:
He spoke as follows: Matthew also produced a written Gospel among the Hebrews in their own language,
"While Peter and Paul were preaching in Rome and establishing the church, and after the departure of these two,
Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, also handed down to us in writing what Peter used to preach. … And in turn [?] the one who was a companion of Paul
set down in a book the gospel that Paul used to preach. And after these,
John, the disciple of our Lord, who had leaned on his breast, also wrote a gospel while he was living in Ephesus of Asia."
These things he says in the third book of the treatise we mentioned before.
In the fifth book, he spoke as follows about John's Revelation and the numerical value of the deceiver's name:
[He also says:] "Since these things are indeed so, and this number is set down in all the ancient and accurate copies with care, and all those who saw John face to face bear witness,
and reason itself teaches us that the number of the name of the beast, according to the Greek way of reckoning, is known from its letters."
And a little further on he says again about him: "We, however, are not compelled, concerning the name of the deceiver,
to declare and speak about it with certainty. For if it had been necessary for his name to be openly proclaimed at this time,

it would have been told by the one who saw the revelation. For it was seen not long ago, but nearly in our own generation, at the end of the reign of Domitian." These things this man we have mentioned related about that Revelation.
He also mentions the first epistle of John and brings many testimonies from it, and likewise the first epistle of Peter. … And as for the book of the Shepherd, he not only knows it,
but also accepts it. He quotes it as follows: “The scripture has rightly said, ‘First believe that there is one God, who created and established everything.’”
but also [?] … And he makes use of the Wisdom of Solomon in his words and quotes from it as follows: "The vision of God brings about life, and life brings one near to God." …

He also mentions something remembered by a certain presbyter who had received [it] from the apostles, whose name he did not hand down to us, and he further sets down that man's interpretations of the divine scriptures.
He also mentioned Justin the martyr and Ignatius, and uses testimonies from their writings. … And he further promises with diligence that he would make [?]
that from among them, from the writings of Marcion, we shall stand against him.

How the Scriptures of the Spirit of God were translated by those Seventy who translated them. Hear what he writes in his words: "God, it says, became man, and he is the Lord who saved us and gave a sign: 'Behold, it says, a virgin shall conceive and bear.'"
It is not as some who now presume to translate the Scriptures have said: ‘Behold, the young woman will conceive and give birth to a son,’

"as Theodotion of Ephesus and Aquila of Pontus translated, both of whom were Jewish proselytes. Following them the Ebionites have gone and say that our Lord was born of Joseph..." And a little later he says again:
“Before Roman rule was firmly established, while the Macedonians still controlled Asia,
Ptolemy was eager to enrich the library he had established in Alexandria with the writings of all peoples, wherever they were worth the effort.
He asked the people of Jerusalem to let him acquire their books and translate them into Greek.
"Since they were subject to the Macedonians at that time, they sent to Ptolemy seventy elders who were learned in the Scriptures and knew both languages. God, however, was doing what he willed.
The king wanted to put them to the test, for he was afraid that they might agree together with one mind and in their translation hide the truth that is in the Scriptures.
He separated them from one another and ordered them all to write a translation of the same text. He did this for all the Scriptures.
When they had assembled and all came together before Ptolemy, he compared each one’s translation.
God was glorified, and the Scriptures were recognized as truly belonging to God, because they all alike spoke the same words and names, from beginning to end.
And all the peoples who were there recognized that the Scriptures had been translated through God's prompting.
And this deed of God was not astonishing. For he also, during the captivity of the people that took place in the days of Nebuchadnezzar, when the Scriptures had been destroyed,
and after seventy years, when the Jews returned to their land in the time of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians,

He gave the Spirit to Ezra the priest, of the tribe of Levi, so that he might write down all the words of the former prophets and give back to the people the law that had been given through Moses." All these things Irenaeus said.
Ninth: The bishops who lived in the days of King Commodus.
When Antoninus had completed nineteen years of his reign, Commodus succeeded him.
In his first year, Agrippinus had completed twelve years of service as bishop of the church of Alexandria, and Julian succeeded him.
Tenth: On Pantaenus the philosopher.

At that time the head of the school of the faithful in Alexandria was a man renowned for his training in wisdom, whose name was Pantaenus. For from ancient custom there had been established among them a school for teaching the holy words, which has continued even to our own time, and it was maintained by men who were powerful in speech and in zeal for the fear of God. And it is said that of all those who excelled at that time,
this man of whom we are speaking was illustrious; and he came from the philosophical school of those called Stoics.

They say this about him: that he showed such a zealous disposition for the word of God that he even became a herald of the gospel of Christ to the peoples of the East, and went as far as the land of India.
For at that time there were still many evangelists of the word of God, who with divine zeal took up the imitation of the apostles, and were eager for the growth and building up of the word of God.
Pantaenus himself was one of them. It is said of him that he traveled as far as India and found the Gospel of Matthew there.

[It is said that it,] before his going there, was with people there who had believed in Christ, to whom Bartholomew, one of the apostles, had preached; and he had left them the book of the gospel of Matthew in Hebrew letters,

and it had been preserved among them until that time. This Pantaenus, then, with all his excellent achievements, at last became head of the school in Alexandria; and both by living voice and by written treatises he laid up the treasure of the teaching of the fear of God.
Eleventh: On Clement of Alexandria. In the days of Pantaenus, Clement was well known in Alexandria, being trained in the Scriptures of God. He was a namesake of the bishop who had been in Rome,

who was a disciple of the apostles — the one who had been in Rome, who was a disciple of the apostles. This Clement, in the treatises that he wrote under his name, mentions Pantaenus as having been his teacher. He does so also in other treatises.
And in the first treatise he alludes to this Pantaenus, when he speaks of notable men who received [the tradition] and were carried on from the apostles.
He speaks thus: "... This account, he says, which I set forth for us, is not a book carefully crafted for display; rather, we are laying up memoranda as a treasury for old age,
and an image of those living and powerful images of the words of blessed men whom I was deemed worthy to hear and see, who are truly worthy of an honoured memorial.
Of them, one was from Greece and another from Syria,
another from Egypt, and another from the East. Of these, one was from Beth Aramaye, and another was a Palestinian, who was by origin of the Hebrews.
Last of all I met the one who was first in power, and I found him hidden and unknown, and I found rest with him in Egypt. These, then, who preserved the perfection of the teaching of the truth,
“directly from Peter, James, John, and Paul, those holy apostles.

They received it as sons from their fathers. But those who are like their fathers are few. Yet by the will of God they have reached even to us, those who sowed in us the holy seed of our fathers the apostles.
Chapter Twelve: The Bishops Who Were in Jerusalem. ... At that time, Narcissus was well known as bishop of the church in Jerusalem.

...who is renowned even to this day. He was fifteenth in the succession from the destruction of the Jews in the years of Hadrian. From that time the church of the Gentiles first began to be established there, after those of the circumcision. We have learned that the first bishop there from the Gentiles was Mark, and after him Cassian, as the list of the succession there shows.
After him came Publius, and after him, in turn, Maximus. After these came Julian, and after him Gaius.
After him came Symmachus and another Gaius, and then another Julian. After these came Capito, and after him Valens.
Then came Dolichianus, and last of all Narcissus. In all, they numbered thirty in the succession after the apostles. ...

Thirteenth: on Rhodon, and on the dissension he records concerning Marcion. At that time there was also Rhodon, who was of Asian origin and had been taught at Rome by Tatian, of whom we spoke earlier, as he himself relates.
Various books are attributed to this man. Among them he also wrote one against the heresy of Marcion, which in his days had split into various opinions.
as is related, when he wrote about those who caused the division, and carefully refuted the false teachings that each one of them had devised and invented.
Listen, then, to what he writes: “They have therefore become divided among themselves because they base themselves on an opinion that has no firm foundation.
“From their own flock, Apelles, who prides himself on his gray hair and old age, acknowledges one first principle.
“He says that the prophecies come from an opposing spirit, because he is persuaded by the utterances [?] of a certain demon-possessed virgin named Philumena.
“Others, however, introduce two first principles, as Marcion did. Among them are Potitus and Basilicus.

"And others followed Potitus. They were not able to distinguish things, just as he himself could not, regarding the things that are explained [?]. They turned and said that there are two principles, simply asserting it without demonstration.
Others of them, again, plunged into worse things than these, for they posit not only two natures,
but even three.
Their head and leader is Syneros, as those who hold his teaching say.
Rhodon also wrote that he came into debate with Apelles, and he spoke as follows: "For the old man Apelles, when he talked with us,
was refuted in many of the things he wrongly said. So he said that the doctrine need not be examined at all, but that each person should remain as he had believed.
For he said that all who hope in the one who was crucified will live, as long as they are found in good works. And he taught things more perverse than all the rest, as I said before.
concerned God: he posited one first principle, as we also say. After positing it, he went on to say that he based it entirely on his own thinking.
And when we said to him in reply, 'Where do you get the demonstration for this?'
or 'How can you say there is one principle? Explain it to us,' he said that the prophecies refute themselves, because they say nothing that is true.
For they do not agree with one another, and they are false and contradict themselves. He said that he did not know how there was one first principle, but only that he was moved to think so.
Again, when I put him under oath to tell the truth, he swore and said: 'I am not persuaded of how there is one self-existent God; I only believe it.'
But I laughed and despised him in my mind, because he said of himself that he was a teacher, yet he did not know how to establish what he taught..."
In this same work he wrote to Callistion and acknowledged that he had been taught by Tatian in Rome.
He said that Tatian had taken pains to compose a book of Questions, in which he promised to demonstrate
what was hidden and unknown in the things written in the divine Scriptures. Rhodon himself, however, promised in his own work to compose solutions to Tatian’s questions.
He also has a book on the Six Days.

Apelles, about whom we have said many things, blasphemed against Moses, and along with him he also blasphemed against the words of God in his many treatises. And as he supposed in his mind, he was very eager to refute the scriptures and to [?] correct them. These things were said about these matters.

Fourteenth: on the false prophets who were in the heresy in Phrygia. But the enemy of God's church, who hates good things and loves hateful ones, left no scheme of deceit untried in working against people.
Again he worked hard to raise heresies against the church. Some of these crept about in Asia and in Phrygia like a cursed, venom-spitting reptile. Montanus boasted that he was the Paraclete.
Prisca and Maximilla were women who belonged to his following, and they too boasted that they were Montanus’s prophetesses....

Fifteenth: on the schism of Florinus and Blastus that took place at Rome. Others were flourishing at Rome, and their head was Florinus, who fell from the presbyterate of the church. With him was Blastus, who likewise fell as well. These men drew many members of the church to their own views.
And each of the two, on his own, was striving to stand against the truth...

Sixteenth: what is said about Montanus and the false prophets who were with him. Against the heresy called that of the Phrygians, the power of truth raised up at that time a strong and invincible one to contend against them: Apolinarius of Hierapolis, whom the account mentioned earlier.

…and to many others with him, men learned in speech, from whom many writings of history have been left to us. Apolinarius, when he began to write against them, shows that he had refuted their error even without writings. At the beginning of his discourse he writes as follows.
"A very long time ago, our beloved Avircius Marcellus, I was urged by you to compose a treatise against the heresy that is called after Miltiades.

I have held back until now. This was not because I was unable to refute the falsehood and testify to the truth. It was because I was diffident and afraid that people might think I wanted to add something to the teaching of the covenant of the new gospel.
For whoever wishes to live according to the teaching of the gospel cannot add anything to it or take anything away from it.
For [?], I went to Ancyra in Galatia and found the church of Pontus disturbed by this ‘new prophecy,’ as they call it.
As the facts make clear, however, it is false prophecy. As far as I was able, with the strength granted by our Lord’s grace,
We spoke in the church about these things, and about whatever was being discussed, for many days, so that the church rejoiced and those who were opposed withdrew for a time.

And those who stood against us were fallen on their faces in distress. The presbyters who were in that place urged us to leave them in writing the things that had been said against those who oppose the word of truth. The presbyter Zoticus was with us in our ministry at the time.
We did not do this, but we promised that, by God’s grace, we would diligently write these things here and send them to them.”
After these things he says other things.

At the beginning of his discourse he tells about the one who was the cause of this heresy, when he comes to it in his account, as follows: "The cause of how the division of their heresy against the church came to light was this.
There is said to be a village in Mysia of Phrygia named Ardabau.

For it is said there about a man named Montanus, who had recently become a believer, in the days of Gratus, proconsul of Asia, that in his great craving and love of leadership… And suddenly he went out of his mind and began to prophesy and to speak strange words.
contrary to the custom of the church's tradition.
Some of those present at that time who heard his strange words were distressed.

They treated him as a man under the working of a demon and a spirit of error that throws the people into confusion. They rebuked him and stopped him from speaking, because they remembered the commandments of our Lord, who warns us to guard watchfully against false prophets.
But there were others who stared at him as though he had the Holy Spirit and the gift of prophecy. They became puffed up in themselves and did not remember our Lord's commandment.

That harmful [?] spirit wounds and blinds the mind and leads the people astray. As people were led astray and deceived by it, they kept urging it on, so that it could no longer be silent. This happened through the craft and skill of the Adversary, who schemed to destroy those who listened to him by having them honor him beyond what was fitting. He stirred up and inflamed their minds, which had fallen asleep away from the true faith.
He also raised up two other women and filled them with the spirit of falsehood.
They spoke in madness, at inappropriate times and outside the proper order, just like Montanus.
To those who gazed at him and were puffed up, that demon himself gave praise.

He made them proud through great promises. At times, though, he also condemned others, with an appearance of reason, so that he might be thought worthy of belief and might also be regarded as one who reproves. Those Phrygians who went astray were few.

And that demon, through his boldness, teaches them to blaspheme the whole church under heaven, because it did not receive him with honour, and that demon found no way into it for the false prophecy. For all the believers in Asia gathered many times, in many places, because of this.

And they examined these loose words that were being spoken, judged that they were profane words, and rejected this heresy. And so they were thrown out of the church and cut off from its communion. … Apolinarius was the first to relate these things.
Throughout his discourse he refuted this error. In his second discourse he spoke as follows about the end of these people: ...
Why, then, do they call us despisers of the prophets because we did not accept their false prophets?
For they say that these are the ones whom our Lord promised to send to that people. Let them answer us, as before God.
Was anyone among the followers of Montanus, or among those women who began speaking falsehoods, persecuted by the Jews or killed by the lawless?
there is not even one. Not a single one of them was seized because of this name and crucified.
Nor in the synagogues of the Jews
was any one of these women of theirs ever scourged or stoned. Instead, they are said to have died by another kind of death. For Montanus and Maximilla,
these two were driven by that destructive spirit and killed themselves. They did not do this together, but each at the time of his or her own death.
And this is the report about them, that they died in this way, like the death of Judas the traitor.
And a story is told about the leader of what they call prophecy, namely Theodotus, who acted as their steward:
he lost his mind and trusted that spirit of deception, believing that he was being raised and carried up to heaven. He fell and died a terrible death.

They say that this was so. But until we see whether you will be persuaded about this, let us not give a decision, O blessed ones. For either it is so or it is not. Montanus, Theodotus and Maximilla have certainly died.
He said in this treatise that the holy bishops of that time wished to refute the spirit that was in Maximilla, but others prevented them, namely those who were helping that spirit.
He writes as follows: "Do not let the spirit that was in Maximilla say, as it is quoted by Asterius Urbanus, 'I am chased like a wolf from the lambs.'"
I am not a wolf. I am word, spirit, and power.’ But if there is power in this spirit, let it show itself in action and expose
and, through that spirit, compel those who came to silence and rebuke the spirit while it was speaking to acknowledge it.
These were distinguished men and bishops: Zoticus from the village of Comana and Julian from Apamea.
The followers of Themison restrained these men and did not allow them to rebuke that spirit and show that it was false and was misleading the people.”
In this same discourse he also said other things to expose Maximilla’s false prophecy. He also spoke about the time when he wrote these things.
He also recalls words of her prophecy in which she foretold that there would be war and disturbance. He exposes her falsehood and says: "How has this too not been shown to be a lie?
For it has now been more than thirteen years up to this day since this woman died."
and there has been no war, either throughout the world or in any particular place. Rather, through God’s mercy, there has been a long peace, especially for Christians.”
These things are from the second book.
From the third book I will set down a few words about those who boast that many martyrs also came from among them.
He says: "When they have been refuted on every point and have nothing to say, they take refuge in the martyrs and say, 'We have many martyrs, and this is a trustworthy proof.'
But that spirit of prophecy said to be among them is false. For this claim, above all the others, is without truth.
For there are also other heresies that have many martyrs. Yet we do not say on that account that their beliefs are sound,
nor do we acknowledge that they possess the truth. Foremost are those of the Marcionite heresy, who say that they have many martyrs,
But they do not truly confess Christ himself." A little further on he says again:

"For this reason, when those who hold the true faith are called from the church to martyrdom together with the martyrs of those called from the heresy of the Phrygians, they separate themselves from them."
and meet their end without entering into fellowship with them, because they are unwilling to believe in the spirit that is in Montanus and these women.
This is true. It happened even in our own days in the city of Apamea, which is on the river Maeander, in the case of Gaius and Alexander and their companions, who suffered martyrdom from Eumenea.”
Seventeenth: on Miltiades and the book he wrote. In this book, written by the man we are speaking about, he also mentions Miltiades, a church writer,

who also wrote a book against this heresy. When he quotes something from their words, he adds: "I found these things in one of their books, which oppose the book of our brother Alcibiades, in which he [?] shows
that a prophet should not speak out of his senses." Then, briefly, as he continues his discussion,

he lists those who prophesied under the New Covenant, among whom he counts a woman named Ammia, and Quadratus. He says: "The false prophet is out of his senses, and for this reason he is without [?] and without fear.
He begins willingly in ignorance,
but against his will he is turned to madness, as I said before. They cannot show that any of the prophets clothed with the Holy Spirit, in either the Old Covenant or the New, behaved in this manner:

not Ada [?], nor Judas, nor Silas, nor the daughters of Philip, nor Ammia of Philadelphia, nor Quadratus, nor any of the others. So let them no longer boast about these, since they have no share with them.
And again, a little later, he said: For if, after Quadratus and Ammia of Philadelphia, as they say, these
the women of Montanus's circle received the gift of prophecy, let them show who among those of Montanus's circle and their women received it.

For the apostle said that the gift of prophecy must remain in the church until the final coming. But they cannot show it, for it has been fourteen years from the death of Maximilla until now." This, then, is what he said.
This Miltiades of whom he spoke has also left us a record of other diligent work on the words of God:
in the book he wrote against the pagans, and in another that he composed against the Jews. After these, he wrote two books each on the rest of these matters.
He also wrote a defense against the pagans on behalf of the philosophy that he followed.

Eighteenth: how Apollonius refuted the heresy of the Phrygians, and whom he mentioned. Apollonius, a writer and a son of the church, also wrote a book of refutation against the heresy called that of the Phrygians, while it was still strong in Phrygia. He shows that the prophetesses named by them are false, and he exposes the kind of conduct that the leaders of this heresy followed.
Hear, then, these words that he says about Montanus:

But who this new teacher is, his works and his teaching show. He is the one who taught the dissolution of marriage and laid down the law of fasting. He called Pepuza and Tymion, which are small cities of Phrygia, 'Jerusalem', and he wanted to gather there everyone who had been persuaded by him from every place.

He appointed collectors of money, and under the name of offerings he contrived to take bribes. He gives wages to those who preach his teaching, so that the teaching of his word may be strengthened through their greed.
These things he said about Montanus. And about his prophetesses, when he came to them in his discourse, he wrote thus: "We show first, then, concerning these his prophetesses..."
that, after they were filled with a spirit of falsehood, they abandoned their husbands. How, then, can they lie about Prisca and call her a virgin?”

And again he goes on to say: You know that all the scriptures forbid a prophet to take gifts and money. So when I see a prophetess who has taken gold, silver and fine garments, how could she not be called to account? And again, as he comes down to the matter,
he spoke thus about one of their confessors: "And again, Themiso also,

who was clothed in covetousness under a guise fit to be accepted, who did not bear the sign of confession but released himself from his bonds with a great deal of money; and when he ought to have been humbled in mind because of this, he boasted as if he were a martyr,
He even dared to imitate the apostle and write a general epistle, to instruct those who had believed more faithfully than he had, so that they would engage with him in empty arguments

and they blaspheme against our Lord and against his apostles and against the holy church." And again, about another one, who was honoured by them as a martyr, he spoke thus: "So as not to speak about many,
let the prophetess tell us about Alexander, who called himself a martyr,

with whom she used to feast, whom many worship, and her too; concerning whose robberies and audacity, and the other things for which he was condemned, we need not speak, but the [?] of the records [?] holds them.
Which, then, forgives sins to which? Does the prophet forgive the martyr his robberies, or does the martyr forgive the prophet his covetousness?
For when our Lord said, 'Do not acquire gold or silver, nor two tunics,'

these men have transgressed in complete opposition, in the very possessions that were forbidden to them. For we show concerning those who are called martyrs and prophets among them that they collect money not only from the rich, but also from the poor, from orphans, and from widows.
But if they have confidence, let them stand on this and lay down a decision that, if they are convicted, they will cease from their transgressions from now on.
For the fruits of the prophet must be tested, since by its fruits the tree is known.

So that those who wish to learn about Alexander may know, we will show it plainly. This man was condemned by Aemilius Frontinus, proconsul at Ephesus, not because of the Name, but because of the robberies he boldly committed.
And when he had become a denier, and swore and lied in the name of our Lord, and led astray the believers who were there:
his own church, the place he came from, did not receive him, because he was a robber. Those who wish to learn about him
have the archive of Asia.
This prophet does not know about him, though he was with her for many years.
We rebuke this one, and through her also her possessions.

And we rebuke this prophet in the same way, and we are able to show this to many. But if they are confident, let them accept the rebuke. Again, in another place in the same treatise, concerning those prophets of whom they boast, he adds and says this:

"If they deny that their prophets have taken bribes, let them admit this: that if they are convicted of having taken them, they are not prophets. And I bring ten thousand proofs of these things. It is necessary that all the fruits of the prophet be tested.
Tell me, then: does a prophet bathe? Does a prophet adorn himself?

Does a prophet love finery? Does a prophet play at gaming tables and dice? Does a prophet lend at interest? Let them admit whether these things are permitted to be done or not; but I will show that they have been done among them." And Apollonius himself relates in this same treatise
Forty years had passed by the time this treatise was written, since Montanus embarked on this supposed prophecy. And he also said:
that Zoticus, whom the earlier writer mentioned, when Maximilla was making herself out to prophesy in Pepuza, rose to rebuke the spirit that was at work in her,
and those who shared her views prevented him. He also mentions Thraseas, a martyr of that time. And again he says, as if from tradition,
that our Savior had commanded his apostles not to go away from Jerusalem for twelve years. He also makes use of testimonies from the Revelation of John.
And he relates that John also raised a dead man in Ephesus by the power of God.
He said other things as well, in which he thoroughly refuted this heresy we have discussed. These things Apollonius said.
Chapter nineteen. What Serapion said about the heresy of the Phrygians.
Serapion, who succeeded Maximinus as bishop in the church of Antioch, mentions what Apollinaris said against this heresy of the Phrygians.
Serapion mentions him in the letter he wrote to Caricus and Pontius, in which he too refutes this heresy.
And he added in it: "So that you may know that the working of the falsehood of what is called the New Prophecy is abhorred by the whole brotherhood throughout the world."
I have also sent you the writings of the blessed Claudius Apollinaris, who was bishop in Hierapolis in Asia.”
In this letter of Serapion the signatures of many bishops are also set down. Some of them signed like this: ...... Aurelius Cyrenius, martyr.

"I pray that you may be well..." Another signed in this form: "Aurelius Publius Julius, bishop of Debeltum in Thrace. As God in heaven lives, the blessed Sotas who was in Anchialus wanted to cast out the demon that was in Priscilla, and the hypocrites did not let him."
Many other bishops who agreed with these also put their signatures to this letter. Such, then, were these matters.
[?] which Irenaeus spoke of in writings against the schisms that existed in Rome. There were men in Rome who were perverting the truth of the laws of the Church. Irenaeus wrote various letters.
One he entitled Against Blastus, Concerning Schism; another, Against Florinus, On the Sole Principle, and That God Is Not the Author of Evil.

For this man held firmly to this opinion. And again, because he had been drawn into the error of the school of Valentinus, Irenaeus also diligently composed a treatise On the Ogdoad, in which he notes
that he himself had received the first succession from the apostles.
At the end of this treatise I found another note, which it is fitting to reproduce in this book. It reads as follows:

"I adjure you who copy this book, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by his glorious coming, in which he comes to judge the living and the dead, to compare what you have copied and correct it against this accurate copy from which you copied it. And [?] you are also to write out this adjuration
and place it in the book you have copied." These things were said by that man to good purpose. We repeat them so that we may have a perfect example of diligence
of the accuracy of those holy and early men.
In the letter we mentioned, which Irenaeus wrote to Florinus, he again reminds him of his association with Polycarp and speaks confidently as follows:

For these teachings are not in agreement with the Church, and they cast whoever is persuaded by them into great wickedness. These teachings not even the heretics outside the Church have ever dared to utter. These teachings...
The presbyters who were before us, those who were disciples of the apostles, did not hand these things down to you.
For I saw you when I was a boy in lower Asia with Polycarp, in the royal court, where you were conducting yourself splendidly and striving to win his approval.
For I remember the things of that time more clearly than things happening now. For what is learned in childhood
grows along with the soul and becomes interwoven with it. For this reason, I can even describe the place where the blessed Polycarp used to sit and teach,
and his goings out and his comings in;

and the manner of his life and the appearance of his body, and the teaching he used to teach the people, and the way he had lived with John and with the others who had seen our Lord, as he used to relate.
and how he remembered their words, and what he had heard from them about our Lord, the miracles he performed, and his teaching.
Polycarp had received these things from those who had seen the living Word with their own eyes, and everything he recounted agreed with the Scriptures.
These things too at that time, because of the grace of God that was upon me,
I listened to carefully and stored them up in memory, not on paper but in my heart. And by the grace of God I constantly and lovingly recall them.
And I can testify before God that if that blessed elder, who learned from the apostles, had heard anything like these things,

He would cry out, stop his ears, and say as was his custom: "O good God, for what times have you kept me, that I should have to endure these things!" And if he heard words like these, he would even flee from the place where he was standing or sitting.

This which I have said can also be known from the letters he wrote, either to the neighboring churches to strengthen them, or to certain of the brothers to teach and admonish them. These things Irenaeus said...
Chapter Twenty-One: How Apollonius suffered martyrdom in Rome. During the reign of Commodus, the persecution had subsided,

And by the goodness of God there was peace [?] for all the churches throughout the whole world, while the teaching of life was turning every soul from the whole race of mankind to the worship of the fear of God,

so that even many of those in Rome who were well known for wealth and great lineage turned to their life, together with all their households and their kindred. But the envious demon who hates good things could not endure this. Instead he contrived to clothe himself again against us with various schemes.
And he brought Apollonius to trial, a man renowned among the [?] of that time for his education and wisdom.
For he stirred up one of his ministers, who are ready for such things, to accuse this man.
But this wicked man himself had his legs broken because he had brought the case at an improper time, since by the emperor's command those who informed about such matters were not allowed to live.
that the judge Perennius pronounced this sentence on him. But this martyr, beloved of God, when the judge earnestly entreated him to speak before the council of the senate,
gave a very wise defense of the faith to which he was bearing witness. Then, as if by a decree of the senate, he was condemned to be beheaded, and so he was crowned. For they had an ancient law
that those who once come into court and do not turn from their opinion are not to be released.
Whoever wishes to learn his words, and the defense he made in answer to what he was asked by Perennis [?], and his whole defense before the senate, may learn them from the writings we have collected.
Twenty-two: Those who were known as bishops at that time...
In the tenth year of his reign, Victor succeeded Eleutherus in the bishopric.
At this time, when Julian had completed ten years in the ministry of the church of Alexandria, Demetrius succeeded him.
In these same times, in the church of Antioch, Serapion was known as bishop, the eighth from the apostles, of whom we spoke earlier. And Theophilus was governing the church of Caesarea in Palestine.
Narcissus too, whom the account mentioned a little earlier, was still holding office in the church of Jerusalem at that time.
At this same time, Bacchylus was bishop in Corinth in Greece. They were renowned in the church at that time
and for their steadfast faith, as we have learned from written accounts. We have listed these men by name because it was appropriate.
Twenty-third [chapter]: On the controversy that arose at that time about Easter. A great question was stirred up at that time, because the churches throughout all Asia, following an older tradition,

kept the fourteenth of the moon and observed it as the day of the feast of the Passover of the Saviour. On that day, it is written, the Jews used to sacrifice the lamb. They held that it was necessary by every means to break the fast on that day,
whatever day of the week it fell on.
But this was not the practice in all the churches throughout the whole world.

For according to the tradition of the apostles, this feast has been kept down to our own day in such a way that no one breaks the fast on any other day except the day of the resurrection of our Saviour.
So the bishops gathered together about this matter, and all of them, of one mind, wrote letters to all the churches everywhere

saying that, according to the law of the church, the mystery of our Lord's resurrection from the dead should be celebrated only on Sunday, and that only on this day should they observe the breaking of the Paschal fast.

Even now there still exist the writings of those who gathered at that time in Palestine. At their head was written Theophilus, bishop of the church of Caesarea, and Narcissus, of the church of Jerusalem.
There is also another document from those who had assembled in Rome concerning this dispute. It names Bishop Victor,

There are also writings of the bishops of other regions, at whose head Palmas was placed; of the churches in Gaul, whose head was Irenaeus; and also of the churches of Mesopotamia and the cities there;
and, individually, of Bacchyllus, bishop of Corinth, and of many others.
those who agreed in one mind and set down a single reckoning.
and that among those who were with us there was this one decision of which we speak.
Twenty-four: On the division that took place in Asia. ... Now the bishops who were in Asia were insisting on keeping that original feast which had been handed down to them.
Polycrates was the head over them.
In the letter he wrote to Victor and the church of Rome, he too set out the tradition he had received in these words:
“We observe the day without alteration, neither adding to it nor taking anything away from it.
[He wrote:] "For in Asia too great luminaries lie asleep, who will rise on the day of our Lord's coming,
when he comes in glory from heaven and seeks out all the saints: Philip, who was one of the twelve apostles, who sleeps in Hierapolis;
and his two daughters, who grew old in virginity. Another daughter of his lived under the guidance of the Holy Spirit and came to rest in Ephesus.
and also John, who had leaned on the breast of Jesus, who was a priest and wore the diadem of holiness, and was a martyr and teacher. He sleeps in Ephesus.
And also Polycarp in Smyrna, who was bishop and martyr; and Thraseas, bishop and martyr, from Eumenia, who sleeps in Smyrna.

What need is there to speak of Sagaris, bishop and martyr, who sleeps in Laodicea; or of the blessed Papirius; or of Melito the eunuch, who was guided by the Holy Spirit all his life, who is laid in Sardis
and awaits the visitation from heaven, when he will rise from the dead?
All these kept the fourteenth day for Easter, according to the Gospel, and did not deviate in anything, but followed the rule of faith.
Again, I too, Polycrates, who am the least of them all,
as I received from my brothers, some of whom I have followed. Seven of my brothers were bishops, and I am the eighth. And these brothers of mine always kept this day, when the people put away leaven.

So I, my brothers, have lived sixty-five years in our Lord. I have conversed with the brothers throughout the whole world and gone through all the holy scriptures, and I am not frightened by those who threaten.
For those who are greater than I have said, "It is right to obey God rather than man."
And to these things he adds, and speaks about the like-minded bishops who were with him when he was writing: "I could mention the bishops who were summoned here,
those whom you asked me to summon, and I summoned them; whose names, if I were to write them, are many. And I summoned them; whose names, if I were to write them, are many.
But these, who know my littleness, agreed to this letter, knowing that my grey hairs did not come in vain, but that I have always lived in Jesus Christ."
Twenty-fifth [chapter]: How there was one agreement everywhere about the Passover.

Now Victor, the bishop of Rome, wished to cut off at once all the churches in Asia, together with all the congregations near them, from the common unity, as if they were people who were divided [from the Church].
He proclaimed and bound them by letters, all the brethren there alike. But this did not please all the bishops.
Instead, they wrote and urged him to consider what made for peace, harmony, and brotherly love.

Their words are also extant in writings that they wrote sharply to Victor. Among them was also Irenaeus, who also wrote as on behalf of the brethren in Gaul who were under his charge. He maintained this: that the mystery of our Lord's resurrection should be celebrated at the Passover only on Sunday.

But he wrote to Victor that it was not right for him to cut off all these churches of God for keeping the tradition of an ancient custom. He asked many other things of him as well. And among his words he added and said this:
"For the difference is not only about the day, but also about the manner of the fast.
For some think that they ought to fast for one day, others for two, and others for several.
And there are some who measure that day as forty hours, day and night.
All this variation exists among those who observe it. And this did not happen only in our days, but also in the years of those who were before us,
who did not keep the feast precisely, but simply and in an ordinary way.
And all these had peace with one another, as we also do. Although there was a difference about the fast, the agreement in faith was confirmed.
And to these things he adds an account [?] which it is fitting to set down now, and it is this: "All the bishops of this church which you govern who were before Soter—
Anicetus, Pius, Hyginus, Telesphorus, and Xystus—
did not themselves observe this day, nor did they persuade those who came after them to observe it. And though they did not observe it,
they had peace with the people from other churches who came to them and who observed it, even though it was a point of opposition that some observed it and some did not.
Nor were people ever cast out because of this matter. Rather, though the bishops who were before you did not observe it, they sent communion to those in other churches who observed it.
When the blessed Polycarp came to Rome in the days of Anicetus, although they had a slight disagreement with one another over other matters as well, they immediately made peace with one another.

And they did not quarrel with one another over this matter. For Anicetus could not persuade Polycarp not to keep this day, because he had lived with John the disciple of our Lord and with the apostles, and had kept this day with them. Nor did Polycarp persuade Anicetus to keep it.
for he told him that we must keep the custom of our fathers, the bishops who came before.
And while things stood thus, they held communion with one another, and in the church Anicetus, by his permission, let Polycarp offer the offering.
And they parted from one another in peace, while there was peace throughout the whole church,

both among those who observe it and among those who do not observe it." Irenaeus, who lived up to his name, for in deed he was a peacemaker—this is what his name means—was asking for these things and urging them for the sake of peace.
And he wrote similar things in his letters about this controversy, not only to Victor but also to many leading men who were in the churches.
Now the bishops who were in Palestine, whom I mentioned a little earlier—Narcissus and Theophilus, and with them Cassius, bishop of the church of Tyre—
And Clarus of Ptolemais, and those who were assembled with them, wrote many things about the tradition of the apostles which they had received concerning the Passover (Pascha).

And at the end of the document they add these words: "Take care, they say, to send copies of this letter to the other churches, so that we may not be to blame for those who easily lead their own souls astray."
And we inform you that they also celebrate in Alexandria on the same day that we celebrate.
For letters go from us to them, and from them they also come to us, so that together, in agreement, we may celebrate this holy day.”

Twenty-sixth [chapter]: How many treatises have come down to us from the diligent labor of Irenaeus. Besides the treatises and letters of Irenaeus that we have mentioned, he also has a concise treatise against the pagans, which is of great value and is entitled "On Knowledge."
And another, written to a brother named Marcianus, on the demonstration of the apostolic preaching.
And another, a book of various discourses, in which he mentions the Epistle to the Hebrews and the Wisdom of Solomon,
and quotes some of their words. These, then, are the writings of Irenaeus that we know of.
Chapter Twenty-Seven. About the many men who were well known in those times.
When Commodus had reigned for thirteen years and died, and Pertinax had reigned for six months after the death of Commodus, Severus succeeded him.
Many writings by numerous ancient members of the church, composed with great care, still survive even to this day.

Those that we know are these: there is that of Heraclitus, which is on the Apostle; and that of Maximus on this question much debated by heretics, where evil comes from, and on this, that matter is created; and again that of Candidus on the Six Days, and that of Apion on this same subject.
And that of Sextus on the resurrection from the dead, and another work by Arabianus, as well as works by many others.
Because we have no evidence concerning them, we have not established their dates in this book or recorded any account of them in this history.
We have also seen writings by many others whose names we cannot give. They were members of the church who held the true faith, as their interpretations show.
But they are unknown because the names of those who wrote them are not recorded.
Twenty-eighth [chapter]: On those who from the beginning belonged to the heresy of Artemon,

what kind of people they were, and how they dared to corrupt the holy scriptures... And from among the learned men we have spoken of, a treatise carefully composed by one of them against the heresy of Artemon contains an account [?fitting] for this history we have undertaken. Paul of Samosata attempted to revive this heresy against us. For this heresy says of our Savior that he was a mere man.

He shows that it had broken away from the church not long before, because those who held to it boasted that it was ancient. He also set down many things to refute the lying words of their party. He speaks in these words:
"They say that all the earlier ones, and the apostles themselves, received and taught the things that we now say,

and that the truth of the preaching was preserved until the times of Victor, who was the thirteenth bishop in Rome after Peter, but that from Zephyrinus, who succeeded him, the truth was falsified. This might perhaps be credible
if the holy scriptures did not first stand against them.
There are also writings by some of our brothers that are older than the times of Victor. They wrote them on behalf of the truth against the pagans and against the heresies that existed at that time.
I mean the writings of Justin, Miltiades, Tatian, Clement, and many others, all of whom speak of the divinity of Christ.
For who does not know the writings of Irenaeus, Melito, and the others, which proclaim that Christ is God and a human being?
The hymns and songs written long ago by faithful brothers praise Christ, the Word of God, and speak of his divinity.
How, then, when the truth of the church is evident throughout all these years, can what these people say be true—that this opinion was preached until the time of Victor?
Oh, how are they not ashamed to slander Victor in this way, when they know for certain that Victor expelled from communion Theodotus, the head and father of this God-denying apostasy,

who was the first to say of Christ that he was a mere man? For if Victor believed according to the teaching of their party, as they say, how did he cast out Theodotus, the very inventor of this heresy?"
These things he said about Victor.
After Victor had served in his ministry for ten years, Zephyrinus succeeded him, in the ninth year of the reign of Severus.
And the one who composed this treatise goes on to tell, about the one who started the heresy we have spoken of, another thing that happened in the years of Zephyrinus. He wrote it in these words:
“I will remind the brothers of something that happened in our own days, which, I think, might have taught even Sodom wisdom if it had happened there.
There was a man named Natalius who was a confessor—not one from long ago, but from our own times.
At one time he was led astray by Asclepiodotus and another Theodotus, who was a banker.
"There were two of them, both disciples of Theodotus, of whom we spoke earlier, whom Bishop Victor separated from communion because of this foolish notion, as I said before.
They persuaded Natalius to accept a fixed [?allowance] from them and to be called bishop of this heresy, and to take from them one hundred and fifty denarii every month.
But while he was associated with them, he was admonished by the Lord many times through visions.
For the merciful God and our Lord Jesus Christ did not want him to be outside the church and perish,

Because he had been a witness of His Passion. But because he paid little attention to them, the visions, since he was ensnared by the leadership among them and by the shameful gains that destroy many, he was finally chastised by holy angels.
And all night long he was severely tortured.
At once he rose early in the morning, put on sackcloth, and scattered ashes over himself. With great earnestness and with tears he fell at the feet of Zephyrinus the bishop.
He threw himself down before everyone, before the people, and poured out his tears before the merciful church of the merciful Christ.
He pleaded and begged greatly, and showed the welts from the blows he had received; and with difficulty they admitted him to communion."
And to these he joins also other words of this writer, which run as follows: They have corrupted the holy Scriptures without fear,

and they have set aside the rule of the original faith, and they do not know Christ. And they do not inquire what the divine Scriptures say, but what form of syllogism they may find that strips the Son of his divinity.
They work hard at this. If someone asks them about a passage from the divine Scripture, they first ask what form of argument the passage can be made into: conjunctive or disjunctive.

They have abandoned the holy Scriptures of God and study geometry instead, as people who are of the earth and speak from the earth, and they do not know the one who came from above. Some of them study Euclid with great care.
Aristotle and Theophrastus are greatly admired by them. Indeed, Galen is practically worshiped by some of them.
They employ the art of unbelievers to support the thinking behind their own heresy,
They mix the craft of those who are without God into the simple faith of the divine Scriptures, though they do not even come near the faith.
Why do we need to say more about them? This is why they have laid hands on the divine Scriptures without fear and say, "We have indeed corrected them."
Anyone who wishes can find out that I am not slandering them.
If anyone is willing to collect the copies of each of them and compare them with one another, he will find that they differ from one another. The copies of Asclepiades differ from those of Theodotus
Many of their copies can be found, because their disciples diligently copy them,

in the "correction" made by each of them, as they call it, though they are really corruptions. Again, those of Hermophilus do not agree with these, and those of Apollonides do not even agree with each other.
If anyone compares the copies they corrected earlier with those they corrupted later, he will find that these also do not agree with one another.
It seems that they themselves also know how great the audacity of this sin is.
For either they do not believe that the holy Scriptures were spoken by the Holy Spirit, [?] they are wiser than the Holy Spirit.
But what else are they but madmen?
For they cannot deny this audacity and claim that it is not theirs, since it is written in their own hands.
For they did not receive the Scriptures in this form from those by whom they were taught.
and they cannot show where they copied them from to make their copies.
Some of them did not even bother to alter them,
Instead, through that lawless and godless teaching of theirs, they completely denied the Law and the Prophets.
and under the pretext of grace they were thrown down to the very depth of destruction. Let this be enough said about these matters.
The fifth book of the Ecclesiastical History is finished.
⁘ / Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, / for ever and ever. Amen.

While he was a fugitive in the regions of Palestine, they saw him for seven years. As for the church of Jerusalem: after Bishop Hymenaeus, whom we mentioned earlier, Zabdas took up the ministry there. But a short time later, when he died,
Hermon, the last, received the throne of the apostles, which was preserved there until the time of the persecution.
In Alexandria, after Marcus had held the episcopate for eighteen years following the death of Dionysius, Theonas succeeded him.
In his days, Achillas was also well known in Alexandria, along with Pierius the presbyter.
He was in charge of teaching the holy faith there. Few people could be found who were like him, for he stood out in the practice of philosophy and in the conduct of a life shaped by gospel teaching.
After Theonas had served for nineteen years, Peter received the episcopate in Alexandria after him, and he was greatly distinguished
during twelve years in the episcopate.
