He led the church for three years before the persecution. For the rest of the time of his leadership he governed himself with great diligence of spirit, and for the benefit of the churches

he cared for them greatly. There, then, in the ninth year of the persecution, his head was cut off and he was adorned with the crown of martyrdom. Up to this point we have composed the account of the succession from the days of the birth of our Savior
until the destruction of the churches in the persecution, which comes to three hundred and five years.

From now on let us give an account of those who fought bravely in the contest for the sake of the fear of God: who they were and what they were like. Let us leave a written record of them for those who come after us.
The seventh book is completed.

First chapter: On the things that happened before the persecution in our days... We have set out the succession of the tradition from the apostles in seven books, and in this eighth book

the things that took place in our days are not a matter to be despised, and it is fitting that we hand them down in writing for the instruction of those who come after us. So let us begin the account from here.

How great, and of what kind, was the freedom and glory that the word of the fear of God enjoyed before the persecution of our days, that word proclaimed through Christ to all humankind, among Greeks and among barbarians: this is too great a task for us to recount as it deserves.

Proof of it may be taken from the honor the emperors showed to those of our people to whom they gave authority to govern over the nations, and from the great love they kept toward the teaching of our faith.
They used to spare them from the vexation of the sacrifices for the peoples.
And what shall we say about those who belonged to the households of emperors, and also to those of high officials?

Those who, in front of their own household members, used to allow them freedom of speech concerning God, in word and in conduct, to their wives, their children and their servants. They allowed them not only to boast of the freedom of the faith, but even to do so gloriously.
and esteemed them more highly than those who had grown up with them. Such was Dorotheus,
He kept truth and faith with them more than anyone else.
Because of these things he was honoured by all who were in positions of authority and in governorships. So was Gregorius, who was famous like him.
All those who were like them were honoured because of the word of God. And how the leaders of the church were received with great honour on account of this by all the procurators and governors!

Second: On the destruction of the churches. But how could anyone describe the vast numbers of people who gathered, who were numerous in every city, and the crowds at the assemblies that took place in the churches on the appointed days?
Because of this they were no longer content with the old buildings. Instead, they enlarged, opened up and built churches from the foundations throughout the cities.

In those times, while these things were growing great and increasing every day, gaining strength and being added to, no envy stood in the way. No evil demon was able to show its jealousy, nor to hinder them through the schemes [?] of men,
as long as the hand of God from heaven was shielding and guarding his people.
as was fitting. But when our conduct changed because of the abundance of peace and freedom, many envied and reviled one another.
And not only this, but it was as though we were waging war against ourselves,
with contempt and wounding words. Leaders fought with leaders, and people rioted against people.

Hypocrisy grew without limit, and mockery increased and grew strong in wickedness. Yet the justice of God, gently, as befits it, stirred up its punishment quietly and moderately while the assemblies were still standing. The persecution began with the brothers who served in the army. But we did not notice it, and we did not take thought for how God might be reconciled to us and have pity on us.
Instead, like godless people, we thought that no one oversaw or punished our affairs, and we kept adding one wickedness on top of another.
Those who were thought to be shepherds pushed the law of the fear of God away from themselves.
They burned with quarrels against one another, and they only multiplied these things: quarrelling and threats, jealousy and strife, hatred toward one another, and tyranny.
They pursued love of power with all their mind. Then it was as in the words of Jeremiah, who said: "The Lord has darkened the daughter of Zion,
and cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth, and did not remember his footstool on the day of his anger.
and the Lord has sunk all the delight of Israel and overthrown all his strongholds."

And as it is said prophetically in the psalm: he rejected the covenant of his servant and cast his holiness to the ground through the destruction of the churches, and he broke down his walls and overthrew his strongholds.
"All who pass along the road have plundered him, and with these he has become a reproach to his neighbours.
He has raised the right hand of his enemies; he has turned back the help of his sword and has not helped him in battle.
He has brought an end to his purification and thrown his throne to the ground.
He has shortened the days of his youth
and covered him with shame." All these things were fulfilled upon us when the houses of prayer were torn down from top to bottom, to their very foundations,
and with our own eyes we saw the holy Scriptures of God being burned in the middle of the marketplace.
And the shepherds of the church were shamefully hiding here and there.
Some of them were seized in disgrace and mocked by enemies. And as it is said in another prophetic saying: he poured contempt on rulers and made them wander in a trackless waste.
But it is not my task to recount these things, nor even the divisions

among one another and the evils that came before the persecution; it is not ours to hand these on to memory. For this reason we did not wish to say anything more about them, except the things by which we vindicate the just judgment of God. So I did not wish to mention those who were tested in the persecution, or those who were utterly and completely shipwrecked and of their own will were cast into the depths of the abyss [?]. We will add to the general history only those things that will be of benefit first to us and then to those who come after us.
[Chapter] three.
On how those who were in the persecution carried on the contest.
Let us therefore now come and record, section by section, the glorious contests of the martyrs of the word of God.
It was the nineteenth year of the reign of Diocletian, in the month of Adar (March),

when the day of the feast of the Passion of our Savior was drawing near, and imperial edicts were published everywhere ordering that the churches be razed to the ground and the books be burned with fire, that those who held rank be degraded, and that those who were in servitude and had been freed,
if they persisted in the Christian way of thinking, be stripped of their freedom. The first edict issued against us was of this kind. But a little later

other edicts came, in which he ordered that all those who stood at the head of the churches everywhere should first be thrown into bonds, and afterwards be forced by every means to sacrifice. Then indeed many leaders of the churches

were the first to be subjected to cruel tortures. But other shepherds' souls gave way out of fear, and they were easily defeated at the very beginning of the battle. As for the rest, different kinds of torture were applied by turns to each one of them. One had his body beaten with blows; another, with tortures and unbearable torments, received [?] on the head, and through these tortures many came to a miserable end of life. Others, again, came out of the contest in other ways.
Chapter Four. Concerning God’s glorious martyrs: how their memorials filled every place, and how they received distinguished crowns for their devotion to God.
For there were some who, when others forcibly subjected them to judgment and brought them forward to the defiled and unclean sacrifice, were released as though they had offered sacrifice,
even though he had not sacrificed. And there was one who had not even come near, yet was brought near [?],

nor had he touched anything defiled; yet because others said that he had sacrificed, he bore the false accusation in silence and went away. Another, half dead, was carried off as though he were alive [?], and was thrown out like a corpse.
And again there was one who was thrown on the ground and dragged by his feet a long distance,

and they counted him among those who had sacrificed. And there was one who cried out and testified in a loud voice, renouncing the defiled sacrifices. Another cried out that he was a Christian, and gloried in confessing the name of the Savior. Another cried out that he had not sacrificed and would not sacrifice.
However, many were struck and silenced in many ways by the Roman troop that had been assigned to this task: they were struck on their faces and jaws and thrown out by force.
So greatly were the enemies of the fear of God satisfied [?] by any means at all.
to make it appear that their wishes had been carried out. But their efforts did not succeed with the holy martyrs, of whom words cannot give an adequate and accurate account.
For there were tens of thousands about whom one could tell, who displayed an extraordinary resolve for the sake of devotion to God,
not only after the persecution was stirred up against everyone, but also long before, while there was peace.
For at once, at first, as if from the top, he [?] who had received the authority of the empire was deeply stirred, and in his madness he secretly began the persecution against the churches
after the interval of time that came after Decius and Valerian.
Suddenly he set himself against us to wage war on us. First, however, he put those serving in the army to the test.

For he thought that by this he could easily overcome all the others, if he first fought against and overcame the many who were soldiers in the army. Then one could see them gladly accepting discharge and becoming like the rest of those who live as ordinary civilians, so that they would not deny the worship of God, the Creator of all.
For when the commander, whoever he was at that time [?], first began the persecution of the soldiers of the army, and was separating out and purging those who were enrolled in military service,
He required them to choose either to comply and remain in the rank they held, or, if they refused to comply and opposed the command, to be stripped of it.

And many who were soldiers of the kingdom of Christ readily and without hesitation valued their confession of him more than the glory they were thought to have and the high rank they held. And some of them, a few, gave up not only their honour

but also endured death for the sake of the true covenant of the fear of God. For at that time the one who was helping along the plot of evil was still emboldened only to shed the blood of a few. It seemed that he was still afraid of the great number of the believers and was holding back from threatening war against everyone. ⁘⁘⁘
Chapter Five. Concerning those who suffered martyrdom in Nicomedia. But when it broke out openly, no one could describe in words
How many these martyrs of God were, and of what kind, a person could see before his own eyes in every city and in the villages.

Then one of the notable men, one of those most highly praised in the ranks of honour esteemed in the world, as soon as this edict against the churches was posted in Nicomedia, was stirred with zeal for God and rushed forward in the fervour of faith. He took this edict, which was posted in a well-known place in the street, brought it down and tore it up, as something that had been posted in impurity and wickedness,
while two kings were in that very city:
that is, the one who was the eldest of them all, and the one who held the fourth rank of the government. This man was the first victor among the martyrs of that time.
In this manner they were glorified. He at once endured the things that are fitting for such daring, and without distress and without agitation he kept himself so until his last breath.

Beyond all the martyrs who have been wonderfully praised and became famous for courage at various times, among the Greeks and also among the barbarians, there were at this time the glorious martyrs of God who were of the company of Dorotheus,
who were members of the kings' households.

They had high honour from their masters, and were not set apart by them from the tender love shown to their own children. Yet they truly reckoned as more abundant wealth, beyond the glory and luxury of this world, the reproaches and pains suffered for the sake of the fear of God,
and the deaths of every kind that were newly devised against them. Of these I will mention one,

and what kind of end of the world he had, so that from it those who read this book may judge also what happened to the others. They brought him into the middle, in this city of which we spoke before, in the presence of these kings.

He was ordered to sacrifice. When he refused, it was ordered that he be hung up naked and his whole body be torn with blows until he should give in, so that he would do what was commanded even against his will.
When he suffered these things and did not change, and his bones could already be seen, they mixed vinegar with salt and poured it on the places of the flesh
that had been torn open. When he despised these pains too, they brought a gridiron of fire into the middle.
And like meat being roasted, the rest of his body was slowly consumed in that fire, little by little and not all at once, so that he would not find release easily.
Those who had placed him on that fire would not let him come up out of it until he agreed, even by a sign, to what he was being ordered to do. But he did not waver from his resolve.
Clothed in victory in those torments, he gave up his soul.
Such was the martyrdom of one of those members of the emperors' households, who was truly worthy of his name as well, for his name was Peter.
We know that the things that happened to the others were no less than these. But so as not to say too much, let us leave the rest and say only this: Dorotheus and Gorgonius, with many others,
who belonged to the royal household, after enduring a struggle involving every kind of suffering, received in return life and the crown of victory in God.

[?]. So much for those who were martyred from the kings' households. At this time Anthimus too, who stood at the head of the church of Nicomedia, had his head cut off because of his testimony on behalf of Christ.
Along with him a multitude of martyrs was suddenly added as well. In those days, I do not know how, a fire broke out in the royal palace in Nicomedia.

And as if on mere suspicion, a report went out that this outrage had openly been committed by our people. From then on, as if by order of the emperor, all the God-fearing people there together were put to death: some were killed by the sword
and some were burned up by fire. And it is said that, as if by the working of the ineffable will of God, men together with women were leaping into that fire and going into it.
The enemies put many others to the sword and threw them into the depths of the sea. As for those members of the royal households,

After they died and had been buried and laid in the earth, as was proper, they dug them up again, brought them out, and ordered that they too be thrown into the sea. For the kings, their masters, supposed
that while they lay in their tombs, people would worship them

and consider them gods. Such were the things that took place at the beginning of the persecution among these martyrs and those like them. * * * * * * After a short time, in the region called Melitene,
And again, in Syria too, other things sprang up [?] in this same kingdom, and they were plotting [?].
that all the heads of the churches in every place should be thrown into prison, by order.

And the sight of what happened in these events was beyond all telling. For multitudes beyond number were imprisoned in every place, and the prisons in every place, which had earlier been prepared for murderers and grave-robbers,
were then filled with bishops, presbyters and deacons,
and readers and exorcists, so that no room was found there for those condemned for evil deeds. Then other letters followed the first ones,

in which it was written about those who were imprisoned that if they sacrificed, they were to be released and go freely wherever they wished; but if they resisted and were not persuaded, it was ordered that they be torn apart with a great many tortures. And from then on, here too, how could anyone count the multitude of martyrs in every place, especially those in Africa and among the people of the Moors,
and in the Thebaid and in Egypt,
those who afterwards went out also to cities and to other regions and were made glorious in martyrdom?

Seventh: On those Egyptians who were martyred in Phoenicia. ⁘ We are well informed about those who came from Egypt and were victorious in Palestine. We also know about those in Tyre of Phoenicia, who filled with amazement anyone who saw them.
with countless blows, and through the endurance of these glorious athletes, in the truth of the fear of God, and in the contests that they were fighting.
who, immediately after their blows, were put with man-eating beasts,

facing the attack of leopards and bears and wild boars and bulls, which were goaded with burns of fire and provoked against them. And people were amazed at the glorious endurance of the brave ones before each one of the beasts.
We ourselves were also present when these things happened, as the power of God and of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ,

He for whose sake they were bearing witness stood by them, and by his deeds showed the martyrs victorious. And we saw savage beasts which for a long time stayed there and did not dare to touch or even approach the bodies of those beloved of God.
But they would rush with slight provocation upon other people, strangers who were from elsewhere [?]. Yet the glorious athletes alone, even while they stood naked,

And with their hands they would provoke them and draw them toward themselves, for this is what they had been ordered to do. Yet the beasts did not reach them at all. There were times when they even charged at them, but they were pushed back as if by the power [?] of God.

And again they would turn back. When this went on for a long time, it caused great astonishment among the spectators. And when the first beast did nothing, they would let loose a second beast against them. One would be amazed at the unshaken courage of these glorious martyrs, and at the steady endurance that lived in the bodies of young men.
For I saw a young man, not yet twenty years old, who stood without fetters and stretched out his hands in the shape of a cross,
and with a mind free of fear or trembling he was intent on God in prayer, and did not move or turn aside at all from the place where he stood,
while bears and leopards, breathing deadly fury, were close to reaching his body.
And so, as if by the power of God, their mouths were shut, and they turned back again.
Such was this man. Again, I saw others who were thrown to a wild [?] bull. Other people, outsiders, who came near it, it tossed into the air with its horns and gored, leaving them half dead.
But against the holy martyrs alone, even when it charged with fury and rage, it could not even approach them.
Instead it stamped its feet and tossed its horns this way and that, and because of the goading of the burns it breathed fury and rage; but by the providence of God it turned back.
Since even this did nothing to them, they again released other wild beasts against them. Finally, after these terrible threats of every kind,
they were all killed with the sword, and instead of being laid in the earth in graves, they were thrown into the depths of the sea.
Such was the contest of these Egyptians, who fought for devotion to God in Tyre.
Chapter Eight: About those who were martyred in Egypt.

One should also marvel at those who were martyred in their own land: how tens of thousands, men together with women and children, for the sake of the teaching of our Savior, despised this temporal life.

And they endured death in every form. After being torn with combs, scourged, and cruelly beaten, and after many kinds of terrible tortures, some of them were thrown into the fire. Others were drowned in the depths of the sea.

Others boldly stretched out their necks to those who cut off their heads. Others died under their tortures, and others wasted away from hunger. Others were crucified, some in the way that is usual for criminals.
Others of them were cruelly fixed head downward.
And they were kept alive until they died of hunger there on the wood.

[Chapter] nine: On those who were martyred in the Thebaid. The blows and pains that the martyrs in the Thebaid endured were beyond words. Instead of combs, their whole bodies were scraped with potsherds

until their lives came to an end. Women, too, were tied by one of their feet, hoisted up into the air by machines, and stretched out as they hung there naked. It was a hateful and merciless sight, harder than anything else for those who saw it.
Others again died tied to trees and branches. Using some device, they bent the hard branches of the trees, this one from one side and that one from the other, to a single point.
And the legs of the martyrs were stretched, one to one side and one to the other.
And they would let the branches go back to their places, for they planned to tear their limbs completely apart. These things were done not for days or a short time, but over a long period of years.
On some days more than ten people were killed, and on some more than twenty, and at times as many as thirty. On some days the number reached sixty, and at other times even a hundred.
In a single day men and women, together with children, were dying. They were [?] with different tortures of every kind. And we ourselves saw this with our own eyes,
when we went to those places. In a single day many people all at once had their heads cut off, and others received the punishment of fire,

so that the sword of the executioner grew blunt and could no longer cut. The killers themselves grew tired and worn out, though they took turns one after another. But we saw an astonishing zeal [?], with a resolve full of the power of God.
in those who believed in the Christ of God.
As soon as the first ones had received their sentence, others would rush in from another side before the judgment seat
and confess of themselves that they were Christians. They despised and scorned the persecutions, those afflictions and tortures of every kind. Without distress, they stood boldly in the fear of God.
With joy, gladness and laughter they received the final sentence of death, singing,
and they offered up praises and thanksgivings to the God of all until their last breath. These people were wonderful.
Even more wonderful were those who were distinguished for wealth, family and glory, and for the discourse of philosophy, and who above all were exalted in the fear of God
and in the faith of the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ.
Such was Polycarpus [?], who did not hold a lowly office but held the administration of Alexandria,
who, while he held his rank and the honor given to him by the Romans, and was attended by soldiers, was busy with lawsuits [?] every day.
and so was Phileas, bishop of the city of Thmuis,

a man renowned in his country for his rank of worldly honour and for his learning in philosophy. Many of their relatives and other friends pleaded with these two men, and so did those who held positions of authority. Even the judge himself pleaded with them to have pity on themselves
and to spare their children and wives. But none of this could draw them to choose and love the life of this present time,

to despise the law of confession, and to deny the Saviour. Instead, with a strong and sound mind, the mind of the fear of God, and with a soul that loved God, they endured all the judge's threats and insults.
At last the heads of both of them were cut off.
[Chapter] ten. [?] From the writings of Phileas to the people of Thmuis.
For all these demonstrations, wonders and excellent proofs are set before us in the holy books of God. The holy martyrs who were with us were not held back by anything.
Instead, they fixed the eye of their soul purely on the God of all.
They accepted death for the fear of God and did not turn away from their calling, because they had found our Lord Jesus Christ, who put on humanity for our sake so that he might cut off all sin.
And he set this before us as the way of life. For he did not count it a thing to be seized to be equal with God, but he emptied himself and took the likeness of a servant.
He was found in the form of a man and humbled himself to the point of death, the death of the cross.
Because of this, the martyrs who had put on Christ strove for the greater gifts. And all the pains and all the devices of torture, not only once,
Some even endured twice, and all kinds of trials. They suffered not only words but also deeds.
which the armed soldiers heaped upon them.
And they did not weaken in their resolve.

For perfect love casts out fear. But what words would be enough for us to tell of their victories and of their courage under every torture? Since anyone who wished to abuse them had the power to do so, some beat them with clubs and others with rods,
others with scourges, others with leather thongs, and others with ropes. Their tortures were a varied sight.
[?] … was to them, so that they would be without fear, after his end, in the fear of Christ.
Of the eleventh chapter: on those who were martyred in Phrygia.

Why then do we need to say much more, and add new stories on top of new stories about the contests and struggles of the martyrs throughout the whole world, who were destroyed under a general law, as if in war? For look: a whole city of Christians in Phrygia, with its men, its women, and the children in it, was surrounded by armed soldiers, who set fire to it and burned it
while the people were crying out and bearing witness before God. For all the people who lived in that city, the curator together with the magistrates,
and the officials together with all the people, confessed that they were Christians. They obeyed in nothing those who ordered them to worship idols.

There was a certain man named Adauctus, who held high rank among the Romans. He was one of the well-known men of Italy and had passed through every rank of honour granted by the emperor, as well as the general administration,
which among them are called magistracies and general offices, and he held them without reproach.
And he, who had gained distinction in all these things, finally, through the victory of devotion to God and through his confession of Christ,
while still holding the office of comptroller, endured the contest for devotion to God and was adorned with the crown of martyrdom.
Chapter Twelve. On the multitude of men and women

who contended in many different ways. Why do I now need to mention the rest by name, or count the multitude of men, or describe the tortures of every kind suffered by the wonderful martyrs? Some of them were cut down with axes, as happened in Arabia.
Some had their legs broken, as happened to those in Cappadocia. Others, in turn, were hung up high by their feet,
A slow fire was set under others, and they were suffocated by the smoke that rose from it, as happened to those in Mesopotamia.

Of others, the tips of their noses, their ears and their fingers were cut off little by little, and the rest of their limbs and the parts of their bodies were cut off, as happened to those in Alexandria.

And why do we need to bring up the memory of those in Antioch, who were roasted on fiery griddles, not to the point of death but to draw out their torture? Others quickly put their right hands into the fire so that they would not offer the abominable sacrifice. Still others fled from these trials,

threw themselves down from the height of the roofs before they could be seized and fall into the hands of the enemies. They regarded death as a prize snatched away, and as better than the wickedness of the wicked.
There was a certain holy woman in Antioch, remarkable for her resolve and distinguished in other respects:
in wealth, in family, and in the esteem of everyone. She had virgin daughters who were lovely in bodily beauty and in stature, and she had brought them up in the laws of the fear of God.

Because the tyrant's envy against them was greatly stirred up, he searched in every way and pursued them while they were in hiding. When he heard that they were in another place, he summoned them to Antioch by a ruse.
When they had been caught in the snare of the soldiers, and she saw that she had no way out,

[?] she and her daughters. She weighed in her mind the evils that come from men, and the most grievous of them all, the threat of fornication. She would not even let her ears hear it, or bear to think about such things.
If not, not even that they should surrender themselves to the worship of demons.

She said that it was more bitter than all deaths and worse than all forms of destruction. But she declared that there was one release from all these things, and this was taking refuge in our Lord. She counselled herself and her daughters, and when they had agreed on this decision,

they all wrapped their bodies modestly in their garments. When they were in the middle of the road, they asked the guards to withdraw a little, and then they threw themselves into the river that was flowing there.

These women, then, cast themselves away by their own hands. There were other virgins in that same Antioch who were of one accord and pleasing to God in everything. They were true sisters, renowned for their family, admirable in their conduct, and young in years.
They were beautiful in body, chaste in soul, beloved for their fear of God, and admirable in their zeal.
As though the earth could not bear to carry such lovely flowers, the servants of the demons ordered them to be thrown into the sea.
These too were treated in the same way as those.
Others in Pontus endured things that are dreadful even to hear. Their persecutors drove sharp reeds into the tips of their fingers, under their nails.
For others, they melted lead in the fire,
and they poured what had been melted (literally: turned) in the fire onto their backs, and they burned those parts of the body that are held in greater honour.
Still others endured hateful sufferings in their hidden parts and in their bowels, sufferings that were pitiless and unspeakable. These the illustrious judges, followers of the laws,

used to display their own ingenuity on them. As if it were an admirable wisdom, they used to devise and multiply [?] (literally: demons). They kept inventing new ones all the time, and they competed with one another for victory as if in a contest. But the end of the afflictions
when they finally grew weary of their excessive wickedness, became tired of killing, and were sated and filled with the outpouring of blood.
was this: they turned, as far as they thought in their minds, to kindness and mercy, so that from then on, as they intended, they would no longer do anything hateful to us. They said:

"For it is not fitting that our cities should be stained [?] with the blood of people of our own race, nor that the exalted rule of the kings, which is gentle and mild toward everyone, should be blamed for harshness."
For it was right, they said, that the clemency of the emperors' authority should extend its help to everyone, so that people would no longer be condemned to death.
"Rather, let this punishment against us be lifted because of the clemency of the emperors."
But orders were given that their eyes should be gouged out and one leg of each of them crippled.
For this was their mercy, and the imposing of light penalties (literally: heads) upon us.
And so, because of this mercy of the wicked, it is impossible for anyone to tell the number of those who endured. Some had their right hands cut off with a sword and were then cauterised with fire.
Others had their left feet burned at the joints and were maimed. And after these things
they were condemned to be sent to the copper mines in various places, not to do useful service.
but for the affliction and humiliation of the condemned. On top of all these, others were victorious in other contests that we cannot recount, for their excellent deeds are beyond words.
Through these things the victorious martyrs of Christ were glorified throughout the whole world, so that those who saw their courage were amazed everywhere.
and the demonstration of the hidden power of God
they openly displayed in the truth of our Saviour.

Thirteenth [chapter]. About those who stood at the head of the churches and showed the truth of the fear of God that they preached by the shedding of their blood. To name all of them would make a long account, and it is not even possible. But let us mention those leaders of well-known churches who bore witness. And first in the remembrance of the faithful
let the martyr of the kingdom of Christ be recorded: Anthimus, bishop of the church of the city of Nicomedia.

whose head was cut off for his confession. Among the martyrs in Antioch was Lucian, a presbyter of the church there, who was excellent all his life. He too was martyred in Nicomedia while the king was there. He proclaimed the heavenly kingdom of Christ before the king, first in word by means of a defence, and afterwards also in deed. Among those martyred in Phoenicia were well-known men, beloved of God in every respect, shepherds of the flock of Christ: Tyrannion, bishop of the church of Tyre; Zenobius, presbyter of the church of Sidon; and Silvanus, bishop of the church of Emesa. Silvanus, together with others, became food for wild beasts in the city of Emesa and was taken up to the companies of the martyrs. The other two honoured the word of God in Antioch itself, and both of them were glorified by endurance unto death. The bishop was thrown into the depths of the sea. Zenobius, who was a skilled physician, was torn with combs on his sides. He bore it bravely and died under his tortures. Among those martyred in Palestine was Silvanus, bishop of the church of Gaza.
At the copper mines at Phaeno, he and others, thirty-nine in number, were beheaded. Also from among the Egyptians, the bishops Peleus and Nilus, together with others, endured death by fire.

And to the great glory of the church of Caesarea, let Pamphilus the presbyter be remembered among these. He was the most wonderful of those who lived in our time, and the glory of his victories will be written at the proper time [?].
Of those at Alexandria: Peter the bishop, a man of God,
is to be recorded among the teachers of the fear of Christ, together with the presbyters who were with him, Faustus, Dius and Ammonius, perfect martyrs of Christ.
Also Phileas, Hesychius and Theodore, bishops of the churches in Egypt.

And there were many others with these, well-known people, who are commemorated by the churches in each place and each region. But as for what happened to all those throughout the whole world, the contests on behalf of the fear of God,
to set down in writing the victories of each one of them precisely

is not our task to recount, but that of those who saw the deeds with their own eyes. Those that I myself witnessed, however, I will make known in another book as a record for those who come after us. In this account, though, I will add to what has already been said the reversal of what happened to us, and what happened from the beginning of the persecution, which will be useful [?] to those who read these accounts.
Fourteenth [chapter] [?]: What the enemies of the fear of God were like.
Concerning the government of the Romans before their war against us: for as long as their rulers were in love and peace toward us,
what words could suffice to recount how many good fruits and how much abundance it was worthy of?
When those who held the authority of rule had completed ten years,
with festivals, feasts and joyful pleasures, and they lived in complete peace.

So it grew great without hindrance, and their authority grew stronger every day. But when it turned away from calm and from peace toward us, they had stirred up a fierce war. Before two years of this war had been completed, something new happened in their empire that overturned all their affairs. Grievous diseases came upon the head of their whole empire, and the disease turned even his mind to madness. He, together with the other one, who held second rank in honour after him, took up a private way of life like everyone else.
And while these things were still happening in this way,
their empire was divided in two in every respect, something that had never happened before.
had happened before.
And after a short time, Constantius was [taken] from the midst [?]. He had been gentle in all his conduct and kind toward those under his authority,

and loving toward God. He left after him, in his place, a beloved son, Constantine, Emperor and Augustus. He ended his life by the law of common nature, and he was the first to be named among the gods.
Even after his death, he received every honor owed to an emperor, this gentle and kindest of emperors,

He alone in our days completed the time of his rule in a way befitting the government of emperors. In other respects too he gave himself in honour and for the benefit of everyone. Nor did he take even the slightest part in the war against us.
Rather, he kept even the God-fearing who were under his hand
free from loss and free from harm. He did not destroy the buildings of the churches, nor did he introduce anything new against us. Because of this he received a good end, complete in blessings,
for he alone departed from this world while still in his reign, in harmony and in glory.
When his beloved son, chaste and God-fearing, received it from him (this was Constantine, who from the very beginning was shown forth as perfect emperor Augustus), he was proclaimed by his soldiers.
The first of them had been named by God, the King of all, and he set himself to imitate his father in the matter of the fear of God.
And this one was like this. ***
[?]-teenth [chapter]: On the things that happened besides these.
Along with these, Licinius too was proclaimed emperor Augustus, as if by a judicial vote of those who held the empire.

To Maximinus the great * * * * * * * * * * * * voices [?] and demons, and he was very eager for the error of idolatry. Apart from the divinations and prophecies of demons, he would not move anything, not even as much as a fingernail. For this reason he also added persecution, harshly and severely,
more than those before him.
so that he built temples in all our cities.
He ordered that the idol temples that had been destroyed long before be rebuilt with diligence, and he appointed priests of the idols for every [?] place and city.

And with these things: in every province he ordered that one priest be appointed, from among the well-known men who were leaders of the city and who had distinguished themselves in the service of an honoured rank.
with the camp of soldiers and armour. He honoured all sorcerers with governorships and great authorities, as though they were just men and lovers of God. And while he was engaged in these things,
in every place and city in the whole province under his authority, through exactions of gold and silver
and of countless possessions, and with a heavy burden of want, he oppressed and crushed [?] them.
From the rich he took the possessions that they held from their fathers, and wealth [?], and he gave heaps of possessions to his flatterers. He was so dissolute in drunkenness
so that, as in a drinking house, he even went out of his mind.
And he gave orders like these in his drunkenness, and when the wine had left him, the next day he came to regret. In his greed he laid on lavish, debauched banquets for everyone.
And he was a teacher of wickedness to his rulers and his subjects.
He urged the soldiers of the army to indulge themselves in luxuries and revelry. And he incited the governors and commanders of the army to oppress those under their authority by plunder and fraud.
so that they would practice tyranny along with him and as he did. But why should we recall this man’s abominable deeds, or count the multitude of women with whom he committed adultery?
so that he did not pass through a city without committing in it the corruption of women
and also the rape of virgins. In these things he succeeded with everyone except the Christians, who despised death, and to whom all this tyranny of his was reckoned as nothing.
For the men endured at his hands fire, the sword, the driving in of nails, being thrown to wild beasts, and being cast into the depths of the sea,
the cutting off of limbs, burns, the gouging out of their eyes, and the gradual mutilation of their entire bodies. Along with these things they also endured hunger, the mines, and imprisonment.
In all things they showed endurance for the sake of the fear of God,
Or rather, that they should exchange the worship of God for idols [?]. Women endured no less than men, for they were strengthened by the teaching of the word of God.

And some endured contests like men and received crowns like the victors. And those who were being dragged off to be defiled quickly handed over their souls to death, [?] their bodies to defilement. One woman, beyond all those the tyrant committed adultery with, was a Christian from Alexandria.
She was well known and highly regarded, and by her courageous resolve she overcame the lust of Maximinus’s soul. She was distinguished in other respects as well:

[distinguished] in wealth, in family, and in the training of wisdom, but she counted everything second to chastity. Though he pressed her greatly, he could not bring himself to kill her, because his desire was stronger than his anger, while she was ready to die. So he banished her and took all her possessions. Many other women, who could not bear even to hear threats of fornication, endured from the judges in every nation all kinds of racks, tortures and torments. These women were indeed admirable.
But more admirable still was one woman from Rome, chaste and renowned for her family,

whom Maxentius, the tyrant there, wanted to violate. He was striving to act like Maximinus. For when she heard that the attendants had come and were standing at her door, the ones who served the tyrant in such matters,

and when she saw that her husband, out of fear of him, allowed them to lead her and take her away, though he himself was prefect of Rome, she, because she was a Christian, asked for a little time, as if to adorn herself.
She went into her bedroom, and when she was alone, she took a sword and stabbed herself in the heart. When she died, she left her corpse to those who were standing there to take her away.

And by deeds that proclaim better than words she showed that, more than all possessions, the chastity of Christians is victorious and incorruptible. [She showed this] to all people, both those who are now and those who will come after us.
Such an abundance of evil was gathered together and perpetrated at the same time by the two tyrants who held power in the East and the West.
For when anyone investigates the cause of these things and where it lies, he cannot be in doubt,
when he says that it came from the persecution against us, since all this turmoil did not stop until the Christians received freedom of speech.

Throughout the ten years of persecution they did not cease plotting against and making war on one another. No one could sail the sea, for wherever someone sailed from, if he was caught, he fell into every kind of rack and torture.
They were flogged, had their sides raked, and were questioned about whether they had been sent by the enemy.
Others were crucified, or went to the fire to be tortured.
Shields and breastplates were being made ready, and arrows and lances,

along with the rest of the equipment of war. Ships fitted out for wartime were being drawn up everywhere, and there was nothing else for anyone to expect from day to day except war. Along with these things there came famine, and afterward [?] overtook [them]. What was fitting about this has been told in its proper time. These and things like them were what took place during the whole persecution.
Sixteenth [chapter]: On the good change of affairs that took place. When these ten years had fully run their course, by the goodness of God (though they had begun to die down after eight years),
the heavenly goodness of God showed us its visitation in peace.

[Chapter] seventeen: On the change of the kings. Then those rulers who had been against us, by whose hands the war against us had formerly been waged, changed their minds in a wonderful way. They reversed their words, and with pleasant letters toward us and gentle orders they put out the great fire of persecution that had been kindled. But the cause of this was not from human beings, nor was it compassion
nor the mercy of the kings, for they were greatly lacking in this.
For every day, from the beginning until that time, they were devising more and more evils against us. With craftiness that took every form, decrees against us were being issued all the time.
But it was a clear visitation of God's providence, who was pleased with his people. Upon that chief author of the evils came the affliction of torment,
which began in his body and went in as far as his soul.

For suddenly an abscess formed in the hidden parts of his body. After that came a deep, penetrating pain, which is a fistula. An incurable ulcerous sore formed in his bowels, and countless worms swarmed out of it.
And a smell of death came from his body, because of the great amount of food.

Before his illness he had become extremely fat. And then, when he was rotting, his appearance was indescribably terrifying to those who came near him. The physicians who could not bear his foul smell were put to death. And while his body was wasting away
and he was without hope of life, because other physicians could not help him,

they were put to death without mercy. And when he had been brought down by all these evils, he became aware of the things he had dared to do against the worshippers of God. He gathered his thoughts, and first he confessed to the God of all.
After that he called those close to him and told them to stop the persecution of the Christians without delay.
He commanded that, by law and imperial decree, they should hurry to rebuild their churches, follow their customs, and offer prayer on behalf of the empire.
Then the deed followed the word. The edicts of the rulers were published in every city, announcing the reversal of what they had said about us. They read as follows:
Emperor Caesar.
Maximian, Maxentius [?], and Augustus.
Emperor Caesar.
Constantine Pius Augustus.
along with the rest of the affairs of the empire.

Among the measures we take for the good and benefit of the public, we had previously wished that everything should be set in order according to the ancient laws and the order of the empire of the Romans,
and that we should also take care that the Christians who had abandoned the religion of their fathers should return to it.
But for some reason such great perversity took hold of them that they would not follow the things the ancients had shown, though their fathers had formerly held to them.
but they acted according to their own minds, each one of them as he pleased,

that they should keep their own law. When we issued an edict that they should return to what had been established by the ancients, many of them were exposed to danger and many were thrown into turmoil.
They suffered every kind of death. And because we see that many have persisted in the same way,
neither offering the gods in heaven the worship due to them
nor taking part in the worship of the Christians,
We, in our clemency and in keeping with our constant custom of granting pardon to all people,

have also in this matter, fully and willingly, agreed to grant them pardon, so that they may again be Christians and may rebuild the houses in which they used to assemble, provided that they do nothing contrary to good order. And by another letter we will inform
the judges what they are required to observe. Therefore, in accordance with this pardon of ours, they are obliged to pray to their God for our life and for the affairs of the empire,
and for themselves, so that in every way well-being may also be granted to the affairs of the empire,

so that they may be able to live free of care in their homes. These things were translated from the Latin language into Greek as well as could be done, and this is how it read. And what happened after these things
it is time for us to consider.
The eighth book is finished.
The ninth book of the Ecclesiastical History.

First chapter.
On the temporary relief that was granted, which came about. Now the change of the emperor's will that had been written was spread through Asia, in every province.
And when these things had been done in this way, there came from all [?]. And he was a persecutor of the fear of God.

He was not pleased with what had been written. Instead of the written decrees that had been set up, he ordered the governors under his hand by word of mouth to ease the war against us. For since he had no power to oppose otherwise
the command of those who were greater than he, he suppressed this law that had been set up, and took care that it should not come openly into the regions under his authority.
And without writing, he ordered the governors under his hand to ease the persecution against us.
They made his command known to one another through writings. Sabinus, who had been honoured by the empire with the highest authority of the prefecture,
revealed and made known the king's mind to the governors in every nation in a Latin letter. They believed that the intention written to them was genuine.
They revealed and made known the king's will through writings to the logistae, the strategoi and those appointed over the villages.
But not in writings [?], so that they should carry out the king's command.
they brought out into the open and set free all those whom they had confined in prison because of their confession of Christ.
They did the same for those in the mines who had been condemned to punishment there, for they believed that this was truly the emperor’s will.
When these things had been done in this way, suddenly, as if out of a deep night, light shone forth. In every city one could see the churches assembling,

and also great crowds gathering, and the services being performed according to their former customs. Every one of the unbelieving pagans was greatly astonished and amazed at these things, at this marvellous reversal that had happened, and they cried out and said

that the God of the Christians alone is the true God. Those of ours who had contended faithfully and bravely in the contests of the persecution received once again the boldness of speech that they had had before everyone.
But all those whose souls had grown sick with regard to the faith were standing in [?] wavering.
They lovingly concerned themselves with the healing of their souls and sought help from those who were healthy.
They asked them for a helping hand and pleaded with God to be reconciled to them. Moreover, the victorious champions of godliness,
When they were freed from the pressure of the sufferings that had come upon them, they all returned to their own places.
Rejoicing and glad, they passed through every city with great delight. Words cannot describe the boldness they had, or the crowds of people on the roads and in the marketplaces.
They travelled on, praising God with hymns and psalms.

Those who a little earlier had been in chains under harsh [?] and driven from their homes were getting their homes back. Even those who had once been murderous toward us saw the wonder that had happened,
which they had not expected to happen, and rejoiced with us over what had taken place.
Chapter Two. On the change that came afterward. The tyrant who hated what was good, and was the opponent of everything good, could not bear what we have described.

This was the man we said was ruler in the regions of the East. He did not put up with this state of affairs even for six months. He worked hard to destroy the peace. First, on a crafty pretext, he banned the gatherings at the cemeteries. Then he used wicked men to send a delegation to himself against us. He stirred up the people of Antioch to ask him to order
that no one at all of the Christians should live in the territory under their control, as though he were showing them great kindness by this [?]. And he also permitted others to do the same.
The instigator and head of this was seen to be Theotecnus at Antioch, a wicked man and a sorcerer, whose nature was strange [?]. He was the logistes (city curator) in that same city.

Of the third. On the statue that was newly set up at Antioch. This man of whom we have spoken was well armed to fight against us, and by every device he was eager to hunt down those who were ours, as if they were wicked men hiding in darkness.
He worked at slander and accusation against us in every way, and he caused the death of many. Finally he set up a statue of Zeus Philius (Baalshamin).

He devised and invented a practice of sorcery, with polluted rites, unclean mysteries and false purifications. He even showed the king a marvellous art of divination. This man too did these things as though to please someone he was eager for [?].
by the one who held power, raised up the demon against the Christians, declaring, “Look! The god has commanded
that the Christians should be driven out beyond the boundaries of the city and of the fields around it.
since they are, he says, enemies of God.
Of the fourth. On the petitions that were planned against us. When this man had at first succeeded as he wished,
also the rest of all the governors who lived in the cities that were under the authority of this emperor

agreed to carry out a similar plan, for the governors of the provinces saw that the emperor was pleased with this, and they urged those under their authority to do this very thing. And the tyrant, with joy, permitted their petition to be carried out by means of his letters. And then the persecution was kindled again from the beginning. And priests, and also high priests, of the idols
were appointed in every city by Maximinus himself. These were men who held the highest ranks of honour in every respect

and were very zealous in the worship of the idols they served. The tyrant's boundless wickedness pushed all the officials, and those under them, to do everything against us in order to please him. They did him this favour in return for the benefits they hoped to receive from him.
As a gift in exchange for a gift, they offered our slaughter, and they renewed their hostility toward us.

Chapter Five. On the forged memoirs that were composed against our Lord. They composed forged memoirs of our Saviour and Pilate, full of blasphemy against Christ. These were sent throughout his whole realm, supposedly by the king's wish.
In letters he ordered that everywhere, in the cities and also in the countryside,
the memoirs should be publicly displayed to everyone, and handed over to all the schoolteachers,

so that they might meditate on the teaching in them and keep their memory. And while these things were being done in this way, another military commander, whom the Romans call a dux, in Damascus of Phoenicia, seized and brought prostitutes from the marketplace,
and ordered that they be scourged severely, and forced them to state in writing that they had formerly been Christians.

and had seen unlawful acts among them. They were to say that the Christians committed acts of impurity in their houses of prayer, along with other things he wanted them to say in order to bring disgrace on our faith. This man too
put these statements into official records and informed the emperor. He ordered these writings to be proclaimed in every place and city.
But a short time later this military commander killed himself with his own hands, paying the penalty for his wickedness.
Chapter Six. Those who suffered martyrdom at this time. Once again our expulsion and a cruel persecution were set in motion.
and the governors in every province again set themselves harshly against us.
Many people known for their teaching of the fear of God were arrested, and they readily accepted the sentence of death.
Three of them, in Emesa, a city of Phoenicia, confessed that they were Christians and were thrown to the wild beasts.
One of them was Silvanus, a bishop who was very old and had served in his ministry for forty years.
At this same time Peter, the bishop who presided over the church of Alexandria, gloriously

He who was a vessel of God because of the glory of his service in the word of God was seized without cause, when nothing of the kind had been expected beforehand; and suddenly, without trial, as if by order of Maximin, his head was cut off. And with him many other bishops from Egypt also suffered the same.
And again Lucian, a man excellent in every respect in the modesty of his conduct and trained in holy learning, who was a presbyter of the church in Antioch, was brought to the city of Nicomedia,
where the emperor was staying at that time. And when he had made a defense before the court concerning the teaching that he proclaimed, he was handed over to prison and was put to death.
Thus, in a short time, the treacherous scheme of Maximinus, the hater of good things, grew stronger, and the persecution he stirred up against us was worse than the former one.
Chapter Seven. Concerning the inscriptions set up against us on pillars. Now the resolutions of the cities against us,

And along with them, the decrees of the emperor were being inscribed on bronze stelae in the middle of the cities, a thing that had never happened before. And every day the children in school recited aloud, as if in mockery, the memoirs of our Savior and of Pilate that had been composed.

Here it seems to me right that we set down the letter of Maximin, the one he had inscribed on stelae, so that this man's boldness, arrogance and vainglory, together with his hatred toward God, may be openly known, and also the just judgment that overtook him at once.
the judgment that does not sleep in its vengeance on the wicked.

When it pressed hard on him a short time later, he changed his mind about these measures against us, and in writing he ordered other laws concerning us. Copy of the translation of this document of the decrees of Maximin the Younger.
which he issued in response to the resolutions [?] against us that were submitted to him, copied from the pillars that stood in Tyre.
Look, even before now, the feeble audacity of human thought has gained strength and has driven away and abolished from itself all the darkness of the gloom of error,
which, a short time ago, was wrapped in the ruinous darkness of error and took the wicked captive.

And especially those of us who are without God should be persuaded of this: that all things are governed and set in order by the care and goodwill of the immortal gods. This truth, however, is not believed merely by being stated.
how we received your kindness with joy and love, and how you showed proof of your disposition, which lies in the love of God,
since even before this it was known to everyone with what watchfulness and reverence you have been disposed toward the immortal gods,
it was not by bare and empty words that people's faith was shown, but by known, glorious and steadfast deeds.
Therefore [?] your city is fittingly established and may be called a dwelling place of the immortal gods. It is therefore clear from many proofs
that it flourishes through the presence of the heavenly gods [?] because of your devotion. Therefore that great and exalted god Baalshamin, who dwells in your splendid city,
who rescued the god of your ancestors, of your wives, and of your children, as well as your dwelling place and your houses, from every destructive calamity,

This healthy will has been stirred up in your souls, revealing and showing how excellent, glorious and beneficial it is to approach the service and ministry of the sacrifices of the immortal gods with the worship that is due them. For who is so lacking in understanding that he could be a stranger to the whole sun [?]
He does not perceive that this happens through the zealous benevolence of the gods, so that the earth should not reject the seeds entrusted to it,
and empty the farmers’ hope and disappoint their expectations; nor that the warfare of the wicked should [?] be settled upon the earth without restraint,
and that the climate of the sky should be corrupted, and that bodies should be dragged to death by corruption,

Nor does the sea rage with its waves under the blowing of violent winds; nor do whirlwinds suddenly rise and bring a storm of destruction; nor again does the earth, the mother and nurse of all, sink down from its edges in the terror of its quakings; nor are the high mountains thrown down into a chasm that opens [?]. For all these evils, and worse than these,
everyone knows had been happening a little before.
And all these things happened together, contrary to law, because of the destructive error of the [?] of those men,
when it had overflowed their souls

and had seized the whole world with shame. And a little further on he says again: Let them look, then, at the broad plains, how their fields flourish with abundant waves of [?] grain, and how the meadows rejoice with the shoots of flowers
because of the abundance of rain and the good order of the air, which has been granted in a mild climate.
Let everyone rejoice in our good religion

and that through the ministry of sacrifices and burnt offerings the divinity, power and steadfastness of the Air has been appeased. Because of this let them rejoice, as they rest truly in the light of peace and in quiet.
And all those who have turned away from that blindness of error

and have been fully helped and have come to a right and excellent mind, let them rejoice greatly that they have been rescued as if from a storm or from a severe illness, and that from now on they enjoy the fruits of the fragrance of life. But if they persist in their accursed vanity, far from your city and from its territory

let them be separated and driven out, as you requested, so that in this way, in accordance with your zeal in this matter, which deserves praise, your city may be kept far from all pollution and impiety, as was the desire implanted in it,
and with the worship that is due to the immortal gods

may be occupied with the service of sacrifices. But so that you may know how lovingly we have received this request of yours, even without a request, without a petition, of my full free will, while I rejoice
our benevolent soul has agreed to do this for your honor and to receive whatever great gift you wish to request in return for this disposition that loves God and [?].
For you receive an unfailing reward: when this is granted to your city, it will give you a good testimony forever,

of your reverence toward the immortal gods, and that you received a gift from the love of our goodness worthy of your distinction, because this petition of your lives will be made known to your children and to your children's children.
Chapter Eight. Concerning what happened afterward through famine, pestilence, and war.
These things, then, were being posted and proclaimed against us in every province, so that, as far as human beings were concerned,

they were driving us away from every good hope, in accordance with that word of God which says that, if possible, even the elect would stumble through these things. But when they had become elated with great expectation,
while those who were carrying out the provisions of this decree issued against us were still traveling along the road from place to place, suddenly
God, who is the helper of his church, not only brought to nothing the tyrant's vainglory against us
But he also showed his heavenly help. So the rain that used to fall in the winter season was held back from the earth, and a severe famine took hold.
And with it also came a deadly plague.
Another disease was spreading: an ulcer that, because of its burning heat, was called a burning coal.
Although it put the whole bodies of those afflicted by it in danger of death, it developed especially in the eyes of many.

And it made tens of thousands of men, with women and children, blind. And it made tens of thousands of men, with women and children, blind. And along with these things a war rose up against him, against the tyrant: the war against the Armenians. They were men who had been friends and allies of the Romans from the beginning.
They too were Christians, and they carried out their worship of God with zeal.

These were completing [?] with zeal toward God. But this hater of God, who wanted to force them to sacrifice to idols and to demons, the enemies, instead set them up as opponents against him in battle. And suddenly all these things were coming on together at one time. And the boldness of the tyrant and his [?] against God were [?] — he who prided himself on his zeal for the idols.
And because of the persecution against us.
there had been neither famine nor pestilence, nor even war, in his days. But these things came together at one time in great measure, and became the beginning of his destruction.
He himself, then, together with all his army, was being worn down in the war against the Armenians.

As for the rest, those under his rule who lived in all the cities, a deadly famine pressed hard on them, so that a single measure of wheat was sold for two thousand five hundred coins. There were myriads of them,
who were dying in every city.

and many of them were people in the villages and in the fields. So those who had once been entered in the [?] registers, who were many, were in a short time almost entirely extinguished, because they suddenly perished from lack of food and from the deadly plague.
Some men even sold their beloved children to the rich for a little food. Others sold off their possessions little by little, until they came to the extreme of want and need, chewing [?] bits of hay
And they ate foolish grass that did harm.

and so wrecking and ruining the health of their bodies. Even well-known women, driven by the pressure of need, went out shamelessly into the marketplaces and wandered about. Yet the evidence of how they had once lived in comfort
showed in the modesty of their faces and the decency of their clothing. Those who had wasted away from famine staggered here and there like dead statues,
while their souls grew faint within them, and they stumbled and fell.
And because they could not stand, they slipped and fell in the streets. As they lay there, they pleaded for someone to hand them a little morsel of bread.
When their breath was about to leave them, they would cry out, "I am hungry", and they had strength only for this bitter cry. The rich were astonished at the great number of those who were begging.
After they had given a great deal, they came to harsh and merciless thoughts,
because they feared that the same thing might happen to them as had happened to those who were begging.
From then on, dead bodies lay naked in the middle of the streets and in the open places, left unburied for many days. They also made a hideous sight for those who saw them,
For many even became food for dogs. For this reason, those still alive turned to killing the dogs,
for fear that they might [?] grow wild and dare to eat human beings. The plague also fed on every household, and especially on those whom the famine had not been able to destroy,

because they had plenty of food. So the rich rulers, the governors, and the many high-ranking men who had been spared by the famine were plainly, by the deadly plague, sharply famine. They were plainly being finished off sharply and quickly by the deadly plague.
Every place was full of groaning, in the streets and in the open places. There was nothing to be seen except weeping, with the playing of pipes and lamentation.

So, as we said before, death came near in these two forms, famine and plague, and in a short time it fed on every family of mankind. You could see two or three bodies at once being carried out to burial in a single funeral procession.

Such was the reward for the boasting of King Maximinus, and for the schemes the cities were devising against us. Meanwhile the zeal and uprightness of the Christians in every respect, and the proof of it, became known among all nations.
For in all this great affliction of evils, they alone showed sympathy, together with the compassion they practised every day.
Some of them tended and buried those who were dying, for there were multitudes who had no one to care for them. Others gathered into one place those who were being tormented by famine in every city,
and they gave bread to all of them and shared it out.

This deed was proclaimed and made known among all people, and they praised the God of the Christians. They confessed that these alone are righteous and truly fear God, since their deeds had shown them to be such.

Ninth [chapter]. On the evil downfall of the lives of the tyrants. While these things were happening in this way, the great and heavenly God, the helper of the Christians, showed His wrath to all people through the things already described, in return for the harsh things they had done to us. Then, in His care for us,
turned toward us again with love and joy, and made the light of peace shine anew upon us as though in the gloom of darkness.
He showed everyone that He is God, and that He faithfully watches over all our affairs.
He disciplines through all kinds of afflictions and chastises His people at all times. Then, after sufficient chastisement, He is reconciled to those who hope in Him and is pleased with them again.
So then, when Constantine arose, the one we said was a king and the son of a king,

righteous and the son of a righteous man, and modest in all things, he rose up against those wicked tyrants through God, the King of all, and through our Savior. He fought them according to the law of war, and God was wonderfully his helper.
Maxentius the tyrant fell in Rome at the hands of Constantine.
The tyrant in the East lived only a short time after him. He too died disgracefully at the hands of Licinius, who at that time had not yet gone mad.
Tenth [chapter]. On the victory of the kings beloved of God. First, then, Constantine,

who was first in honor and in rank of kingship, had pity on those in Rome who were being oppressed by the tyrant. He called in prayer upon the God of heaven and upon His Word, who is the Savior of all, our Lord Jesus Christ,

to be his helper. He went out to battle with his whole army, because he was concerned to restore to the Romans the freedom of their fathers. Maxentius, however, relied on the craft of sorcery more than on the loyalty of those who obeyed him. He did not dare to go even a little way outside the city. Instead, with a countless multitude of armed men and tens of thousands of cavalry,
Every place and city around Rome and Italy that had been enslaved under their hands was armed. But Constantine the emperor,
who had been raised up by help from God, attacked the first, the second, and the third of the tyrant's camps.
and he overcame them mightily. He then advanced and entered Italy.

Eleventh [chapter]. On the final destruction of the enemies of the fear of God. When he had come near to Rome, God Himself drew the tyrant out beyond the gate of the city as if in chains, so that Constantine would not be forced to fight against the Romans because of the tyrant.
There were things said of old about the wicked, written in the holy books, which many people regarded as fables and which no one except believers believed. Then, through the actual event,
they were believed by believers and unbelievers alike, when they witnessed the wonder and saw it with their own eyes.
For just as in the days of Moses and the first generation of the Hebrews, he cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea,

"And his chosen warriors sank in the Red Sea; the deeps covered them." In the same way Maxentius and the armed men with him "sank into the depth like stones" when they turned their backs to the power of God that was with Constantine.
As he was crossing the river that he himself had yoked with boats, making a bridge over it, he built a device for his own destruction.
Of him it may be said: "He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and fell into the ditch that he had made."
'His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall come down upon his crown [?].'
For this bridge that he had built over the river came apart suddenly when the crossing was filled with men, and the ships sank into the depth, full of men.
And this wicked one himself went first, and all his friends with him. And as the word of Scripture says:
"They sank like lead in the mighty waters." Therefore, not in words but in deeds, like those of the house of Moses the servant of God,
who received victory from God, let us here also praise and say these things which were said concerning that first wicked tyrant:
"Praise the Lord, the exalted one, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea. Helper and protector, the Lord has become my saviour."
"Who is like you, O Lord? Who is like you among the gods? Who is like you, glorious in his holiness, awesome and praised, doing wonders?" These things, and others like them and greater than them,
Constantine sang through his deeds, praising God, the Ruler of all and the Giver of victory, and he entered Rome in a victory triumph.
All of them together, with women and children,

along with the senate and the men of rank and all the people of Rome, with joyful faces and rejoicing souls, [?] received him with praises and abundant joy as their redeemer, saviour and benefactor. But he, who possessed the fear of God
as something planted in him by nature, was not shaken by the shouting or puffed up by the praises, because he was keenly aware of God's help.
Then he gave orders that the victory of the Passion of our salvation be inscribed on his statue, which held in its right hand the sign of our salvation, that is, the cross.
And he set it up in a well-known place, in a street in Rome.
And they wrote above it in the Roman language as follows: "By this sign of salvation, which is the token of true valour,
I have saved your city from the yoke of the tyrant and set it free. And I have also restored the senate and the people of the Romans to their former glory and splendour."
After these things, Constantine, and with him also Licinius, acted together. At that time Licinius had not yet fallen into the madness that later came upon him when his mind was perverted.

Both of them praised God, who had been the cause of all good things for them. With one counsel and one will they established a complete law on behalf of the Christians, together with an account of what God had accomplished for them.

This was in wonder at the victory over the tyrant that had come to them. They sent this law to Maximinus, who was still ruling over the peoples in the East and was still deceitfully showing them friendship.

But the tyrant was pained by the things that had happened. He did not wish to appear to have obeyed others, and yet he was not able to disregard what had been commanded, out of fear of those who had commanded it. Then, as if on the authority of his own will, he wrote this first letter to the governor,
as though under compulsion, on behalf of the Christians.
And nothing whatever was done in it.
In a pretended [?] manner he lied about himself.
Translation of the copy of the letter of the tyrant Jovius Maximinus Augustus to Sabinus. To your Honour also, and to all people, we make it known that our lords and fathers Diocletian and Maximian
when they saw that everyone had abandoned the worship of the gods and had joined the Christian people, rightly commanded
...that all men who had departed from the worship of the immortal gods should be brought back to the worship of the gods by well-known persecutions and penalties [?].

But when I first came to the land of the East, I learned that in various places there was a multitude of men who could be useful to the affairs of the state, and that they were being persecuted by the judges for the reason mentioned above.
I gave orders to each of the judges that from now on they should not deal harshly with any of these inhabitants of the provinces.

[I commanded] rather that they should turn them back to the worship of the gods by enticement and persuasion. Then, when this was being observed by the judges as I had commanded, no one from the regions of the East was persecuted or afflicted.
Rather, because nothing harsh was done to them, they were turning all the more to the worship of the gods. But after these things,
when in the following year I entered Nicomedia and was staying there, the citizens came to me with the images of their gods and earnestly asked me
that such a people should by no means be given permission
to dwell in their country. But I gave them this answer:
I received their petition favorably, but I saw that this request had not come from everyone.
If, however, there are some who persist in this religion, each of them should have control over his own choice, according to his own judgment.
"And if they are willing [?] to be persuaded to the worship of the gods..." But not only [?] to the citizens of Nicomedia, but also to the rest of the other cities,
which also made the same request of me with similar eagerness, that none of the Christians should dwell in their cities, it was necessary to give an answer in love. Because this very thing
had been observed by all the former emperors. It also pleased the gods themselves, in whose hands are all human beings
and the administration of the affairs of the empire, that I should now approve such a petition, presented for the sake of worshiping their divinity.
Although, before this time, written instructions were also sent to Your Honor, and an order was issued with authorization that this practice should not be observed
toward the inhabitants of the provinces, care should be taken for them, so that they are approached not with harshness but with gentleness and moderation. Nevertheless,
they must suffer neither insult nor loss at the hands of the officials or anyone else. I therefore thought it right to remind Your Honor of this in this letter as well:

…that, above all, you should deal with the people of our provinces by persuasion and encouragement, so that they may recognize the worship of the gods. (The manuscript repeats this phrase: "by persuasion and encouragement you should deal with the people of our provinces, so that they may recognize the worship of the gods.")
