Therefore, if anyone of his own will agrees to the worship of the gods, we should receive him. But if there are people who wish to persist in the worship of their own religion,

leave them free to exercise their own freedom. Therefore your excellency must observe what you have been commanded. No one is to be given authority to harass [?] the people of our provinces with insult and loss, since, as I said before, it is with encouragement and persuasion
above all that it is proper to bring the people of our provinces back to the worship of the gods.
And so that this command of ours may become known to all the people of our provinces, it is to be made known through an order that you issue.
This is what was commanded. You may be sure of this: he was compelled by necessity to give this command, and did not give it of his own will.
So no one believed or trusted him, because of the earlier toleration he had granted, which was like this one, and which he had reversed, going back on his own word.
So none of our people dared to hold an assembly, or even to show himself in public. His letter did not command this either. It only permitted one thing: that we should be protected from harm.
He did not permit us to hold assemblies, or to build church buildings, or to do anything else that was customary among us.
Yet those emperors who were leaders of peace and of the fear of God had written to him and permitted this, and to all who were under their authority, through commands and laws,

they had granted this toleration. But this wicked man would not submit to it until he was pursued by the just judgement of God. In the end he came to it against his will, because of the following cause.
He was not able to carry the greatness of the government that had been entrusted to him, which he did not deserve,
and he did not conduct affairs with the sober, prudent judgement that kingship requires.

He went about matters unskilfully and in everything. In pride and boasting he even set himself above those who shared the kingdom with him, men who surpassed him in every respect: in family, in upbringing, in education, in the honour of authority and in understanding,

and also in modesty, which is the chief of all virtues, and in the fear of the true God. He dared to exalt himself and to name himself first in rank. He was carried away by the heights of his madness, broke the treaty he had made with Licinius,
and in hostility prepared for war against him. In a short time he went round every place and threw all the cities into turmoil.

He gathered his whole army of countless tens of thousands and marched out to do battle against him. He put his hope in those demons whom he considered gods, and he grew proud because of his tens of thousands of armed men.
But when he joined battle, he was abandoned by God, without any deed [of help], and victory was given by the one God
to the one who at that time held the government of the kingdom. First he lost the army of armed men in which he had trusted, and the guards who surrounded him left him naked.

And in that which held authority he took refuge [?]. Cowardly and hastily he took off the adornment of kingship, which did not befit him. Then in a cowardly, base and feeble way he hid himself among the crowd of people. He fled and hid in villages and fields, and only barely [?] escaped from the hands of the soldiers and lived.
By what he did, he showed that the words of God are true and trustworthy, which say:
“A king is not saved by a great army, nor does a warrior escape through his great strength. A horse is a false hope for deliverance;
with all its strength it cannot rescue its rider. The Lord's eyes are on those who fear him, who wait for his grace, to rescue their lives from death.”

So the tyrant, full of shame, came to the provinces under his control. First, in the rage of his madness, he killed many priests and prophets of the gods he had once admired, whose prophecies had urged him on to start the war, treating them as sorcerers and deceivers

and as betrayers of his life. After this he gave glory to the God of the Christians and established a full and complete law for their freedom. But he fell into a severe, deadly illness, and since he was given no more time to live, he departed from the world.
The law that he sent out read as follows.
Emperor Caesar Gaius Valerius Maximinus.
Germanicus, Sarmaticus, Pius, Fortunate, Invincible, Augustus. In every matter we are exceedingly careful for the benefit of our provinces,
and we wish to provide for them those things by which everything may be plainly brought to completion for them.
We believe that everyone should know and acknowledge, through their implementation, the measures that promote the orderly administration of the empire and are welcome to everyone's mind.
Even before this, it had come clearly to our knowledge that, because our illustrious fathers had ordered

Diocletian and Maximian, that the assemblies of the Christians should be suppressed. And they suffered great loss at the hands of the officials, and this has gone on until now against the inhabitants of our provinces,
for whose affairs we are eager to take care, as is fitting.
Because their possessions were being ruined, letters were issued before this year to the governors in every province, in which we laid down a law
that if there is anyone who wishes to adhere to this custom, or to a similar observance of worship,
that person should have authority over his own will without hindrance, so that he is neither hindered nor prevented by anyone,
and that each one of them should be free, without fear and without suspicion, to do what seems good to him. However, even now this could not be hidden from us:
some of the judges were in two minds about the commands.

that people were being troubled over orders: they were being made to approach the worship of the cults in faith. Those who are pleased to do so, let them do it. But so that every fear and every uncertainty about religion may be removed, we have laid down a law
that this order be added, that they should have authority.
namely, those who wish to conduct themselves according to this belief and this worship,
by this grant of ours,

as each one of them wishes and is pleased to adhere to this, so that, as by a custom, he may choose to worship in it. And they are permitted to build the houses of their churches. And so that this grant of ours may be great, we also wish to order this: that if there are houses or places
that previously belonged by right to the Christians, and by order of our fathers passed into another's ownership,
or were seized by one of the cities, or were actually sold,
or were given to anyone as an honor, we command that all these be restored to the Christians' original ownership,

...so that in this too everyone may perceive our diligence and our kindness. These are the words of the tyrant, at a time when not even a full year had passed since he had put up an order against the Christians on steles.
And by him, the Christians, who a little earlier were regarded as wicked and godless, and as the cause of all calamities for the world,
so that he did not allow us to live in cities, in villages, or in the desert; by this man laws and orders were being issued against the Christians;
and those who a little earlier were being thrown to fire and sword and as food for beasts before his eyes, and were leaving the world miserably through every kind of torture and [?],
and had endured these things as wicked and godless people—to these very people he himself now grants permission,

these he permitted to worship in their religion, to build churches, and to receive back the rights to whatever they had possessed. But when he had made such confessions as these, as though they would be of some help to him, because of these things

he suffered less than what he deserved. He was struck by a blow from God suddenly, and at the second engagement of the battle he was overthrown. This was how he left the world. For he did not, like great generals, victors and warriors who win their battles on the field of famous victories, have the good fortune to meet a glorious end bravely. He died instead as a wicked man and an enemy of God. For when the army was standing in the field, as a wicked man and enemy of God; for when the army was standing in the field, he was hiding inside a house. And [?], as he deserved, he was struck by a blow from God suddenly: his whole body was being lashed, and he was hounded by evil and severe pains.
He was lying prostrate and thrown down, he wasted away from hunger, and his whole body was melting away in an invisible fire that had been sent upon him from God.
And when he had wasted away entirely, that former appearance was destroyed; only bones remained alive, and he had become [?] like a withered image after a long time.
Those who met him and saw him thought nothing else about him except that his body was a tomb for his own soul, which was buried like a corpse that had completely wasted away.
Then a fever burned him severely, as if from the depths of his brain. And his eyes burst out of their sockets and fell out.

And he was left blind. But his soul was still in him, and he was confessing to our Lord and asking for death. And at last, confessing that he was suffering these things because of his outrage against Christ, by a just judgment his soul left him. Thus, then, his soul [?] from the world.
Maximinus, the only one left of the enemies of the fear of God.
He was known to be the worst of them all. But by the goodness of God Almighty the churches were being rebuilt from their foundations, and the word of Christ was shining forth to the glory of God.
And it received the freedom of speech that it had had before, and more. Their wickedness [?] received the freedom of speech that it had had before.
But the wickedness of the enemies of the fear of God was filled with shame and disgrace. And first of all Maximinus, who was the adversary of all people.

He was openly proclaimed and named in writings, by those who held the kingdom, as wicked, insolent, a hater of God and a tyrant. And of the images that had been set up in every city in his honour and that of his sons, some were thrown down from on high to the ground and smashed, and some had their faces blackened in [their] form [?].
And the statues that had been standing as if in his honour
were likewise thrown down and smashed.
And they were set up as an object of laughter and mockery for those who wished to insult and scorn them. Then the honours of those other enemies of the fear of God were also stripped away.
And all those he had especially honoured with positions of authority were killed. Out of flattery toward him they had arrogantly insulted our teaching. These were:

The one he honoured more than everyone else, who was more distinguished and beloved than the others: Peucetius, who had been consul twice and three times and had been appointed by him prefect over everything.
And also Culcianus, who had risen through every rank of government, and who also took pride in the great amount of Christian blood he had shed in Egypt.
And besides these, many others, by whose hands the greatness of Maximinus had grown and become strong.

Just judgment, which forgets nothing, also caught up with Theotecnus for what he had done against the Christians. For because of the image he had set up in Antioch, through which he thought he had succeeded, he had even been honoured by Maximinus with a governorship.
Now when Licinius entered the city of Antioch, he made a search for sorcerers. He had the prophets and priests of that new image that had been set up tortured.
He was asking them by what means they had been showing off this deception. And since they could not hide it under the pressure of torture,
they revealed and made known that the whole secret of the deception lay in the craft devised by Theotecnus. And after him his partners in sorcery were also put to death after many tortures.

And in addition to all these, the sons of Maximinus were also added, who until then had shared his imperial honour and the images set up to them. And also those who had formerly prided themselves on being related to the tyrant,
who had also exalted themselves and lorded it over all people.
also suffered terrible disgrace, like those we mentioned earlier, because they had not accepted correction
and had not recognized and understood the command in the Holy Scriptures: “Do not trust in a ruler or in a human being, who has no power to save.
For his spirit goes out and he returns to his earth, and on that day all his thoughts perish.
Thanks then be to God for all things, who is the Almighty and King of all,

and to Jesus Christ, the Saviour and Redeemer of our souls, the Only-begotten of God and his Word. Through him we pray always that peace may be kept for us, firm and undisturbed by troubles from outside or of the mind.
The ninth book is finished.
The tenth book, again, of the History of the Church.
The first chapter: On the peace that was given to us by God. / [Chapter] two.
On the rebuilding of the churches.
/ Third: On the festivals for the dedication of the churches that took place in every place. / Fourth:
Discourse on the splendour of affairs. / Fifth:
Translation of the imperial law concerning the things that are due to the Christians.
And the history concerning Licinius.

Chapter One. The peace given to us by God.
But thanks be to God for everything, to the Father and King of all,

And to the Redeemer and Saviour of our souls, Jesus Christ, the Only-begotten of God and his Word, by whose hand we always pray that peace may be kept for us, firm and unshaken by troubles from outside or troubles of the mind. And with these let us pray.
This tenth book we also add to the other books of the Church History that were set down before. We dedicate it to your name, O holy [?Paulinus; the text reads "labourer" or "work"].
And we name you as the seal of the whole history. Fittingly, the discourse of the perfect number is placed here, for the dedication of the completed church.
For we are persuaded by the Spirit of God, who commands thus: "Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done wonders.
His right hand and his holy arm have saved him. The Lord has made known his salvation; before the eyes of the nations he has revealed his righteousness."

And in keeping with the word that commands us to sing a new song, let us also respond and say that, after histories and dark and hateful sights, we have been counted worthy to see such things as these and to celebrate festivals.
Many righteous people and martyrs of God who came before us longed to see these things on earth and did not see them, and to hear them and did not hear them.
But they hastened on swiftly and were counted worthy of things better than these. They eagerly pressed on to heaven and paradise, to delight in God.
We, however, acknowledge that even these things are beyond our worth, and we marvel at the gracious gift of the Giver. We are filled with wonder, as is fitting.
And with all our soul and strength we worship, and we bear witness to the truth of what was spoken prophetically in Scripture,
which says: “Come, see the works of God, who has done wonders on earth and puts an end to wars from the ends of the earth.

"He breaks bows and shatters spears, and the chariots of the earth." "He breaks bows and shatters spears, and burns chariots with fire." And as we rejoice in these things that have been done, it has been fulfilled in us. From here on let us proceed with the history.
Second: On the dedication of the churches. The whole race of the enemies of God had been extinguished, as we said above, and the sight of those men was suddenly wiped away,
so that once again the word of God would be fulfilled, which says: "I saw the wicked boasting and lifted up like the trees of the forest.
And when I passed by, he was not there; I sought him, and did not find him."
And now the day is cheerful and bright, without even the shadow of clouds, for the rays of heavenly light have illuminated all creation through the church of Christ.
And there were no envious people. Even those who are outside our faith shared with us in these good things that were given to us by God, if not equally, then at least to some small degree.

Freedom from the slavery of the tyrants was given to all people, and they found relief from their former evils. Each and every person confessed that there is truly one God, who is the helper of those who fear him.
And this was especially so for us, who hang our hope on the Christ of God. Joy in God burned in everyone, with an unspeakable delight.
And people saw every place that a little earlier had been laid waste by the wickedness of the tyrants being restored, as if from a long and bitter sickness unto death.
Temples were being rebuilt from their foundations and adorned, and those that had earlier been destroyed received glory in abundance.
Moreover, those supreme emperors, through frequent laws on behalf of the Christians, confirmed God's gift to us as well, with magnificence and power.
Letters from the emperors also came, addressed to bishops, together with honours, gifts, and possessions [?] of this kind.
Since we are now recalling this matter, let us record their words in this book, as if on holy pillars, so that they may be known and remembered by those who come after us.

Third: On the festivals for the dedication of the church that took place in every place. Along with these things came the sight that we all love and pray for: dedication festivals were being held [?] in every city.
New houses of prayer were being built. Bishops gathered together, along with crowds of people from distant regions.

And people became known to people in the love of distant members; and people became known to people in the love of the members of the body of Christ. They were willing and were gathering into oneness and peace.

As was said in prophecy, which made known in a mystery something that was going to happen: bone was drawing near to bone, and joint to joint. And the rest of the things that the word of God had spoken beforehand in prophecy, in a symbol, were being fulfilled without falsehood.
And one power of the Spirit of God was establishing all the members. There was one soul for all of them and one mind of faith, and from all of them one hymn of praise resounded.
and the complete ministry of the leaders of the churches, as befits God, and the offerings of the priests and the laws of the Church, as befits God.

There was a place where psalms and the words given to us by God were heard, and there was a place where the ministrations of the mystery of God were performed, which are the hidden symbols of the passion of our Redeemer.
And all together, every race and age of men and women, with all the strength of their minds,
in prayers and thanksgivings, rejoicing in soul and understanding, were praising God, the giver of good things. And all who wished were delivering orations on the dedication festivals.
according to the ability each of them had, and they were honoring and delighting the festival gathering.
And one of them, among the least of them, stood in the middle and delivered an address to the assembly of the church, while many shepherds were gathered there.
They were ready to listen quietly and modestly. He addressed one bishop in particular, who excelled in everything and was worthy of God,
who was renowned for his zeal, especially in Tyre in Phoenicia, and had built a magnificent temple there. He delivered the following address.

Of the fourth. Oration on the splendour of the affairs of the Church. Oration on the festal assembly, on the building of the church, which was delivered in the presence of Paulinus, bishop of the church of Tyre. O priests, beloved of God,
Those who are clothed in the holy garment and the heavenly crown of glory, and the anointing of God, and the robe of the priesthood, and the Holy Spirit; and you, O glory of the holy temple of God,
who are honoured with the wisdom that comes from God, and who are glorious in deeds and excellent works of new virtue and splendour,
for that God who holds the whole world has honoured you with an excellent gift: that you should build on earth a house for Christ, his Word and Only-begotten.
and for his holy Church, glorious to God. If anyone wished to call you a new Bezalel,
chief of the craftsmen of the tabernacle of God, or Solomon, king of a new and more excellent Jerusalem,
or a new Zerubbabel, who made the latter glory of the temple greater and better than the first.

But you also, O lambs of God's flock, dwelling-place of good words, school of modesty, and beloved hearers of the fear of God: formerly you received through your hearing, in the divine readings, the glories of the fear of God, the wonders of our Lord, and his help toward people, and you offered praises to God. It is now permitted to say, even while we are being taught: "We have heard God with our ears; our fathers also have told us what you did in their days, in the days of old." But now it is not as from hearsay, nor as from a report in words, that we receive the high arm and the heavenly hand of our good King and our God. Rather, by the deeds themselves we see with our eyes that the things handed down long ago for our help are true and trustworthy. Let a second hymn of victory go up, and let us cry out as with a loud voice and say: "As we have heard, so have we seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God." In which city? In this one, which has been newly built and dedicated to God, which is the Church of the living God, the firm pillar of truth.

For another word of God also announces this: "Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God." Since God has gathered us into it by the grace of his Only-begotten, let each one of those who have been called give praise, cry out and say: "I was glad when they said to me, Let us go to the house of the Lord," and "Lord, I have loved the service of your house and the place where your glory dwells." And not only each one of us by himself, but all of us together, with one spirit and one soul, let us honour and praise Christ, who is greatly honoured and praised in the city of God and on his holy and glorious mountain.

For he is truly great, and his temple is great, exalted and glorious, and fairer in appearance than the sons of men. Great is our Lord, who alone does wonders. Great is he who does wonders without end and mighty deeds without number. Great is he who changes times and seasons, who removes kings and sets up kings, who raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dunghill. He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and lifted the lowly from the earth. He has filled the hungry with good things and brought low the arm of the proud. Not only for believers but also for those who do not believe, he has confirmed the record of the ancient stories: he who does great wonders, the Lord of all and Creator of the whole world, Almighty and good over all, he who is one, God alone. To him we offer a new praise, answering and saying: "To him who alone does great wonders, for his mercy is forever. Who struck great kings, he alone, for his mercy is forever. Who struck great kings and killed mighty kings, for his mercy is forever. Who remembered us in our lowliness …" [?: gap in the text] … [?] let those on earth who enter give thanks to him. The King is not like a lowly man, but like the beloved Son of God, and as the Word of God he is rightly worshipped. For what king has ever had such glory that the tongue and ears of all people on earth should be filled with his name? What king has laid down such just, pure and true laws, that from the ends of the earth to the farthest edge of creation they should be read aloud continually in the hearing of all people? Or who has tamed rebellious nations of barbarous and bitter custom with his gentle laws full of mercy? Who, while persecuted among all the nations, has shown such glory before all people that his teaching flourishes every day and is renewed throughout the whole world? Who has established such a people, the like of which has never been heard of since the beginning of the world, a people not hidden in a corner of the earth but established throughout all creation under heaven? Who has so strongly armed his worshipers with pure weapons that their souls are firmer than adamant in the contest against the adversary? What king like this has conquered and won victory in battle even after his death, and taken victory over his enemies, and filled every place and city, among Greeks and barbarians alike, with temples of his kingdom and shrines set apart for his divinity? There are these adornments, decorations and offerings of this temple, which are truly glorious, great and worthy of wonder, and these demonstrations, in deed, of the kingdom of our Savior. For even now he spoke and they came into being; he commanded and he established them. For who was there to oppose its being established at his nod, the nod of him who is King of all and Governor of all, he who is the Word of the teaching of God? His words, when they are explained, require understanding and interpretation, and not only according to the thinking of those who toil at the work, that he is also with this one who is named [?] and who is God. For he sees the temples within the souls of all, and he is discerned in the house built of living stones that have been gathered together, the house firmly founded on the foundation of the prophets and apostles, of which Jesus Christ is the cornerstone of the building. He was rejected not only by those builders of old, who are now no more, but also by those who to this day are evil builders of a building of evil people. Yet he was chosen by the Father, both then and now, to be the cornerstone of the building of this common church. He has therefore established this living temple, which has been built out of you for the living God, a temple that is great, worthy of God, and truly holy. Its hidden interior is not seen or searched out by everyone, for it is truly the Holy of Holies. Who dares to look upon it or to speak of it? And who can rightly enter within the sanctuary, except the one who alone is the great High Priest, to whom alone belongs the authority to search the hidden things of the spiritual soul? But perhaps another, second after him, is also able to enter within. Only one: this governor who sits at the head of this flock, whom the first and great High Priest has honored after himself in this church. He made him shepherd of this divine flock of yours, appointing him over your people by the counsel and judgment of his Father, to be his minister and prophet. This is the new Aaron, or Melchizedek, who resembles the Son of God. May he remain and be preserved by him forever through the prayers of us all. To this man alone, then, after the great and first High Priest, let there be authority to see and examine the understanding of the inner part of your souls. Through trial and length of years he has tested each person accurately, and by his zeal and care he loves [?] all of you in orderly conduct and in the word that is in the fear of God. He is more able than anyone to account for the things done by the power of God, so as to render words equal to his deeds. For our great and first High Priest imitates whatever he sees his Father doing. This first teacher, too, looks with the pure eye of the mind upon him as upon the first example and model, and as far as his strength allowed he imitated, built and helped [?], and was in no way inferior to Bezalel, whom God himself filled with the spirit of wisdom, understanding and knowledge of the craft of building the tabernacle, which was built according to a heavenly model and in symbols. So too this man bore in his own soul the image of Christ, the Word of God, the Wisdom and the Light. It cannot be told how he was enabled to resemble him in rich wisdom, in goodness of soul, and in generosity [?] of expense. This temple, greatly befitting God, he established gloriously as a likeness, with a surpassing demonstration, so that what is invisible was gloriously established in this visible nature. And first of all it is right to speak of its place: it had been buried in filthy dung through the malice of the enemies. He did not neglect it or abandon it to the ruin of many years, though he could have found many other places in the cities and easily been spared the hardship of the labor. Instead he was the first to rouse himself to the work, and by his resolve he filled the whole people with strength and gathered from all of them one great hand. This was the triumph of the first contest that he undertook: this church, which had been taken captive and afflicted by the enemies and had endured persecution even before us, and which like a mother had been bereaved of her children, he judged it right that she should share joy with us in the great gift of God's goodness. For since the great Shepherd had driven away the beasts and wolves, every bitter and savage kind, and had broken the teeth of the lions, as it is said in the word of God, and had gathered the children of the church, it was right that he too should set up the fold of the flock, to put to shame the enemy and avenger. He established it as a reproach to the audacity of the wicked, the enemies of God. And now those enemies of God are no more, because they never truly existed from of old. For in a short time they caused confusion and were themselves thrown into confusion, and by just judgment they received a fitting penalty on their own heads: they, their friends and their households perished together. Just as the things spoken beforehand in prophecy in the holy scriptures, let us know that they have been confirmed in deed. The word of God is to be believed in other matters too, but also in what he decreed concerning them when he says: "The wicked have drawn the sword and bent the bow to kill the poor and the needy and those who are upright in their ways; their sword shall enter their own heart, and their bows shall be broken." And again: "Their memory has perished and is no more, and their name has been blotted out forever and ever." And when evils overtook them, they cried out, and there was no one to save them.

"And they passed away from the Lord, and he did not answer them. But they bowed down and fell, while we rose up and stood upright." And the words spoken about these: "The Lord in the city will despise their image" — this became known as plainly true before the eyes of everyone. But those who, after the manner of the giants, raised a war of enmity against God, such was the deadly overthrow that came upon them. But to the church, which had been laid waste and despaired of by men, such an end was seen to come because of her endurance toward God, that she might cry out and speak the prophecy of Isaiah, which says thus: "Let the thirsty wilderness rejoice, and let the desert exult and blossom like a lily; let it blossom and let the wilderness exult. Be strong, you slack hands, and you trembling knees, be made firm. Say to the faint of heart: Be strong and do not fear; behold, your God comes and executes your judgment. He comes and saves you. For waters have broken forth in the wilderness, and rivers in the dry land; for the wilderness has been turned into pools, and the thirsty land into a spring of water." These words were spoken in prophecy long ago and recorded in the holy Scriptures; but the deeds have been fulfilled among us not as by hearsay but in actual events. And she who was like a wilderness and like a thirsty land, and like a widow who had no one; she whose gates they hacked down with axes like a forest of trees, and together with hatchets and hammers broke and destroyed her books, and burned with fire the sanctuary of God, and profaned to the ground the dwelling-place of his name; she whom all who passed along the way plucked, whose fences they broke down, whom the boar of the forest devoured and the wild beasts of the field grazed upon — behold, by the wonderful power of Christ, now [?] ... "who comforted you, out of all the sons whom you bore, and there was none who took hold of your hands. Behold, I have taken from your hands the cup of staggering and the cup of my wrath; you shall not drink it again any more."

"…and I will put it into the hands of those who humbled you." "Awake, awake, and put on the strength of glory. Shake yourself from the dust, and rise up and sit. Loose the band from your neck. Lift up your eyes round about, and see your children gathering together and coming to you. As I live, says the Lord, you shall put them all on like an ornament, and adorn yourself with them like a bride. For your ruins and your desolate places, and the land of your overthrow, will now be too narrow for those who live in it, and those who swallowed you up will flee far away. And the children of your bereavement will say in your ears: 'The place is too narrow for us to live in; make room for us so that we may live.' And you will say in your heart: 'Who has borne me these? For I am bereaved and a widow. Who has brought these up? For I was left alone; where were these?'" Isaiah prophesied these things.

These things were written down for us long ago in the holy Scriptures, and it was necessary that we should receive their truth in deed. These things the Bridegroom, who is the Word of God, said to his bride, who is the holy Church. And this friend of the Bridegroom, through the prayers of all of us, stretched out your hands and raised her up, she who had been desolate and overthrown and without hope in the eyes of men. By the sign of the will of God, the King of all, and by the great dawning of the goodness of Jesus Christ, he raised her up and established her in this way, as he had learned from the book of prophecy.

This is a great wonder and a cause of much amazement for those who look at it in their minds only with outward sight. But more excellent than any wonder is the renewal of the soul in the fear of God. That renewal shows forth the knowledge of God, and of it these things are types and patterns. It is the soul that the Son of God created in his own image. In every respect he gave it the image of God: a nature that is incorruptible and bodiless, and foreign to every earthly substance; a rational being, of the light of the Word. Once, in the beginning, he fashioned it out of nothing so that it might exist, and he made it a bride and a holy temple for himself and for his Father. He plainly confesses and shows this when he says: "I will dwell in them and be to them, and they shall be my people."

This, then, is the pure and perfect soul, which from the beginning was thus [?] so that it might wear the image of the heavenly Word. But through the envy and jealousy of the demon who loves evil, and by the choice of her own will, she came to love passions and to love hateful things. She was forsaken by God like a wilderness, so that she came to belong to those who envied her, to destroy her and take her captive. She was swept away by the crafty schemes of hidden enemies, and her fall was astonishing, until not one stone upon another of the victories of righteousness was left in her. She was even thrown to the ground like a corpse, completely stripped of all the right thoughts of nature.

While this soul, which had been created in the image of God, lay overthrown, she was devoured. It was not a wild boar visible to us that devoured her, but the demon who works corruption, together with the hidden beasts of the wilderness. They shot at her the burning arrows of their wickedness. They threw down the sanctuary of God and burned it with fire, and they levelled to the ground the dwelling place of his name. They buried the wretched soul under the heap of their wickedness, and they changed her and left her without hope of life.

But the Word, who is God, Light and Saviour, took care of her and carried her burden, since he received the penalty that was due for her sins. He took her up again anew, by the will of his merciful Father. First he chose for himself the souls of those exalted kings. Then, through the hands of those who love God, he purified the whole creation of all the guilty and destructive men, and of the evil tyrants who hated God. Next there were the men who were close to him, who had long been serving him as priests in secret and had been hidden under his wing. He revealed them and brought them out into the light, and he honoured them with the great gifts of the Father, as they deserved. And again, through the hands of these men, he cleansed the souls that a little earlier had been stained and lay buried in fear of the tyrants' decrees. With the [?] of his teaching he purified them and scoured them clean. He gave light and brightness to the place of your minds, and from then on handed it over to this wise governor, worthy of God. In other matters he is distinguished and intelligent, but above all he knows well the souls entrusted to him. From the first day until now he has been setting them in order and building them up without ceasing. And now he has set shining gold and costly, glorious stones in your souls, so that once again the mystery of the holy prophecy may be fulfilled in you in deed. In that prophecy it is said: "Behold, I make your stones of beryl, and I will lay your foundations with stones of sapphire, and I will build your battlements with stones of jasper, and your gates with choice stones."

"And all your children shall know me, and great shall be the peace of your children, and in righteousness you shall be established." And so this is the great temple, which stands in the whole creation under heaven. God the Word, the Creator of all, above heaven and also again upon earth, made its shining likeness, so that his Father might be honoured and worshipped by the whole creation and by all human beings. And that place above heaven, of which there are here below [?] its counterparts, is the Jerusalem above, and the heavenly Mount Zion, and the glorious city of the living God. In it are the great hosts of angels and the church of the firstborn who are written in heaven, who with surpassing and unspeakable praises glorify their Creator, the Governor of all. And no one among mortals is able to praise him as is fitting, because eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and it has not entered into the heart of man, these things which God has prepared for those who love him. Since, then, we have been made worthy of these things, a little out of much, men together with women,

and little children together with the grown, all of us together with one spirit and one soul, let us not cease confessing and praising him who became for us the cause of all these good things: him who forgives the iniquity of all of us, him who heals the diseases of all of us, him who satisfies our desire with good things, who has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. For as far as the east is distant from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us; and as a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him. Then, now as well and at all times, as these things are continually renewed in their places, and also on this feast of joy and this glad and bright day, let us keep him who is the cause and head of this feast seen before our eyes, by day and by night, at every moment and with every breath, loving and worshipping him with all our strength and soul. Now also let us rise and with a voice of love entreat him to shelter us under his wings and keep us alive to the end, and to send us from his presence his peace forever, which is not shaken or broken, in Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom be glory to him in all the ages. Amen.

Of the fifth [book?]. The laws of the emperors concerning the Christians, and the account of Licinius.

Such were the things that the heavenly goodness of God granted at the dawning of our redemption, and such were the abundant good things given to all people in our peace. In this way, then, festivals were being celebrated with rejoicing. But envy, which hates what is good, could not bear the sight of these things, nor could the demon who loves evil. Even what had happened to the tyrants we spoke of earlier was not enough to bring Licinius to a sober mind. His rule was prospering, he held the second rank in honour, and he was the brother-in-law and kinsman of the great emperor Constantine. Yet he was very far from imitating good things. Instead, he vied with the perverse wickedness of the wicked tyrants. He had seen with his own eyes how their lives ended in ruin, yet he wanted to follow their way of thinking rather than remain in the love and friendship of the emperor who was his superior. He envied the very man who was his benefactor, and he waged a hateful and bitter war against him. He had no regard for the law of nature, or for oaths, or for blood, and he did not even remember the covenant between them.

Constantine, as a good emperor, had given him a sign of true love. He did not refuse to make him a kinsman, but gave him his sister as his wife. He also judged him worthy to share in his ancestral lineage and in the ancient royal family. He gave him authority to rule over all as his brother-in-law and partner in the kingdom, and he empowered him in the same way to administer and govern the peoples under Roman rule. But Licinius did the opposite. Every day he plotted against the man who was his superior and spread every kind of deceit, so that he might repay his benefactor with evil. At first he hid the snares of his deceit and appeared to be his friend. Many times, though, he attacked him with fraud and in secret, and he easily believed he would get what he wanted. But God was Constantine's friend and his guardian and protector. God brought to light the deceit that was being forged against him in hiding and in darkness. So great was the armour of the fear of God that he had, to punish his enemies and to be a force that guarded his life. By it our God-loving emperor was protected, and from the very structure of his deceit this hated man was [?].

When Licinius saw that his hidden deceit did not succeed as he wished, because God [exposed] all his deceit and the wickedness of his mind was revealed to the emperor who was worthy of God, he no longer acted in secret. He at once launched an open war against Constantine and against God, because he was convinced that Constantine worshipped Him. Then he began to destroy those who feared God, who [?] at all not [?]. At first, however, in peace [?]… and he did these things craftily [?]… who was compelled [?]… the evil that was planted [?]… in him. He did not set [?]… before his eyes the memory of those before him [?]… to the Christians. Also [?]… that he destroyed [?]… them. But when he had turned away from sober thought and his mind had gone mad, he made war on God, who was Constantine's helper, instead of on the one who was helped by Him.

First he persecuted the Christians who were in his household. The wretch thereby robbed himself of the prayers to God that they offered on his behalf, for they had received this teaching from their fathers, that they should pray for all people. After that he ordered the soldiers in every city to be separated and stripped of the honour of their rank if they would not sacrifice to demons. Yet these things were small when compared with his greater ones. But why do we need to mention one by one the deeds of this hater of God, and how [?]… himself from the law [?]… and this man did not transgress the law [?]. For concerning those who [?]… were in prison [?]… there was a law that no one [?]… with a piece of bread [?]… to them, and no one [?]… those who were perishing [?]… from hunger. No one was even to be good, or to do anything good, though people are drawn by nature to have compassion on their neighbours. It was a law contrary to humanity, harsh and alien to every gentle nature. He made it and set a penalty on those who showed compassion: those who showed mercy were to be bound and shut in prison just like the people they pitied, and to receive the same punishment. Such were the commands of Licinius.

Why do we need to list the new laws he made about marriage and about those who depart from the world? With them he dared to change the ancient laws of the Romans, which had been well and wisely established, and in their place he set barbarous and harsh legislation. He spread great loss and laid all kinds of exactions on those under his rule: gold and silver, land surveys, and a head-tax that he collected even for people in the villages who had died long before. Besides this, when this hater of humanity found people who had done no wrong, he drove them from their homes. He banished honoured men of distinguished lineage, separated their wives from them, and handed the women over to vile slaves for a shameful purpose. How many married women and virgin girls this wicked old man defiled, filling up the lust of his wanton soul! But why should we lengthen the account of these things, when the excess of his last deeds made his earlier ones seem like nothing?

At the end of his madness he dared to act against the bishops. He regarded them as servants of God and as opposed to what he was doing. But because he still feared the one who was his superior, he did not plot evil against them openly but in secret. He had the most eminent of them killed through the deceit of the governors, and the manner of their death was strange, such as had never been heard of before. What was done at Amasea and in the other cities of Pontus surpassed [?] all cruelty. There some of the churches of God were torn down from top to bottom, and others were closed, so that no one could gather in them or minister in them, or offer to God in them the service owed to Him. He thought that the prayers in them were not offered on his behalf, and he was convinced that they did everything to win God's favour for Constantine, the God-loving emperor. From then on he attacked us in his wrath. The flattering governors were persuaded that they were doing what pleased the wicked man. Some of them put the bishops on trial as though they were criminals and imposed penalties on them, and the bishops were led away and executed without cause. Others met a strange and evil end in other ways: their bodies were cut up with the sword piece by piece and thrown away. Again those who feared God were persecuted and fled, and again the fields, deserts, mountains and hills were filled with the servants of Christ our Lord.

Because the wicked man succeeded in these things, he resolved to stir up persecution against everyone in his whole land. And he would have done so, had not God, the helper of our souls, quickly made a great light and saviour for all, Constantine His servant, shine out suddenly, as if from darkness and the gloom of night. With a lofty arm He raised him up and brought him forward, and from heaven He gave him the fruit of righteousness that he deserved: victory over the wicked man. This vile man, together with his counsellors and all his friends, He cast down prostrate before Constantine's feet. For when Licinius went to the very limit of madness and attacked him, this friend of God came to a sober decision. He mixed the firmness of justice with mercy, and so he resolved to avenge those who were oppressed by the tyrant and to save the great mass of humanity by destroying a few wicked men. Before this time he had dealt only with mercy toward a man who did not deserve it. Yet Licinius did not turn from his evil ways; instead his madness grew even worse against the peoples under his authority. Those who were suffering had no hope or life left, because the tyranny of the evil serpent was crushing them. For this reason the helper of the good mixed hatred of evil with love of good, and he went out to stretch the right hand of life to all who were perishing. Then he called on God, the King of all, and on His Son, the Saviour of all, to be his helper and his guide. He arranged his army around him against the enemies of God and easily won the victory, and God suddenly made everything in the war go smoothly before him. Those who only shortly before had been breathing threats of death were gone, and not even their names remained in memory. Their inscriptions and their images received the disgrace they deserved.

The same things that Licinius had seen with his own eyes happen to those earlier, wicked tyrants now happened to him. He too would not accept correction, and he did not learn from the blows that struck his fellows. Because he followed the path of their wickedness, he was justly condemned to a sentence like theirs. So he lay cast down and overthrown. But the victorious Constantine, who was glorious in all the strength of the fear of God, together with his God-loving sons, who resembled their father in everything, took the eastern land, which was theirs. As before, they established a single rule of the Romans, and their peace prevailed from the risings of the sun and around all the corners of creation. All the fear that had once held people was taken away from them. They kept the days of glorious festivals, and light shone everywhere. With joyful faces and bright eyes, as they had been before, everyone looked at one another. In all the cities and villages, with hymns of praise and psalms, they praised first of all God, the King of all, as they had been taught. After him, all who loved God extolled the God-fearing king. The former evils and wickednesses were extinguished. People delighted in the good things that were present and looked forward to those that were to come. And the decrees of the victorious king were spread out in every place.

which were full of mercy and great laws, and contained generous gifts and proofs of the truth of the fear of God. And so, when all tyranny had been purged away, the kingdom that rightly belonged to them was preserved for them alone, firmly and without envy: for Constantine and his sons, who swept from the world the hatred toward God of all those before them. And they recognized the good things given to them by God, and, as they showed by their love of virtue and their love of God, they openly displayed to all people thanksgiving and worship toward God. Here ends the writing of the ten books of the Ecclesiastical History composed by Eusebius of Caesarea. The first book: thirteen ecclesiastical narratives. The second book: twenty-six ecclesiastical narratives. The third book: thirty-nine ecclesiastical narratives. The fourth book: twenty-six ecclesiastical narratives. The fifth book: twenty-eight ecclesiastical narratives. The sixth book: forty-five ecclesiastical narratives.

The seventh book: thirty ecclesiastical narratives. The eighth book: seventeen ecclesiastical narratives. The ninth book: eleven ecclesiastical narratives. The tenth book: five ecclesiastical narratives. Altogether the narratives number two hundred and forty, written by Mar Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea of Palestine.
Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen and amen.

Blessed be God and His Christ, who strengthened His servant, the deficient and sinful Isaac, and he wrote this book for the honoured, excellent and chosen of God, Mar [?]. Therefore let everyone who reads and learns remember the owner and the scribe, and pray that the Lord God may bring them through that fearful place, the house of dread, and bring them to the kingdom of His Son and Beloved, our Lord Jesus Christ, and seat them at the table of His glory with His holy chosen ones, when they are served by the blessed angels. Yes, and amen and amen. It was written and completed in the month of Nisan of the year seven hundred and seventy-three [?] the city [?]. May all who fear Christ remember them forever, amen. May there truly be a good remembrance before God for Mar the priest [?], of the village of [?], his sister [?] of Mar P[?] [?]. Say: yes and amen. By the prayer of all the upright and chosen, may mercy be upon the scribe who wrote carelessly, as he supposes. Yes and amen.
Another notice: concerning the different versions of the divine Scriptures. From the work of Eusebius of Caesarea.
From chapter sixteen of the sixth book of the Ecclesiastical History: how Origen devoted himself to the holy Scriptures.

Origen studied the holy scriptures so thoroughly that he even learned the Hebrew language. He also acquired the books kept among the Jews in Hebrew writing. He also studied the transmitted versions of the holy translations that others had made besides those Seventy. Besides the translations of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, he found other translations of the holy scriptures that differed from them. These had been hidden and concealed for a long time, and he searched them out and brought them to light. Because it was not known who had translated them, he reported only this about them: that he had found one of them in Nicopolis and the others in another place. In the translation of the Psalms that he made, he showed that after those four well-known translators there was another translation, a fifth, a sixth and a seventh. He reports about one of them that it was found in Jericho in a jar in the days of King Antoninus, son of Severus. He gathered all these translations together, worked through them, and set them side by side, one against another, with the Hebrew characters. He left us copies of the works called the Hexapla. And [?] he also set out those of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion
together with that of the Seventy-two

From chapter 17: Symmachus, who translated the scriptures.

We should know that Symmachus, one of those who translated the scriptures, was an Ebionite. The heresy called that of the Ebionites consists of those who say that Christ was born of Joseph and Mary. They regard him as a mere man, and they say that the law must be kept in the Jewish manner, as we have already explained earlier in this history. Symmachus also has treatises that survive to this day. In them he argued against the Gospel of Matthew in order to support this heresy. Origen gives information about these. He says that he obtained them, together with other translations of the scriptures that Symmachus made, from a certain woman named Juliana. He says of her that she had received these books from Symmachus himself.

From chapter 25: How Origen mentions the books that are accepted in the church.

While writing on the first Psalm, Origen set out the list and count of the holy scriptures of the Old Testament. He spoke as follows: *** "We should know that the accepted books, as the Hebrews have handed them down to us, are twenty-two, the same as the number of their letters." A little further on he added: "These are the twenty-two books of the Hebrews. The book we call Genesis is called by the Hebrews after the beginning of the book, that is, Bereshit. Exodus is called in Hebrew Zalmaot [?], which means 'And these are the names.'"
Leviticus is ‘Weniqra,’ that is, ‘And he called.’ Numbers is called ‘Aspequdim’; Deuteronomy, ‘Ellehdebarim,’

These, then, are the words: Joshua son of Nun: Yesuebnun. Judges and Ruth are called Aphusphtim. The Books of Kings, two, are called Ana [?]. Dabrimin, one, that is, Chronicles (the Words of the Days). Ezra, two, which among them is called Ehiezra, which means "helper." The Book of Psalms, which is called Sph Tlim. The Proverbs of Solomon are called Maloth. Ecclesiastes, which is called Qohelet. The Song of Songs they call Sir Sirim. Isaiah: Yaisia. Jeremiah with his Lamentations: Aharmia. Daniel: Daniel. Ezekiel: Hezqiel. Job: Iyob. Esther: Esther. Besides these there are also the books of the Maccabees, on which is written Sabna Eli [?]. He set these down in the treatise we mentioned.

In the first treatise that he wrote on the Gospel of Matthew, he kept to the canons of the church and testified that he knows only four Gospels. He wrote as follows: "As I have learned by tradition about the four Gospels, which alone are undisputed in the whole church of God under heaven: Matthew wrote first. He had earlier been a tax collector and later became an apostle of Jesus Christ. He wrote it in Hebrew letters for those who had come to faith from Judaism. The second is Mark, who wrote as Peter told him. Peter called him 'my son' in his catholic epistle, when he wrote: 'The chosen church that is in Babylon, like you, greets you, and so does Mark my son.' The third is the Gospel of Luke, which Paul praises. Luke made it for those who had come to faith from the Gentiles. And after all of them comes the Gospel of John."

In the fifth volume of his commentary on the Gospel of John, he spoke about the epistles of the apostles as follows: "Paul was made worthy to be a minister of the new covenant, not of the letter but of the spirit. He fulfilled the gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, and he wrote letters also to all the churches of God in which [?]. But even the letters he did write are few in words. Peter, on whom the church of Christ was built, against which the gates of Sheol do not prevail, left only one epistle that the church acknowledges. Perhaps there are also two, since there is dispute about the second. What shall we say about John, who [?] could have made many books, for which the world would not have been enough? He also wrote the Revelation, and he was commanded to be silent and not to write down the voices of those thunders. He also left one epistle of few words. Perhaps also a second and a third, since not everyone acknowledges that they are his. Still, both of them together do not contain even a hundred lines."

Again, when he was commenting on the Epistle to the Hebrews, he spoke about it as follows: the style of the diction of that epistle to the Hebrews, when he was commenting on it, the style of the diction of that epistle to the Hebrews, is not that of an unskilled writer, as the apostle himself confesses that he was unskilled in speech. For in the composition of its speech in the Greek language this epistle is more skilful than the apostle's other epistles. Everyone who can judge differences of style acknowledges this. On the other hand, the thoughts in it are wonderful and not inferior to those the apostle wrote. Everyone who knows how to read the apostle carefully agrees that this is true.

After this he adds: "For my part, I decide and say that the thoughts in this epistle [?] are those of someone who remembered what the apostle used to say, and who wrote down what his master said, as a disciple would. So whatever church holds this epistle to be the apostle's, let them keep to that. But who truly wrote this epistle, God alone knows. The account that has come down to us about it is this: some say that Clement wrote it, who is said to have been bishop of the church of Rome. Others have said that Luke wrote it, who wrote the Gospel and the Acts." These things, then, have been said up to this point....
